docs.title: Valid parentheses
docs.text: Medium Stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given a string of ()[]{}, return true if every opener is closed by the same type in the correct order.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The most recent unmatched opener must be closed first, which is LIFO. So use a stack.
  2. Trick: push the expected closer instead of the opener. Then the check is just pop() == c.
  3. A mismatch, or a pop from an empty stack, means invalid. Leftovers at the end also mean invalid.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Brute force
docs.text: Repeatedly remove "()", "[]" and "{}" until nothing changes. Valid if the string ends up empty. That's O(n²).

docs.title: Approach 2 — Stack (optimal)
docs.text: char Action Stack (top on the right) { push } } [ push ] } ] ( push ) } ] ) ) pop ) ✅ } ] ] pop ] ✅ } } pop } ✅ empty → valid

docs.title: Approach 3 — Single bracket type
docs.text: With only ( and ), a counter is enough: it must never go negative and must end at 0. That's O(1) space.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Valid parentheses: "{[()]}" with a stack of expected closers
  1. Trick: when we see an opener, push the closer we expect. Then a closer only has to equal the top of the stack.
  2. { opens: push }, the closer we now expect.
  3. [ opens: push ], the closer we now expect.
  4. ( opens: push ), the closer we now expect.
  5. ) closes: pop ), and it matches.
  6. ] closes: pop ], and it matches.
  7. } closes: pop }, and it matches.
  8. End of the string and the stack is empty: valid. With "([)]" the pop at index 2 would give ']' instead of ')', and we'd return false right there.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Brackets "()[]{}" are balanced if every opener is closed by the same type in the correct order. */
public final class ValidParentheses {
    private ValidParentheses() {}

    /** Brute force: repeatedly delete "()", "[]", "{}" until nothing changes. O(n^2). */
    public static boolean bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        String prev;
        do {
            prev = s;
            s = s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "");
        } while (!s.equals(prev));
        return s.isEmpty();
    }

    /** Optimal: stack of expected closers. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean optimal(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            switch (c) {
                case '(' -> stack.push(')');                 // push what we EXPECT to see later
                case '[' -> stack.push(']');
                case '{' -> stack.push('}');
                default -> {
                    if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != c) return false;
                }
            }
        }
        return stack.isEmpty();                              // leftover openers → unbalanced
    }

    /** Only one bracket type? A counter is enough. O(1) space. */
    public static boolean singleTypeCounter(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        int open = 0;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (c == '(') open++;
            else if (c == ')' && --open < 0) return false;   // closed more than opened
        }
        return open == 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Stack: O(n) time and O(n) space. Counter: O(n) time and O(1) space.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
• Minimum additions to make the string valid. Count the unmatched openers and closers.
  • Longest valid parentheses (Hard). Use a stack of indexes, or DP.
  • Generate all valid combinations of n pairs (backtracking).

docs.title: Count vowels & consonants
docs.text: Easy Classification Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the vowels (a e i o u) and consonants in s. Ignore digits, spaces and symbols. Return {vowels, consonants}.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: "Hello World 2026" → {3, 7} (e, o, o | h, l, l, w, r, l, d)

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Is y a vowel? (No, here.) Upper case? (Count it, case-insensitively.) Non-English letters? (Ignore them.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Each char falls into one of three buckets: vowel, consonant, or ignored.
  2. Lower-case once, check the range a..z, then test membership in "aeiou".
  3. One pass, so O(n). A 5-char lookup is effectively O(1).

docs.title: Approach 1 — Loop (optimal)
docs.text: For each char c in s.toLowerCase(): skip it if it's not in a..z. Otherwise increment vowels if "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0, else consonants.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Recursive
docs.text: Classify s[i], then recurse on i+1. Base case: i == length. Pass an index, not a substring.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Streams
docs.text: Count the vowels, then count the letters. Consonants = letters − vowels.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

/**
 * Count vowels and consonants (English letters only; digits, spaces and symbols are ignored).
 * Result is {@code int[]{vowels, consonants}}. {@code null}/empty → {0, 0}.
 */
public final class VowelConsonantCount {
    private VowelConsonantCount() {}

    /** Loop + {@code indexOf} lookup in a vowel string. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static int[] optimal(String s) {
        int vowels = 0, consonants = 0;
        if (s == null) return new int[]{0, 0};
        for (char c : s.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
            if (c < 'a' || c > 'z') continue;                // not an English letter
            if ("aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0) vowels++;
            else consonants++;
        }
        return new int[]{vowels, consonants};
    }

    /** Recursive: count first char, recurse on the rest by index (no substring copies). */
    public static int[] recursive(String s) {
        int[] acc = new int[2];
        if (s != null) recursive(s.toLowerCase(), 0, acc);
        return acc;
    }

    private static void recursive(String s, int i, int[] acc) {
        if (i == s.length()) return;                         // base case
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') acc["aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0 ? 0 : 1]++;
        recursive(s, i + 1, acc);
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: filter letters, then count twice. */
    public static int[] streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return new int[]{0, 0};
        String lower = s.toLowerCase();
        long vowels = lower.chars().filter(c -> "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0).count();
        long letters = lower.chars().filter(c -> c >= 'a' && c <= 'z').count();
        return new int[]{(int) vowels, (int) (letters - vowels)};
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: All approaches take O(n) time. The loop and streams use O(1) extra space; the recursive version uses O(n) stack.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Character.isLetter accepts é, ß and so on. Decide whether you want "English letters" or "any letter".

docs.title: Z-algorithm
docs.text: Expert Pattern matching Z-box Linear time

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build the Z array of a string: z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of the string (z[0] is defined as 0). Then use it to find every occurrence of a pattern in a text in O(n + m).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
s z aabcaabxaaaz 0 1 0 0 3 1 0 0 2 2 1 0 aaaaa 0 4 3 2 1

Search: text = "AABAACAADAABAABA", pattern = "AABA" → [0, 9, 12].

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Overlapping matches? Yes, they are all reported ("aa" in "aaaa" → 0, 1, 2).
  • Empty pattern? Return an empty list.
  • Alphabet? Any char. The trick needs one separator that never appears in the input; '\u0000' is used here.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for every i, compare s[i..] with s[0..] char by char. Worst case O(n²) on "aaaa…".
  2. Waste: if we already know s[l..r) equals the prefix s[0..r−l) (a Z-box), then for any i inside the box, s[i..r) equals s[i−l..r−l). We have already computed z[i−l] for that position.
  3. Insight: start z[i] at min(r − i, z[i − l]) and only compare characters beyond r. Each such comparison pushes r right, and r only moves forward, so the total work is O(n).
  4. Pattern search: compute Z of pattern + '\0' + text. A position with z == m is a full match. The separator caps every z value at m.

docs.text: i inside box [l, r)? start z compared z[i] new box 1 no 0 a=a, b≠a 1 [1, 2) 2 no 0 b≠a 0 — 4 no 0 aab then x≠c 3 [4, 7) 5 yes, z[1] = 1, r − i = 2 1 b≠a 1 — 6 yes, z[2] = 0 0 b≠a 0 — 8 no 0 aa then a≠b 2 [8, 10) 9 yes, min(1, z[1] = 1) = 1 1 a=a, z≠b 2 [9, 11)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Z-algorithm. z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s (z[0] := 0).
 * Pattern search: build Z of pattern + '\u0000' + text; every z == m marks an occurrence.
 */
public final class ZAlgorithm {
    private ZAlgorithm() {}

    /** Brute force Z array: compare from every i. O(n²) worst case ("aaaa…"). */
    public static int[] zBrute(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int[] z = new int[n];
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            while (i + z[i] < n && s.charAt(z[i]) == s.charAt(i + z[i])) z[i]++;
        }
        return z;
    }

    /**
     * Linear Z array. [l, r) is the rightmost "Z-box": s[l..r) equals the prefix s[0..r-l).
     * Inside the box, z[i] starts from the mirrored value z[i-l] (capped at the box edge), so each char past r is
     * compared once overall. O(n) time.
     */
    public static int[] z(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int[] z = new int[n];
        int l = 0, r = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            if (i < r) z[i] = Math.min(r - i, z[i - l]);              // reuse what the box already proved
            while (i + z[i] < n && s.charAt(z[i]) == s.charAt(i + z[i])) z[i]++;  // extend past the box
            if (i + z[i] > r) {                                       // new rightmost box
                l = i;
                r = i + z[i];
            }
        }
        return z;
    }

    /** All start indexes of pattern in text (overlaps included), via Z of pattern + sentinel + text. O(n + m). */
    public static List<Integer> search(String text, String pattern) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (pattern.isEmpty() || pattern.length() > text.length()) return out;
        String joined = pattern + '\u0000' + text;                    // sentinel never matches, so z ≤ m
        int[] z = z(joined);
        int m = pattern.length();
        for (int i = m + 1; i < joined.length(); i++) if (z[i] == m) out.add(i - m - 1);
        return out;
    }

    /** Naive search, used as the oracle in tests. O(n·m). */
    public static List<Integer> searchBrute(String text, String pattern) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (pattern.isEmpty()) return out;
        for (int i = 0; i + pattern.length() <= text.length(); i++) if (text.startsWith(pattern, i)) out.add(i);
        return out;
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute-force Z O(n²) O(n) Z-algorithm O(n) O(n) Search via Z O(n + m) O(n + m)

docs.title: Z vs KMP
docs.text: Both are linear. KMP's LPS table looks at suffixes ending at i, while Z looks at prefixes starting at i. Z is often easier to write from memory, and its array answers more questions directly: "how many prefixes occur at each position", "string period", "number of distinct substrings" (with a loop).

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting the separator: without it, z values can run past the pattern into the text and exceed m.
  • Using z[i − l] without the r − i cap. The mirrored value is only trustworthy inside the box.
  • Strings of length 0 or 1.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: KMP & Rabin–Karp · Longest palindromic substring (Manacher uses the same "reuse the mirror inside a box" idea).

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• Contiguous memory gives O(1) index access. Inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because elements shift.
  • An "in place" answer usually means O(1) extra space, using read/write pointers or swaps.
  • Most array problems are one of: two pointers, prefix/suffix accumulation, Kadane, hashing, sorting first, reversal tricks, or a monotonic stack.

docs.title: Best time to buy & sell stock
docs.text: Medium Running minimum Greedy

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: prices[i] is the price on day i. Buy once and sell later to maximise profit, or return 0 if no profit is possible. [7,1,5,3,6,4] → 5 (buy at 1, sell at 6).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every (buy, sell) pair with buy < sell. That's O(n²).
  2. Insight: if you sell on day j, the best buy is the minimum price before j.
  3. So keep a running minSoFar, and each day compute price − minSoFar. That's O(n) and O(1).
  4. Unlimited transactions: collect every rise from one day to the next. Summing the up-moves equals buying at every valley and selling at every peak.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: day price minSoFar profit today best 0 7 7 0 0 1 1 1 0 0 2 5 1 4 4 4 6 1 5 5

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Best time to buy and sell: track the cheapest day so far
  1. If we sell today, the best buy day is the cheapest day so far.
  2. Day 0, price 7: cheapest so far 7 (day 0), selling today earns 0.
  3. Day 1, price 1: cheapest so far 1 (day 1), selling today earns 0.
  4. Day 2, price 5: cheapest so far 1 (day 1), selling today earns 4. New best 4.
  5. Day 3, price 3: cheapest so far 1 (day 1), selling today earns 2.
  6. Day 4, price 6: cheapest so far 1 (day 1), selling today earns 5. New best 5.
  7. Day 5, price 4: cheapest so far 1 (day 1), selling today earns 3.
  8. Buy on day 1 at 1, sell on day 4 at 6: profit 5. One pass, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Stock prices by day. Max profit from ONE buy then a later sell (0 if no profit). Plus multi-transaction variant. */
public final class BuySellStock {
    private BuySellStock() {}

    /** Brute force: every buy/sell pair. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] prices) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < prices.length; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < prices.length; j++) best = Math.max(best, prices[j] - prices[i]);
        return best;
    }

    /** Optimal: track the minimum price so far; profit if sold today. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int optimal(int[] prices) {
        int minSoFar = Integer.MAX_VALUE, best = 0;
        for (int p : prices) {
            minSoFar = Math.min(minSoFar, p);
            best = Math.max(best, p - minSoFar);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Unlimited transactions (LeetCode 122): sum every positive day-to-day rise. Greedy, O(n). */
    public static int unlimitedTransactions(int[] prices) {
        int profit = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) profit += Math.max(0, prices[i] - prices[i - 1]);
        return profit;
    }
}

docs.text: I (one transaction) ✅ · II (unlimited) ✅ · III / IV (at most k transactions, a DP over states) · with cooldown · with a transaction fee. These are covered in DP.

docs.title: First missing positive
docs.text: Expert Cyclic sort Index as hash O(1) space

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the smallest positive integer that does not appear in an unsorted array. You must use O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output [1, 2, 0] 3 [3, 4, -1, 1] 2 [7, 8, 9, 11, 12] 1 [] 1

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• May I modify the input? The O(1)-space solutions need to (or you copy it, which costs O(n)).
  • Duplicates and negatives? Both allowed, and both must be ignored.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try 1, 2, 3, … and scan for each one. O(n²).
  2. Hash set: O(n) time, but O(n) space. Sorting: O(n log n). Neither meets the bound.
  3. Key bound: with n numbers, the answer is in [1, n + 1]. Values ≤ 0 or > n can never be the answer, so ignore them.
  4. Use the array as its own hash table: value v "belongs" at index v − 1. Swap each in-range value to its home (cyclic sort). Afterwards, the first index i holding something other than i + 1 means i + 1 is missing.
  5. Why O(n): every swap puts one value in its final home, and it never moves again. So there are at most n swaps in total, even with the inner while.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Smallest positive integer that is NOT in the array. Required: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. */
public final class FirstMissingPositive {
    private FirstMissingPositive() {}

    /** Brute force: try 1, 2, 3, ... with a linear scan each. O(n²). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a) {
        for (int k = 1; ; k++) {
            boolean found = false;
            for (int x : a) if (x == k) { found = true; break; }
            if (!found) return k;
        }
    }

    /** Hash set. O(n) time, O(n) space. The answer is at most n + 1, so the loop is bounded. */
    public static int hashing(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) set.add(x);
        int k = 1;
        while (set.contains(k)) k++;
        return k;
    }

    /** Sorting, then walk the positives. O(n log n) time. */
    public static int sorting(int[] a) {
        int[] b = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(b);
        int expect = 1;
        for (int x : b) {
            if (x == expect) expect++;
            else if (x > expect) break;               // gap found
        }
        return expect;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal — cyclic sort: the answer is in [1, n+1], so value v belongs at index v-1. Swap every in-range value
     * to its home; then the first index i with a[i] != i+1 gives i+1. Each swap fixes one value permanently, so
     * there are at most n swaps: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Mutates its input.
     */
    public static int cyclicSort(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            // keep swapping a[i] home while it is in range and its home doesn't already hold it (handles duplicates)
            while (a[i] >= 1 && a[i] <= n && a[a[i] - 1] != a[i]) {
                int home = a[i] - 1;
                int t = a[home];
                a[home] = a[i];
                a[i] = t;
            }
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] != i + 1) return i + 1;
        return n + 1;
    }

    /**
     * Alternative O(1) space: index-as-hash with sign marking. First replace non-positives / out-of-range by n+1,
     * then for each value v in [1, n] make a[v-1] negative. The first positive slot is missing. Mutates its input.
     */
    public static int signMarking(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] <= 0 || a[i] > n) a[i] = n + 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int v = Math.abs(a[i]);
            if (v <= n && a[v - 1] > 0) a[v - 1] = -a[v - 1];
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] > 0) return i + 1;
        return n + 1;
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n²) O(1) Hash set O(n) O(n) Sorting O(n log n) O(n) for the copy Cyclic sort O(n) O(1) Sign marking O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Duplicates loop forever if the swap condition is a[i] != i + 1. Check a[a[i] − 1] != a[i] (the home already has this value) instead.
  • In sign marking, read Math.abs(a[i]): the slot may already have been negated.
  • All of 1..n present → the answer is n + 1.

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: The code is short, but it needs two insights at once: bounding the answer to [1, n + 1], and reusing the input as a hash table without losing information.

docs.title: Majority element (Boyer–Moore voting)
docs.text: Easy Voting Hashing O(1) space

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the value that appears more than ⌊n/2⌋ times. The classic version guarantees that one exists. The follow-up asks you to report "none" when it doesn't.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output [3, 2, 3] 3 [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2] 2 [1, 2, 3] none (follow-up) [1, 1, 2, 2] none: exactly n/2 is not a majority

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Is a majority guaranteed? If not, you need a second pass to verify.
  • "More than n/2" or "at least n/2"? It changes the [1,1,2,2] case.
  • Can I modify or sort the array?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: count each value with a nested loop. O(n²).
  2. Hash map: count once. O(n) time but O(n) space. The interviewer then asks for O(1) space.
  3. Sorting insight: a value covering more than half the array must cover the middle index. O(n log n), no counting.
  4. Voting insight: pair each occurrence of the majority with a different value and cancel both. The majority has more copies than everything else combined, so something of it always survives. Keep one candidate and a votes counter: +1 for a match, −1 otherwise, and pick a new candidate whenever votes hits 0.

docs.title: Dry run: [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
docs.text:
x candidate votes 2 2 1 2 2 2 1 2 1 1 2 0 1 1 (restart) 1 2 1 0 2 2 (restart) 1

Result: 2. Note that the candidate changed twice. Voting only promises the right answer at the end, and only when a majority exists.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.OptionalInt;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/**
 * Majority element: the value that appears MORE than n/2 times.
 * The "guaranteed" variants assume one exists (LeetCode 169); {@link #verified} returns empty when none does.
 */
public final class MajorityElement {
    private MajorityElement() {}

    /** Brute force: count every candidate. O(n²) time, O(1) space. */
    public static OptionalInt bruteForce(int[] a) {
        for (int x : a) {
            int count = 0;
            for (int y : a) if (y == x) count++;
            if (count > a.length / 2) return OptionalInt.of(x);
        }
        return OptionalInt.empty();
    }

    /** Hash map counts. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static OptionalInt hashing(int[] a) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) if (counts.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum) > a.length / 2) return OptionalInt.of(x);
        return OptionalInt.empty();
    }

    /** Sorting: if a majority exists it must occupy the middle index. O(n log n). Assumes one exists. */
    public static int sorting(int[] a) {
        int[] b = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(b);
        return b[b.length / 2];
    }

    /**
     * Boyer–Moore voting. Pair each majority vote with a different value and cancel both; the majority survives
     * because it has more votes than all others combined. O(n) time, O(1) space. Assumes one exists.
     */
    public static int boyerMoore(int[] a) {
        int candidate = 0, votes = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            if (votes == 0) candidate = x;            // previous prefix cancelled out completely: restart
            votes += (x == candidate) ? 1 : -1;
        }
        return candidate;
    }

    /** Boyer–Moore + a second pass to confirm, so arrays without a majority return empty. O(n), O(1). */
    public static OptionalInt verified(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 0) return OptionalInt.empty();
        int candidate = boyerMoore(a), count = 0;
        for (int x : a) if (x == candidate) count++;
        return count > a.length / 2 ? OptionalInt.of(candidate) : OptionalInt.empty();
    }

    /** Java 8: frequency map, then the entry above n/2. */
    public static OptionalInt streams(int[] a) {
        return Arrays.stream(a).boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()))
                .entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getValue() > a.length / 2)
                .mapToInt(Map.Entry::getKey)
                .findFirst();
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n²) O(1) Hash map / streams O(n) O(n) Sorting O(n log n) O(n) for the copy Boyer–Moore (+ verify pass) O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Without a guaranteed majority, Boyer–Moore still returns some candidate. Always run the verification pass.
  • Empty array: there is no candidate.
  • Sorting the caller's array in place is a side effect. The code sorts a clone.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text: Majority II (values appearing more than n/3 times): at most two can exist, so keep two candidates and two counters, then verify both. In general, more than n/k needs k − 1 candidates.

docs.title: Find max & min of an array
docs.text: Easy Linear scan Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return {min, max} of a non-empty array. GfG asks for the version with the minimum number of comparisons.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sorting gives the min and max at the ends, but O(n log n) is overkill.
  2. One scan: update min and max per element. That's O(n) and about 2n comparisons.
  3. Pairwise trick: compare the two elements of a pair with each other first, then the smaller with min and the larger with max. That's 3 comparisons per 2 elements, about 1.5n.
  4. Divide & conquer: solve each half and combine. It also takes about 1.5n comparisons, and it's a nice recursion example.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.IntSummaryStatistics;

/** Find {min, max} of a non-empty int array. Throws IllegalArgumentException on null/empty. */
public final class MaxMin {
    private MaxMin() {}

    /** Sort then take ends. O(n log n) — mutates a copy only. */
    public static int[] sorting(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        return new int[]{c[0], c[c.length - 1]};
    }

    /** Optimal: one linear scan. O(n) time, O(1) space, ~2n comparisons. */
    public static int[] linear(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        int min = a[0], max = a[0];
        for (int x : a) {
            if (x < min) min = x;
            if (x > max) max = x;
        }
        return new int[]{min, max};
    }

    /** Pairwise comparison: ~1.5n comparisons (classic GfG "minimum comparisons" answer). */
    public static int[] pairwise(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        int i, min, max;
        if (a.length % 2 == 0) {
            min = Math.min(a[0], a[1]);
            max = Math.max(a[0], a[1]);
            i = 2;
        } else {
            min = max = a[0];
            i = 1;
        }
        for (; i < a.length; i += 2) {                       // compare the pair first, then 1 vs min, 1 vs max
            int small = Math.min(a[i], a[i + 1]), big = Math.max(a[i], a[i + 1]);
            if (small < min) min = small;
            if (big > max) max = big;
        }
        return new int[]{min, max};
    }

    /** Recursive (divide & conquer): min/max of halves. O(n) time, O(log n) stack. */
    public static int[] recursive(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        return dc(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int[] dc(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return new int[]{a[lo], a[lo]};
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        int[] l = dc(a, lo, mid), r = dc(a, mid + 1, hi);
        return new int[]{Math.min(l[0], r[0]), Math.max(l[1], r[1])};
    }

    /** Java 8: IntSummaryStatistics gives min, max, sum, avg, count in one pass. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        IntSummaryStatistics s = Arrays.stream(a).summaryStatistics();
        return new int[]{s.getMin(), s.getMax()};
    }

    private static void requireNonEmpty(int[] a) {
        if (a == null || a.length == 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("array must be non-empty");
    }
}

docs.title: Maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm)
docs.text: Medium Kadane DP Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray. [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6 ([4,-1,2,1]).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every (i, j) with a running sum. That's O(n²).
  2. DP view: let best(i) = the best sum of a subarray ending at i. Then best(i) = max(a[i], best(i-1) + a[i]). In words: extend the previous run, or restart here.
  3. Restart exactly when the previous run is negative, because it can only hurt.
  4. The answer is max over i of best(i). Since you only need the previous value, space is O(1).

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: i a[i] current = max(a[i], current + a[i]) best 0 −2 −2 −2 1 1 max(1, −1) = 1 (restart) 1 2 −3 −2 1 3 4 max(4, 2) = 4 (restart) 4 4 −1 3 4 5 2 5 5 6 1 6 6 7 −5 1 6 8 4 5 6

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Kadane on [−2, 1, −3, 4, −1, 2, 1, −5, 4]
  1. Start with the first element: current = best = −2. The highlighted window is the best subarray ending here.
  2. i = 1: 1 beats -1 → restart here. New best = 1.
  3. i = 2: extend: current + a[i] = -2. best stays 1.
  4. i = 3: 4 beats 2 → restart here. New best = 4.
  5. i = 4: extend: current + a[i] = 3. best stays 4.
  6. i = 5: extend: current + a[i] = 5. New best = 5.
  7. i = 6: extend: current + a[i] = 6. New best = 6.
  8. i = 7: extend: current + a[i] = 1. best stays 6.
  9. i = 8: extend: current + a[i] = 5. best stays 6.
  10. Done. The best subarray is [4, −1, 2, 1] (indices 3–6), sum 6. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Maximum sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray (Kadane). [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6. */
public final class MaxSubarraySum {
    private MaxSubarraySum() {}

    /** Brute force: all subarrays with running sum. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            int sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                best = Math.max(best, sum);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Kadane: best subarray ending here = max(a[i], a[i] + best ending at i-1). O(n), O(1). */
    public static int kadane(int[] a) {
        int current = a[0], best = a[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            current = Math.max(a[i], current + a[i]);        // extend or restart
            best = Math.max(best, current);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Kadane returning the subarray bounds {sum, start, end}. */
    public static int[] kadaneWithIndices(int[] a) {
        int current = a[0], best = a[0], start = 0, bestStart = 0, bestEnd = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (a[i] > current + a[i]) {
                current = a[i];
                start = i;                                   // restart here
            } else {
                current += a[i];
            }
            if (current > best) {
                best = current;
                bestStart = start;
                bestEnd = i;
            }
        }
        return new int[]{best, bestStart, bestEnd};
    }

    /** Divide & conquer (recursive): max of left, right, crossing. O(n log n). */
    public static int divideAndConquer(int[] a) {
        return dc(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int dc(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return a[lo];
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        int leftBest = Integer.MIN_VALUE, sum = 0;
        for (int i = mid; i >= lo; i--) leftBest = Math.max(leftBest, sum += a[i]);
        int rightBest = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        sum = 0;
        for (int i = mid + 1; i <= hi; i++) rightBest = Math.max(rightBest, sum += a[i]);
        return Math.max(Math.max(dc(a, lo, mid), dc(a, mid + 1, hi)), leftBest + rightBest);
    }
}

docs.title: Merge intervals
docs.text: Hard Sort + sweep

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge all overlapping intervals. [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]] → [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. Touching intervals ([1,4],[4,5]) merge.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Unsorted intervals can overlap anywhere, so comparing every pair is O(n²).
  2. Sort by start. Now an interval can only overlap the current merged block.
  3. Sweep: if next.start <= current.end, extend with current.end = max(current.end, next.end). Otherwise close the block and start a new one.
  4. Use max for the end because a later interval can sit entirely inside the current one ([1,10],[2,3]).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

/** Merge overlapping intervals. [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]] → [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. Touching ([1,4],[4,5]) merges. */
public final class MergeIntervals {
    private MergeIntervals() {}

    /** Optimal: sort by start, then extend or append. O(n log n) time, O(n) output. */
    public static int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
        if (intervals == null || intervals.length == 0) return new int[0][];
        int[][] sorted = intervals.clone();
        Arrays.sort(sorted, Comparator.comparingInt(iv -> iv[0]));
        List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int[] current = sorted[0].clone();
        for (int i = 1; i < sorted.length; i++) {
            if (sorted[i][0] <= current[1]) {                // overlaps → extend
                current[1] = Math.max(current[1], sorted[i][1]);
            } else {                                          // gap → close current
                out.add(current);
                current = sorted[i].clone();
            }
        }
        out.add(current);
        return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }

    /** Follow-up: insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list. O(n). */
    public static int[][] insert(int[][] intervals, int[] add) {
        List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int i = 0, n = intervals.length;
        int[] merged = add.clone();
        while (i < n && intervals[i][1] < add[0]) out.add(intervals[i++]);          // fully left
        while (i < n && intervals[i][0] <= merged[1]) {                              // overlapping
            merged[0] = Math.min(merged[0], intervals[i][0]);
            merged[1] = Math.max(merged[1], intervals[i][1]);
            i++;
        }
        out.add(merged);
        while (i < n) out.add(intervals[i++]);                                       // fully right
        return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }
}

docs.title: Missing number
docs.text: Easy Math XOR

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: An array holds n distinct numbers from 0..n, with exactly one missing. Find it. [3,0,1] → 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sort, then find the first i where a[i] != i. That's O(n log n).
  2. HashSet: insert everything, then check 0..n. That's O(n) time but O(n) space.
  3. Math: the expected sum is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum. That's O(1) space. Use long to avoid overflow.
  4. XOR: since x ^ x = 0, XOR-ing all the indexes 0..n and all the values leaves only the missing number. It can't overflow.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Array has n distinct numbers from 0..n; one is missing. Find it. [3,0,1] → 2. */
public final class MissingNumber {
    private MissingNumber() {}

    /** Sort and find the first index where a[i] != i. O(n log n). */
    public static int sorting(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        for (int i = 0; i < c.length; i++) if (c[i] != i) return i;
        return c.length;
    }

    /** Gauss sum: n(n+1)/2 − sum. Use long to avoid overflow. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int sumFormula(int[] a) {
        long n = a.length, expected = n * (n + 1) / 2, sum = 0;
        for (int x : a) sum += x;
        return (int) (expected - sum);
    }

    /** XOR trick: x ^ x = 0, so XOR of all indexes and values leaves the missing one. Overflow-free. */
    public static int xor(int[] a) {
        int x = a.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) x ^= i ^ a[i];
        return x;
    }

    /** Java 8. */
    public static int streams(int[] a) {
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(0, a.length).sum() - Arrays.stream(a).sum();
    }
}

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• 1..n with one missing and one duplicated: use sum and sum-of-squares equations, or XOR partitioning.
  • First missing positive (Hard): cyclic sort, putting each value v at index v−1.

docs.title: Move zeros to end
docs.text: Easy Two pointers In place

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Move all 0s to the end in place, keeping the order of the non-zero elements. [0,1,0,3,12] → [1,3,12,0,0].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Extra array: copy the non-zeros, and the remaining slots are zeros by default. That's O(n) space.
  2. In place: a write pointer marks where the next non-zero goes. A read pointer scans.
  3. When a[read] != 0, swap it into write and advance write. The relative order is preserved because write ≤ read.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Move zeros: read and write pointers
  1. Everything before write is a finished non-zero, in order.
  2. a[0] is 0: skip it. write stays at 0.
  3. a[read] = 1 is non-zero: swap it to write (0) and advance write.
  4. a[2] is 0: skip it. write stays at 1.
  5. a[read] = 3 is non-zero: swap it to write (1) and advance write.
  6. a[read] = 12 is non-zero: swap it to write (2) and advance write.
  7. Non-zeros in order, zeros at the end, one pass and minimal writes.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Move all zeros to the end, keeping the relative order of non-zero elements. In place. */
public final class MoveZeros {
    private MoveZeros() {}

    /** Extra array: copy non-zeros, fill rest with zeros. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static int[] extraSpace(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        int k = 0;
        for (int x : a) if (x != 0) out[k++] = x;           // remaining slots are already 0
        return out;
    }

    /** Optimal: write pointer + swap. O(n) time, O(1) space, minimal writes. */
    public static void optimal(int[] a) {
        int write = 0;                                       // next position for a non-zero
        for (int read = 0; read < a.length; read++) {
            if (a[read] != 0) {
                int t = a[write];
                a[write++] = a[read];
                a[read] = t;
            }
        }
    }

    /** Java 8: concatenate non-zeros and zeros. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        return IntStream.concat(Arrays.stream(a).filter(x -> x != 0), Arrays.stream(a).filter(x -> x == 0)).toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Next permutation
docs.text: Hard Pivot · swap · reverse

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Rearrange the array, in place, into the next lexicographically greater permutation. If none exists, return the smallest. [1,2,3] → [1,3,2] · [3,2,1] → [1,2,3] · [1,1,5] → [1,5,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. To get the next bigger number, change the rightmost position you can.
  2. A suffix that is non-increasing is already at its maximum, and no rearrangement of it gets bigger.
  3. So find the pivot i: the first index from the right with a[i] < a[i+1].
  4. Swap a[i] with the smallest element in the suffix that is greater than it. Since the suffix is descending, that is the rightmost element > a[i].
  5. The suffix is still descending. Reverse it to make it ascending, which is the smallest possible arrangement.
  6. If there is no pivot, the whole array is descending. Reverse everything to get the smallest permutation.

docs.title: Dry run ([1,3,5,4,2])
docs.text:
pivot: from right, 2<4? no, 4<5? no, 5>3 → a[1] = 3 is the pivot (3 < 5)
swap 3 with the rightmost > 3 in [5,4,2] → 4  →  [1,4,5,3,2]
reverse suffix [5,3,2]                         →  [1,4,2,3,5] ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Rearrange to the next lexicographically greater permutation; if none, the smallest (sorted). In place. */
public final class NextPermutation {
    private NextPermutation() {}

    /**
     * 1. From the right, find the first i with a[i] < a[i+1] (the "pivot").
     * 2. If none → array is fully descending → reverse whole array.
     * 3. From the right, find first j with a[j] > a[i]; swap a[i], a[j].
     * 4. Reverse the suffix a[i+1..] (it was descending, now ascending = smallest).
     * O(n) time, O(1) space.
     */
    public static void next(int[] a) {
        int i = a.length - 2;
        while (i >= 0 && a[i] >= a[i + 1]) i--;
        if (i >= 0) {
            int j = a.length - 1;
            while (a[j] <= a[i]) j--;
            swap(a, i, j);
        }
        for (int l = i + 1, r = a.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) swap(a, l, r);
    }

    private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.title: Product of array except self
docs.text: Hard Prefix / suffix

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return out[i] = the product of every element except a[i], without division, in O(n). [1,2,3,4] → [24,12,8,6].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: a nested loop, O(n²).
  2. Why not division? It fails on zeros, and the interviewer forbids it anyway.
  3. Insight: out[i] = (product of everything LEFT of i) × (product of everything RIGHT of i).
  4. Prefix/suffix arrays take O(n) space. Optimisation: store the prefix products in out, then sweep from the right with a single suffix variable, for O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** out[i] = product of all elements except a[i], WITHOUT division, in O(n). */
public final class ProductExceptSelf {
    private ProductExceptSelf() {}

    /** Brute force: nested loop. O(n^2). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            int p = 1;
            for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) if (i != j) p *= a[j];
            out[i] = p;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Prefix and suffix product arrays. O(n) time, O(n) extra. */
    public static int[] prefixSuffix(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] pre = new int[n], suf = new int[n], out = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) pre[i] = i == 0 ? 1 : pre[i - 1] * a[i - 1];
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) suf[i] = i == n - 1 ? 1 : suf[i + 1] * a[i + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = pre[i] * suf[i];
        return out;
    }

    /** Optimal: store prefix in output, multiply by a running suffix on the way back. O(n), O(1) extra. */
    public static int[] optimal(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        out[0] = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) out[i] = out[i - 1] * a[i - 1];   // product of everything left of i
        int suffix = 1;
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            out[i] *= suffix;                                         // × product of everything right of i
            suffix *= a[i];
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array
docs.text: Easy Slow/fast pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: In place, keep each value once and return the new length k. The first k slots hold the result. [0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4] → k = 5, [0,1,2,3,4,…].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sorted means duplicates are adjacent, so you only need to compare with the last kept value.
  2. k = the length of the unique prefix. For each i, if a[i] != a[k-1], write it to a[k++].
  3. Generalisation: to allow at most m copies, compare with a[k-m].

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Remove duplicates from a SORTED array in place; return the new length k (first k slots hold uniques). */
public final class RemoveDuplicatesSorted {
    private RemoveDuplicatesSorted() {}

    /** Set-based (works unsorted too, but O(n) extra space). */
    public static int withSet(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) seen.add(x);
        int k = 0;
        for (int x : seen) a[k++] = x;
        return k;
    }

    /** Optimal: slow/fast pointers — sorted means duplicates are adjacent. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int optimal(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 0) return 0;
        int k = 1;                                           // a[0..k-1] are unique
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (a[i] != a[k - 1]) a[k++] = a[i];
        }
        return k;
    }

    /** Variation (LeetCode 80): allow each value at most twice. */
    public static int atMostTwice(int[] a) {
        int k = 0;
        for (int x : a) if (k < 2 || x != a[k - 2]) a[k++] = x;
        return k;
    }

    /** Java 8: returns a new array of distinct values. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        return Arrays.stream(a).distinct().toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Reverse an array
docs.text: Easy Two pointers Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse a in place. [1,2,3,4,5] → [5,4,3,2,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Element i belongs at n-1-i.
  2. Swapping the pair (l, r) fixes two positions at once, so you only need n/2 swaps.
  3. Stop when l >= r. The middle element of an odd-length array stays where it is.

docs.title: Approaches
docs.text:
• Iterative two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space.
  • Recursive: swap (l, r), then recurse on (l+1, r-1). Base case l >= r. O(n) stack.
  • Streams (new array): IntStream.range(0,n).map(i -> a[n-1-i]).toArray().

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Reverse an int array in place (and a copy-returning streams version). */
public final class ReverseArray {
    private ReverseArray() {}

    /** Optimal: two pointers swap. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static void inPlace(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return;
        for (int l = 0, r = a.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) {
            int t = a[l];
            a[l] = a[r];
            a[r] = t;
        }
    }

    /** Recursive: swap ends, recurse inward. O(n) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static void recursive(int[] a) {
        if (a != null) recursive(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void recursive(int[] a, int l, int r) {
        if (l >= r) return;
        int t = a[l];
        a[l] = a[r];
        a[r] = t;
        recursive(a, l + 1, r - 1);
    }

    /** Java 8: new reversed array. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return null;
        return IntStream.range(0, a.length).map(i -> a[a.length - 1 - i]).toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: Reversing a sub-range [l, r] is the building block of Rotate array and Next permutation.

docs.title: Rotate array by k
docs.text: Medium Reversal trick

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Rotate right by k in place. [1,2,3,4,5,6,7], k = 3 → [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. k may be larger than n.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Normalise: k %= n, because rotating n times gives back the original.
  2. Brute force: rotate by one, k times. That's O(n·k).
  3. Extra array: out[(i+k) % n] = a[i]. That's O(n) time and O(n) space.
  4. Reversal insight: the last k elements must come first. Reversing the whole array puts them at the front, but backwards. Reverse each part again to fix the order.

docs.title: Reversal, visualised
docs.text:
original      1 2 3 4 | 5 6 7
reverse all   7 6 5 | 4 3 2 1
reverse [0,k) 5 6 7 | 4 3 2 1
reverse [k,n) 5 6 7 | 1 2 3 4   ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Rotate array to the RIGHT by k steps in place. [1..7], k=3 → [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. */
public final class RotateArray {
    private RotateArray() {}

    /** Brute force: rotate by one, k times. O(n·k). */
    public static void bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0) return;
        k %= a.length;
        for (int step = 0; step < k; step++) {
            int last = a[a.length - 1];
            System.arraycopy(a, 0, a, 1, a.length - 1);
            a[0] = last;
        }
    }

    /** Extra array: element i goes to (i+k) % n. O(n), O(n). */
    public static void extraArray(int[] a, int k) {
        int n = a.length;
        if (n == 0) return;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out[(i + k) % n] = a[i];
        System.arraycopy(out, 0, a, 0, n);
    }

    /** Optimal: reverse all, reverse first k, reverse rest. O(n), O(1). */
    public static void reversal(int[] a, int k) {
        int n = a.length;
        if (n == 0) return;
        k %= n;                                              // k may exceed n
        reverse(a, 0, n - 1);
        reverse(a, 0, k - 1);
        reverse(a, k, n - 1);
    }

    /** Left rotation by d is right rotation by n - d. */
    public static void rotateLeft(int[] a, int d) {
        if (a.length == 0) return;
        reversal(a, a.length - d % a.length);
    }

    private static void reverse(int[] a, int l, int r) {
        while (l < r) {
            int t = a[l];
            a[l++] = a[r];
            a[r--] = t;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Second largest element
docs.text: Easy Linear scan

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the second-largest distinct value. [12, 35, 1, 10, 34, 1] → 34. [10, 5, 10] → 5. [10, 10] → none.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Distinct or not? (Here: distinct.) What should we return if there is none? (Here: OptionalInt.empty(), not −1, because −1 may be a valid value.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sort, then walk back from the end until a value differs from the max. That's O(n log n).
  2. One pass: keep first and second.
    • x > first: the old first becomes second, and first = x.
    • first > x > second: second = x. The strict < skips duplicates of the max.
  3. Use long sentinels so that an input containing Integer.MIN_VALUE still works.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.OptionalInt;

/** Second largest DISTINCT element. [10, 5, 10] → 5. Empty if it does not exist. */
public final class SecondLargest {
    private SecondLargest() {}

    /** Sort and walk back skipping duplicates of the max. O(n log n). */
    public static OptionalInt sorting(int[] a) {
        if (a == null || a.length < 2) return OptionalInt.empty();
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        for (int i = c.length - 2; i >= 0; i--) if (c[i] != c[c.length - 1]) return OptionalInt.of(c[i]);
        return OptionalInt.empty();
    }

    /** Optimal: track first and second in one pass. O(n), O(1). Uses long sentinels so MIN_VALUE works. */
    public static OptionalInt optimal(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return OptionalInt.empty();
        long first = Long.MIN_VALUE, second = Long.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int x : a) {
            if (x > first) {
                second = first;                              // old max becomes second
                first = x;
            } else if (x < first && x > second) {
                second = x;                                  // strictly less than max → candidate
            }
        }
        return second == Long.MIN_VALUE ? OptionalInt.empty() : OptionalInt.of((int) second);
    }

    /** Java 8: distinct, sort descending, skip 1. */
    public static OptionalInt streams(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return OptionalInt.empty();
        return Arrays.stream(a).boxed().distinct().sorted((x, y) -> Integer.compare(y, x))
                .skip(1).mapToInt(Integer::intValue).findFirst();
    }
}

docs.text: The Kth largest element is a heap of size k (O(n log k)) or Quickselect (O(n) on average).

docs.title: 3Sum
docs.text: Medium Sort + two pointers Dedup

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return all unique triplets of values [a, b, c] with a + b + c = 0. A triplet uses three different indexes, but the output must not repeat the same set of values.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Unique by values or by indexes? By values.
  • Does the order of the output matter? Here each triplet is ascending and the list is sorted, so all approaches can be compared directly.
  • Can the sum overflow? With values near ±2³¹, yes. The code adds in long.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: three nested loops, sort each triplet, put it in a set to remove duplicates. O(n³).
  2. Reduce to two-sum: fix a[i]. Now you need two numbers summing to −a[i]. A hash set solves that in O(n), giving O(n²) overall.
  3. Sort first: on a sorted array, two-sum is a two-pointer sweep. If the sum is too small, move lo up. If too big, move hi down.
  4. Dedup without a set: after sorting, equal values sit together. Skip an i equal to the previous i, and after a hit skip equal values at lo and hi. Every triplet is then produced exactly once.
  5. Early exit: if a[i] > 0, every remaining number is positive, so stop.

docs.title: Dry run: sorted [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]
docs.text: i (a[i]) lo hi sum action 0 (−4) −1 2 −3 lo++ … always < 0 no triplet with −4 1 (−1) −1 2 0 [-1, -1, 2], skip dups, lo++, hi-- 0 1 0 [-1, 0, 1] 2 (−1) — — — same as previous i → skip 3 (0) 1 2 3 hi-- → lo = hi, stop

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * 3Sum: all UNIQUE triplets [a, b, c] (as values, each sorted ascending) with a + b + c == 0.
 * Output order: triplets sorted lexicographically, so every approach returns the same list.
 */
public final class ThreeSum {
    private ThreeSum() {}

    /** Brute force: every i < j < k, dedupe with a sorted set. O(n³) time. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> bruteForce(int[] nums) {
        Set<List<Integer>> seen = new TreeSet<>(ThreeSum::compare);
        int n = nums.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
                for (int k = j + 1; k < n; k++)
                    if ((long) nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0) {
                        int[] t = {nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]};
                        Arrays.sort(t);
                        seen.add(List.of(t[0], t[1], t[2]));
                    }
        return new ArrayList<>(seen);
    }

    /** Fix i, then two-sum with a hash set on the rest. O(n²) time, O(n) space. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> hashing(int[] nums) {
        int[] a = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a);
        Set<List<Integer>> out = new TreeSet<>(ThreeSum::compare);
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;
            Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) {
                int need = -a[i] - a[j];
                if (seen.contains(need)) out.add(List.of(a[i], need, a[j]));   // need ≤ a[j]: it came earlier
                seen.add(a[j]);
            }
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(out);
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: sort, fix the smallest element, two pointers on the rest. Skip equal values at every level so each
     * triplet is produced exactly once — no Set needed. O(n²) time, O(1) extra (besides output and the sort).
     */
    public static List<List<Integer>> twoPointers(int[] nums) {
        int[] a = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a);
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 2; i++) {
            if (a[i] > 0) break;                              // smallest is positive: no sum can reach 0
            if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;          // same first value → same triplets
            int lo = i + 1, hi = a.length - 1;
            while (lo < hi) {
                long sum = (long) a[i] + a[lo] + a[hi];
                if (sum < 0) lo++;                            // need bigger: move the small end up
                else if (sum > 0) hi--;                       // need smaller: move the big end down
                else {
                    out.add(List.of(a[i], a[lo], a[hi]));
                    while (lo < hi && a[lo] == a[lo + 1]) lo++;   // skip duplicate second values
                    while (lo < hi && a[hi] == a[hi - 1]) hi--;   // skip duplicate third values
                    lo++;
                    hi--;
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    private static int compare(List<Integer> x, List<Integer> y) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            int c = Integer.compare(x.get(i), y.get(i));
            if (c != 0) return c;
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Brute force + set O(n³) O(k) for k triplets Fix one + hash set O(n²) O(n) Sort + two pointers O(n²) O(1) extra besides the sort

O(n²) is essentially optimal here: there can be Θ(n²) triplets in the output.

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Skipping duplicates before recording a hit loses [-1, -1, 2]. Skip i against i − 1 (the previous value), never against i + 1.
  • Forgetting the duplicate skips at lo/hi after a hit produces repeated triplets.
  • Arrays shorter than 3.

docs.title: Trapping rain water
docs.text: Expert Two pointers Prefix max Monotonic stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given bar heights, compute how much water is trapped after rain. [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] → 6.

                 █
         █ ≈ ≈ ≈ █ █ ≈ █
     █ ≈ █ █ ≈ █ █ █ █ █ █
   ───────────────────────
h: 0 1 0 2 1 0 1 3 2 1 2 1      (≈ = water, total 6)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Key formula: water above bar i = min(maxLeft(i), maxRight(i)) − h[i].
  2. Brute force: compute maxLeft and maxRight by scanning for each i. That's O(n²).
  3. Waste: those maxima get recomputed every time. Precompute them as prefix-max and suffix-max arrays, for O(n) time and O(n) space.
  4. Two-pointer insight: if h[l] < h[r], then maxRight(l) ≥ h[r] > h[l], so the water at l depends only on leftMax. Process l and move it. Mirror the logic for r. That's O(n) time and O(1) space.
  5. Alternative view: a monotonic decreasing stack fills water layer by layer whenever a taller bar closes a basin.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Trapping rain water with two pointers
  1. Water above a bar = min(tallest on its left, tallest on its right) − its height. Move the pointer with the lower wall: its side's max is the binding limit.
  2. h[l] = 0 < h[r] = 1: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (0) decides. +0.
  3. h[l] = 1 ≥ h[r] = 1: rightMax (1) decides for r. +0.
  4. h[l] = 1 < h[r] = 2: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (1) decides. +0.
  5. h[l] = 0 < h[r] = 2: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (1) decides. +1.
  6. h[l] = 2 ≥ h[r] = 2: rightMax (2) decides for r. +0.
  7. h[l] = 2 ≥ h[r] = 1: rightMax (2) decides for r. +1.
  8. h[l] = 2 ≥ h[r] = 2: rightMax (2) decides for r. +0.
  9. h[l] = 2 < h[r] = 3: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (2) decides. +0.
  10. h[l] = 1 < h[r] = 3: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (2) decides. +1.
  11. h[l] = 0 < h[r] = 3: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (2) decides. +2.
  12. h[l] = 1 < h[r] = 3: the right wall is taller, so leftMax (2) decides. +1.
  13. The pointers met: 6 units of water, one pass, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Water trapped between bars. [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] → 6. */
public final class TrappingRainWater {
    private TrappingRainWater() {}

    /** Brute force: for each bar, scan left max and right max. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] h) {
        int water = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
            int leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0;
            for (int l = 0; l <= i; l++) leftMax = Math.max(leftMax, h[l]);
            for (int r = i; r < h.length; r++) rightMax = Math.max(rightMax, h[r]);
            water += Math.min(leftMax, rightMax) - h[i];
        }
        return water;
    }

    /** Precompute prefix-max and suffix-max arrays. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static int prefixMax(int[] h) {
        int n = h.length;
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        int[] left = new int[n], right = new int[n];
        left[0] = h[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) left[i] = Math.max(left[i - 1], h[i]);
        right[n - 1] = h[n - 1];
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) right[i] = Math.max(right[i + 1], h[i]);
        int water = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) water += Math.min(left[i], right[i]) - h[i];
        return water;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: two pointers. The side with the smaller max is the bottleneck — its water level is
     * already known, so process it and move inward. O(n) time, O(1) space.
     */
    public static int twoPointers(int[] h) {
        int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0, water = 0;
        while (l < r) {
            if (h[l] < h[r]) {
                leftMax = Math.max(leftMax, h[l]);
                water += leftMax - h[l++];
            } else {
                rightMax = Math.max(rightMax, h[r]);
                water += rightMax - h[r--];
            }
        }
        return water;
    }

    /** Monotonic decreasing stack: fill "layers" when a taller bar closes a basin. O(n). */
    public static int monotonicStack(int[] h) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int water = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && h[i] > h[stack.peek()]) {
                int bottom = stack.pop();
                if (stack.isEmpty()) break;                  // no left wall
                int left = stack.peek();
                int width = i - left - 1;
                int bounded = Math.min(h[left], h[i]) - h[bottom];
                water += width * bounded;
            }
            stack.push(i);
        }
        return water;
    }
}

docs.title: Two sum
docs.text: Medium Hashing Two pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target (exactly one solution). [2,7,11,15], 9 → [0,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: check every pair. That's O(n²).
  2. Waste: for each x, we search for target − x with a linear scan.
  3. Hashing: remember the values we've seen, mapped to their indices. Each lookup is then O(1), for O(n) total.
  4. Look up before inserting, so an element never pairs with itself ([3,3], 6 works, [3], 6 doesn't).
  5. If the array is sorted (or you're allowed to sort), use two pointers, which needs O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Dry run (hash map, [2,7,11,15], 9)
docs.text: i a[i] need seen Result 0 2 7 {} → 1 7 2 found 2 → idx 0 [0,1] ✅

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Two Sum with a hash map: [2, 7, 11, 15], target 26
  1. One pass. For each number, ask the map: have I already seen its complement?
  2. i = 0: need 26 − 2 = 24. Not in the map yet.
  3. Remember 2 → 0 for later numbers. Putting it after the lookup stops an element pairing with itself.
  4. i = 1: need 26 − 7 = 19. Not in the map yet.
  5. Remember 7 → 1 for later numbers. Putting it after the lookup stops an element pairing with itself.
  6. i = 2: need 26 − 11 = 15. Not in the map yet.
  7. Remember 11 → 2 for later numbers. Putting it after the lookup stops an element pairing with itself.
  8. i = 3: need 26 − 15 = 11. It's in the map at index 2: answer [2, 3].

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Indices of two numbers adding to target (exactly one solution assumed). Returns {} if none. */
public final class TwoSum {
    private TwoSum() {}

    /** Brute force: every pair. O(n^2), O(1). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a, int target) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++)
                if (a[i] + a[j] == target) return new int[]{i, j};
        return new int[0];
    }

    /** Optimal: one-pass hash map value → index; look up the complement first. O(n), O(n). */
    public static int[] optimal(int[] a, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            Integer j = seen.get(target - a[i]);
            if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
            seen.put(a[i], i);                               // insert AFTER lookup so we don't pair with self
        }
        return new int[0];
    }

    /** Sorted input variant: two pointers. O(n), O(1). Returns indices into the sorted array. */
    public static int[] sortedTwoPointers(int[] sorted, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = sorted.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int sum = sorted[l] + sorted[r];
            if (sum == target) return new int[]{l, r};
            if (sum < target) l++;                           // need bigger → move left up
            else r--;                                        // need smaller → move right down
        }
        return new int[0];
    }

    /** Unsorted + two pointers: sort index array by value (O(n log n)), keep original indices. */
    public static int[] sortThenTwoPointers(int[] a, int target) {
        Integer[] idx = new Integer[a.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) idx[i] = i;
        Arrays.sort(idx, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(a[x], a[y]));
        int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int sum = a[idx[l]] + a[idx[r]];
            if (sum == target) return new int[]{Math.min(idx[l], idx[r]), Math.max(idx[l], idx[r])};
            if (sum < target) l++;
            else r--;
        }
        return new int[0];
    }
}

docs.title: Armstrong number
docs.text: Easy Digits Recursion Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: An Armstrong (narcissistic) number equals the sum of its digits, each raised to the number of digits. 153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³, 9474 = 9⁴ + 4⁴ + 7⁴ + 4⁴. Also: list every Armstrong number up to a limit.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Count the digits d once.
  2. Extract each digit with % 10 and / 10, and add digit^d.
  3. Compare the sum with the original. Keep a copy, because the loop destroys n.
  4. Pitfall: Math.pow returns a double. Use an integer power loop to avoid rounding errors.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Armstrong (narcissistic) number: sum of each digit^(number of digits) equals the number. 153 = 1³+5³+3³. */
public final class ArmstrongNumber {
    private ArmstrongNumber() {}

    /** Iterative: count digits, then sum powers. O(d). */
    public static boolean isArmstrong(int n) {
        if (n < 0) return false;
        int digits = String.valueOf(n).length();
        long sum = 0;
        for (int x = n; x > 0; x /= 10) sum += pow(x % 10, digits);
        return sum == n;
    }

    /** Recursive sum of digit powers. */
    public static boolean recursive(int n) {
        return n >= 0 && sumPowers(n, String.valueOf(n).length()) == n;
    }

    private static long sumPowers(int n, int p) {
        return n == 0 ? 0 : pow(n % 10, p) + sumPowers(n / 10, p);
    }

    /** Java 8: digits as chars → power sum. */
    public static boolean streams(int n) {
        if (n < 0) return false;
        String s = String.valueOf(n);
        return s.chars().mapToLong(c -> pow(c - '0', s.length())).sum() == n;
    }

    /** All Armstrong numbers in [1, limit]. */
    public static List<Integer> upTo(int limit) {
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, limit).filter(ArmstrongNumber::isArmstrong).boxed().collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new));
    }

    private static long pow(int base, int exp) {             // integer power — avoid Math.pow double rounding
        long r = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) r *= base;
        return r;
    }
}

docs.text: O(d²) per number with the naive power, or O(d log d) with fast power. Since d ≤ 10, that's effectively O(1).

docs.title: Number base conversion
docs.text: Medium Division / Horner Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Convert integers between bases 2–36: decimal → binary (10 → 1010), hex → decimal (ff → 255), and any base → any base.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. To base b: n % b is the last digit, and n / b drops it. Repeat until n is 0. The digits come out least-significant first, so reverse them at the end.
  2. Recursive version, no reversal: convert n / b first (the higher digits), then append n % b.
  3. From base b, Horner's rule: read left to right with value = value × b + digit. "ff" → 0×16+15 = 15 → 15×16+15 = 255.
  4. Any → any: parse into a long, then format. Reject digits that are invalid for the base.
  5. Handle 0 and negative numbers explicitly.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

/** Convert integers between bases 2..36 (digits 0-9 then a-z), without Integer.toString(n, radix) as the main answer. */
public final class BaseConversion {
    private BaseConversion() {}

    private static final String DIGITS = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";

    /** Repeated division: remainders are the digits from LEAST significant upward → reverse at the end. */
    public static String toBase(long n, int base) {
        check(base);
        if (n == 0) return "0";
        boolean negative = n < 0;
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        long x = Math.abs(n);                                // fine for |n| < 2^63
        while (x > 0) {
            sb.append(DIGITS.charAt((int) (x % base)));
            x /= base;
        }
        if (negative) sb.append('-');
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    /** Recursive: convert n / base first (the higher digits), then append the last digit — no reversal needed. */
    public static String toBaseRecursive(long n, int base) {
        check(base);
        if (n < 0) return "-" + toBaseRecursive(-n, base);
        if (n < base) return String.valueOf(DIGITS.charAt((int) n));
        return toBaseRecursive(n / base, base) + DIGITS.charAt((int) (n % base));
    }

    /** Parse: Horner's rule — value = value * base + digit, left to right. */
    public static long fromBase(String s, int base) {
        check(base);
        boolean negative = s.startsWith("-");
        long value = 0;
        for (char c : (negative ? s.substring(1) : s).toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
            int d = DIGITS.indexOf(c);
            if (d < 0 || d >= base) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad digit '" + c + "' for base " + base);
            value = value * base + d;
        }
        return negative ? -value : value;
    }

    /** Any base to any base via a long in the middle. */
    public static String convert(String s, int from, int to) {
        return toBase(fromBase(s, from), to);
    }

    private static void check(int base) {
        if (base < 2 || base > 36) throw new IllegalArgumentException("base must be 2..36");
    }
}

docs.text: O(log_b n) for both directions.

docs.title: Excel column title ↔ number
docs.text: Medium Bijective base 26 Horner's rule

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Excel names columns A, B, …, Z, AA, AB, …, AZ, BA, …, ZZ, AAA, … Convert a title to its column number, and a number back to its title.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Title Number A 1 Z 26 AA 27 AZ 52 ZZ 702 AAA 703 FXSHRXW 2147483647

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Uppercase only? Here, yes: other characters throw.
  • Largest input? Return a long so large titles don't overflow.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Title → number is base conversion with Horner's rule: n = n * 26 + digit, where A = 1 … Z = 26.
  2. Number → title: the trap. Plain base 26 uses digits 0..25, but here the digits are 1..26 with no zero. Doing n % 26 on 26 gives 0, which has no letter.
  3. Fix: subtract 1 before each step. (n − 1) % 26 picks the letter (0 → A, 25 → Z), and (n − 1) / 26 is the rest. This system is called bijective base 26.
  4. The recursive form writes the same idea top-down: title(n) = title((n − 1) / 26) + letter((n − 1) % 26).

docs.title: Dry run: 702 → title
docs.text:
n n − 1 (n − 1) % 26 letter (n − 1) / 26 702 701 25 Z 26 26 25 25 Z 0

Read in reverse: ZZ. Without the −1, 702 % 26 = 0 has no letter.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

/**
 * Excel column titles: A..Z = 1..26, AA = 27, AZ = 52, BA = 53, ZZ = 702, AAA = 703.
 * This is "bijective base 26": digits run 1..26 and there is no zero, which is why naive base conversion fails.
 */
public final class ExcelColumn {
    private ExcelColumn() {}

    /** Title → number with Horner's rule: n = n * 26 + digit, digit in 1..26. O(L). */
    public static long toNumber(String title) {
        if (title == null || title.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("empty title");
        long n = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < title.length(); i++) {
            char c = title.charAt(i);
            if (c < 'A' || c > 'Z') throw new IllegalArgumentException("not A..Z: " + c);
            n = n * 26 + (c - 'A' + 1);
        }
        return n;
    }

    /**
     * Number → title. Shift to 0-based before each division: (n - 1) % 26 picks the letter, (n - 1) / 26 is the rest.
     * Without the -1, 26 would become "A@" instead of "Z". O(log₂₆ n).
     */
    public static String toTitle(long n) {
        if (n < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be >= 1");
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (n > 0) {
            n--;                                        // make this digit 0-based
            sb.append((char) ('A' + n % 26));
            n /= 26;
        }
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    /** Recursive form of toTitle: title(n) = title((n-1)/26) + letter((n-1) % 26). */
    public static String toTitleRecursive(long n) {
        if (n < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be >= 1");
        long m = n - 1;
        String last = String.valueOf((char) ('A' + m % 26));
        return m / 26 == 0 ? last : toTitleRecursive(m / 26) + last;
    }

    /** Brute force for tests: count up from "A" with an odometer increment. O(n · L). */
    public static String toTitleBrute(int n) {
        char[] t = {'A'};
        for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) t = increment(t);
        return new String(t);
    }

    private static char[] increment(char[] t) {
        for (int i = t.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (t[i] != 'Z') {
                t[i]++;
                return t;
            }
            t[i] = 'A';                                  // carry
        }
        char[] grown = new char[t.length + 1];          // all Z → one longer, all A
        java.util.Arrays.fill(grown, 'A');
        return grown;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Direction Time Space Title → number O(L) O(1) Number → title O(log₂₆ n) O(log₂₆ n) Odometer brute force (tests only) O(n · L) O(L)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• 26 → "Z" and 27 → "AA". These are the boundary cases that break a naive % 26.
  • Building the title with insert(0, c) is O(L²). Append, then reverse once.
