docs.title: Add two numbers
docs.text: Hard Carry Dummy head Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Two non-negative numbers are stored as digit lists in reverse order (342 is 2→4→3). Return their sum in the same form. 2→4→3 + 5→6→4 → 7→0→8 (342 + 465 = 807). Follow-up (LeetCode 445): the digits are in forward order.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Can the lists have different lengths? (Yes.) Leading zeros? (No, except for the number 0 itself.) Could the numbers exceed long? (Yes, which is why converting to a number is wrong.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Tempting but wrong: convert to long, add, and convert back. It overflows after 19 digits.
  2. Reverse order is a gift: the head is the ones digit, exactly where grade-school addition starts.
  3. At each step, sum = carry + digitA + digitB. Emit sum % 10 and carry sum / 10.
  4. Loop while either list has digits or the carry is non-zero. That last condition produces the extra leading digit (99 + 1 = 100).
  5. Forward-order follow-up: reverse both lists, add, and reverse the result. A stack-based version also works.

docs.title: Dry run (342 + 465)
docs.text: a b carry in sum digit carry out 2 5 0 7 7 0 4 6 0 10 0 1 3 4 1 8 8 0

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Numbers stored as digit lists in REVERSE order (342 = 2→4→3). Return their sum in the same form. */
public final class AddTwoNumbers {
    private AddTwoNumbers() {}

    /** Iterative: grade-school addition with a carry. O(max(m,n)). Works for any length — no overflow. */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
        int carry = 0;
        while (a != null || b != null || carry != 0) {       // carry != 0 emits the final extra digit
            int sum = carry + (a != null ? a.val : 0) + (b != null ? b.val : 0);
            tail = tail.next = new ListNode(sum % 10);
            carry = sum / 10;
            if (a != null) a = a.next;
            if (b != null) b = b.next;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Recursive: add this digit pair plus carry, recurse on the rest with the new carry. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        return add(a, b, 0);
    }

    private static ListNode add(ListNode a, ListNode b, int carry) {
        if (a == null && b == null && carry == 0) return null;
        int sum = carry + (a != null ? a.val : 0) + (b != null ? b.val : 0);
        return new ListNode(sum % 10, add(a != null ? a.next : null, b != null ? b.next : null, sum / 10));
    }

    /** Follow-up (LeetCode 445): digits in FORWARD order. Reverse both, add, reverse the result. */
    public static ListNode forwardOrder(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        return ReverseLinkedList.iterative(iterative(ReverseLinkedList.iterative(a), ReverseLinkedList.iterative(b)));
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(max(m, n)) time. O(max(m, n)) for the output, plus O(max(m, n)) stack in the recursive version.

docs.title: Copy list with random pointer
docs.text: Hard Hashing Interleaving

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Each node has next and a random pointer to any node or null. Return a deep copy. No pointer in the copy may reference an original node.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Copying next is easy. The trouble is that random may point forward to a node you haven't copied yet.
  2. Two passes with a map: pass 1 creates every copy (original → copy). Pass 2 sets copy.next = map.get(orig.next) and copy.random = map.get(orig.random). O(n) space.
  3. O(1) space insight: the map exists only to find "the copy of X". Put each copy right after its original (A → A' → B → B'). Then the copy of X is simply X.next.
  4. Three passes: insert the copies, set copy.random = orig.random.next, then unweave the two lists, restoring the original.

docs.title: Interleaving, visualised
docs.text:
original:     A → B → C
interleaved:  A → A' → B → B' → C → C'
random:       A'.random = A.random.next
split:        A → B → C      A' → B' → C'

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Deep-copy a list whose nodes also have a {@code random} pointer to any node (or null). */
public final class CopyRandomList {
    private CopyRandomList() {}

    /** Node with an extra random pointer. */
    public static final class Node {
        public int val;
        public Node next, random;

        public Node(int val) {
            this.val = val;
        }
    }

    /** HashMap original → copy, then wire next/random in a second pass. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static Node withMap(Node head) {
        Map<Node, Node> copy = new HashMap<>();
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) copy.put(n, new Node(n.val));
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {
            copy.get(n).next = copy.get(n.next);             // get(null) → null, which is exactly right
            copy.get(n).random = copy.get(n.random);
        }
        return copy.get(head);
    }

    /**
     * Interleave: A→A'→B→B'→… so every copy sits right after its original (original.next IS the map).
     * Then set randoms, then unweave. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
     */
    public static Node interleave(Node head) {
        if (head == null) return null;
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next.next) {    // 1. insert copies
            Node c = new Node(n.val);
            c.next = n.next;
            n.next = c;
        }
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next.next) {    // 2. copy.random = original.random's copy
            if (n.random != null) n.next.random = n.random.next;
        }
        Node copyHead = head.next;
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {         // 3. split the two lists, restoring the original
            Node c = n.next;
            n.next = c.next;
            c.next = c.next != null ? c.next.next : null;
        }
        return copyHead;
    }
}

docs.title: Intersection of two linked lists
docs.text: Medium Two pointers Hashing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Two lists may merge into a shared tail (the same nodes, not just equal values). Return the first shared node, or null.

A:      4 → 1 ↘
                8 → 4 → 5
B:  5 → 6 → 1 ↗

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each node of A, scan B. That's O(m·n).
  2. HashSet: store A's nodes, then walk B. O(m + n) time, O(m) space.
  3. Length insight: after the merge point both lists are identical, so the only difference is the head part. Skip the extra |m − n| nodes of the longer list, then walk both together.
  4. Elegant version: walk A then B with one pointer, and B then A with the other. Both travel m + n, so they meet at the intersection, or reach null at the same moment if there isn't one. You never need to count lengths.

docs.title: Why switching heads works
docs.text: Pointer p travels a + c + b and pointer q travels b + c + a, where c is the shared tail. The totals are equal, so they arrive at the start of c together.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Return the node where two lists merge (by identity), or null. Lists are not modified. */
public final class IntersectionOfTwoLists {
    private IntersectionOfTwoLists() {}

    /** Store every node of A, walk B until one is found. O(m+n) time, O(m) space. */
    public static ListNode withSet(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        Set<ListNode> seen = new HashSet<>();
        for (ListNode x = a; x != null; x = x.next) seen.add(x);
        for (ListNode y = b; y != null; y = y.next) if (seen.contains(y)) return y;
        return null;
    }

    /** Align by length: skip the longer list's extra head, then walk together. O(m+n), O(1). */
    public static ListNode lengthDiff(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        int la = length(a), lb = length(b);
        for (; la > lb; la--) a = a.next;
        for (; lb > la; lb--) b = b.next;
        while (a != b) {
            a = a.next;
            b = b.next;
        }
        return a;
    }

    /**
     * Switch heads: each pointer walks its list then the other one. Both travel m+n, so they arrive at the
     * intersection together — or at null together when there is none. O(m+n), O(1), no length counting.
     */
    public static ListNode switchHeads(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode p = a, q = b;
        while (p != q) {
            p = p == null ? b : p.next;
            q = q == null ? a : q.next;
        }
        return p;
    }

    private static int length(ListNode n) {
        int len = 0;
        for (; n != null; n = n.next) len++;
        return len;
    }
}

docs.title: Detect a cycle & find its start
docs.text: Medium Floyd's tortoise & hare Hashing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Does the list contain a cycle?
  2. If so, which node does the cycle start at (LeetCode 142)?
  3. How long is the cycle?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: remember every node you visit in a HashSet. The first repeat is the cycle start. O(n) space.
  2. O(1) insight: on a circular track, a runner going 2 steps per tick gains 1 step per tick on a runner going 1, so it must land on it. It can't jump over, because the gap shrinks by exactly 1.
  3. Finding the start: let F = distance from head to the start, and a = distance from the start to the meeting point. Slow walked F + a and fast walked 2(F + a). The difference F + a is a whole number of loops, so F ≡ −a (mod loop). A pointer from the head and a pointer from the meeting point, both moving 1 step, therefore meet exactly at the start.

docs.title: Picture
docs.text:
head → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
               ↑       ↓
               7 ← 6 ← 5        F = 2 (head..3), loop length 5

docs.title: Approach 1 — HashSet
docs.text: O(n) time, O(n) space. The first node that add rejects is the start.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Floyd (optimal)
docs.text:
1. slow and fast both start at head. Loop while fast and fast.next exist.
  2. If slow == fast, there's a cycle.
  3. To find the start, set p = head and step p and slow together until they meet.
  4. For the length, walk around once from the start.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Floyd's tortoise and hare on a list whose tail loops back to node 3
  1. Both pointers start at the head. slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2.
  2. slow → node 2, fast → node 3. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  3. slow → node 3, fast → node 5. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  4. slow → node 4, fast → node 7. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  5. slow → node 5, fast → node 4. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  6. slow → node 6, fast → node 6. They meet: inside a loop the faster runner must land on the slower one, because the gap shrinks by exactly 1 each round.
  7. Phase 2: put p at the head and keep slow at the meeting point (node 6). Both now move 1 step at a time.
  8. p → node 2, slow → node 7.
  9. p → node 3, slow → node 3. Same node!
  10. They meet exactly at the start of the cycle, node 3: the distance from the head equals the distance from the meeting point, modulo the loop length. O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Does the list loop back on itself? If so, where does the loop start, and how long is it? */
public final class LinkedListCycle {
    private LinkedListCycle() {}

    /** HashSet of visited nodes (identity, not value). O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean hasCycleWithSet(ListNode head) {
        Set<ListNode> seen = new HashSet<>();                // ListNode has no equals(): identity semantics
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {
            if (!seen.add(n)) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    /** Floyd: fast gains one step per round on slow; inside a loop it must land on slow. O(n), O(1). */
    public static boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
            if (slow == fast) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    /**
     * Start of the cycle. After slow and fast meet, a pointer from head and a pointer from the meeting
     * point, both moving 1 step, meet exactly at the cycle start (distance head→start = meet→start mod loop).
     */
    public static ListNode cycleStart(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
            if (slow == fast) {
                ListNode p = head;
                while (p != slow) {
                    p = p.next;
                    slow = slow.next;
                }
                return p;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

    /** Length of the cycle (0 if none): from the meeting point walk once around. */
    public static int cycleLength(ListNode head) {
        ListNode start = cycleStart(head);
        if (start == null) return 0;
        int len = 1;
        for (ListNode n = start.next; n != start; n = n.next) len++;
        return len;
    }
}

docs.title: LRU cache
docs.text: Expert HashMap Doubly linked list Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Design a cache of fixed capacity with O(1) get(key) and put(key, value). When it's full, put evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: What does get return for a missing key? (−1.) Does updating an existing key count as a use? (Yes.) Thread safety? (Not required here. Mention synchronized or a ConcurrentHashMap + lock as a follow-up.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. O(1) lookup needs a HashMap.
  2. O(1) "who is the oldest?" needs an order. An array costs O(n) to shift, so use a list.
  3. O(1) "move this entry to the front" means you must unlink a node from the middle in O(1), which needs a doubly linked list (you need prev).
  4. The map stores key → node, so the node is found instantly and moved in O(1).
  5. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove every null check.
  6. Each node must store its key too: on eviction you have the tail node and must remove its key from the map.

docs.text:
map: { 1 → ●, 3 → ●, 4 → ● }
head ⇄ [4] ⇄ [3] ⇄ [1] ⇄ tail

package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Least-Recently-Used cache with O(1) get and put. When full, put evicts the key used longest ago.
 * {@code get} returns -1 for a missing key.
 */
public final class LruCache {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<Integer, Entry> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Entry head = new Entry(0, 0), tail = new Entry(0, 0);   // sentinels: no null checks

    /** Doubly linked node: most recent right after head, least recent right before tail. */
    private static final class Entry {
        final int key;
        int value;
        Entry prev, next;

        Entry(int key, int value) {
            this.key = key;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    public int get(int key) {
        Entry e = map.get(key);
        if (e == null) return -1;
        moveToFront(e);                                      // reading counts as "use"
        return e.value;
    }

    public void put(int key, int value) {
        Entry e = map.get(key);
        if (e != null) {
            e.value = value;
            moveToFront(e);
            return;
        }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {                        // evict least recently used
            Entry lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru);
            map.remove(lru.key);                             // that's why Entry stores its key
        }
        e = new Entry(key, value);
        map.put(key, e);
        addFront(e);
    }

    public int size() {
        return map.size();
    }

    private void moveToFront(Entry e) {
        unlink(e);
        addFront(e);
    }

    private void unlink(Entry e) {
        e.prev.next = e.next;
        e.next.prev = e.prev;
    }

    private void addFront(Entry e) {
        e.next = head.next;
        e.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = e;
        head.next = e;
    }

    /** Production shortcut: LinkedHashMap in access order + removeEldestEntry. Know it, but expect to hand-roll. */
    public static <K, V> Map<K, V> withLinkedHashMap(int capacity) {
        return new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
            @Override
            protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
                return size() > capacity;
            }
        };
    }
}

docs.text: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) (access order) plus removeEldestEntry is a two-line LRU, and the class shows it. Interviewers usually ask you to build the structure yourself, so know both.

docs.title: Merge K sorted lists
docs.text: Expert Min-heap Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list. [1→4→5, 1→3→4, 2→6] → 1→1→2→3→4→4→5→6. Let N be the total number of nodes.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Collect and sort: O(N log N). It ignores the fact that the input is already sorted.
  2. Merge one by one: merge list 1 with 2, the result with 3, and so on. The growing result is re-walked k times, which gives O(k·N).
  3. Heap insight: at any moment the next output node is the smallest of the k current heads. A min-heap of size k gives that in O(log k), so the total is O(N log k).
  4. Divide & conquer: merge lists in pairs, like merge sort. There are log k rounds and each touches every node once, so it's also O(N log k), with no heap.

docs.title: Heap trace (first steps)
docs.text: Heap (heads) Pop Push 1a, 1b, 2 1a 4a 1b, 2, 4a 1b 3b 2, 3b, 4a 2 6 3b, 4a, 6 3b 4b

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list. N = total nodes. */
public final class MergeKSortedLists {
    private MergeKSortedLists() {}

    /** Brute force: collect all values, sort, rebuild. O(N log N) time, O(N) space. */
    public static ListNode collectAndSort(ListNode[] lists) {
        List<Integer> all = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ListNode l : lists) all.addAll(ListNode.toList(l));
        Collections.sort(all);
        return ListNode.of(all.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray());
    }

    /** Sequential: merge list 1 into 2, result into 3, … O(k·N) — the first list is re-walked k times. */
    public static ListNode sequential(ListNode[] lists) {
        ListNode result = null;
        for (ListNode l : lists) result = MergeTwoSortedLists.iterative(result, l);
        return result;
    }

    /** Min-heap of the k current heads: pop smallest, push its successor. O(N log k) time, O(k) space. */
    public static ListNode heap(ListNode[] lists) {
        PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Integer.compare(x.val, y.val));
        for (ListNode l : lists) if (l != null) pq.offer(l);
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            ListNode smallest = pq.poll();
            tail = tail.next = smallest;
            if (smallest.next != null) pq.offer(smallest.next);
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Divide & conquer: merge pairs like merge sort. log k rounds, each O(N) → O(N log k), O(log k) stack. */
    public static ListNode divideAndConquer(ListNode[] lists) {
        if (lists.length == 0) return null;
        return merge(lists, 0, lists.length - 1);
    }

    private static ListNode merge(ListNode[] lists, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return lists[lo];
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        return MergeTwoSortedLists.iterative(merge(lists, lo, mid), merge(lists, mid + 1, hi));
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Collect + sort O(N log N) O(N) Sequential merge O(k·N) O(1) Min-heap O(N log k) O(k) Divide & conquer O(N log k) O(log k) stack

docs.title: Pitfall
docs.text: PriorityQueue<ListNode> needs a comparator, because ListNode isn't Comparable. Use Integer.compare(a.val, b.val) rather than a.val - b.val, which overflows for extreme values.

docs.title: Merge two sorted lists
docs.text: Easy Dummy head Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list by splicing the existing nodes. 1→2→4 + 1→3→4 → 1→1→2→3→4→4.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The smallest overall node is one of the two heads, so take it and repeat. This is the merge step of merge sort.
  2. Dummy head: start with a fake node, so "append to result" is always tail.next = x, with no special case for the first node.
  3. When one list runs out, the rest of the other is already sorted, so attach it in one assignment.
  4. Use <= to take from a on ties. That keeps the merge stable.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Iterative with a dummy head (optimal)
docs.text: O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Recursive
docs.text: merge(a, b): whichever head is smaller becomes the answer, and its next = merge(rest, other). The base case is when either list is empty. It's elegant, but uses O(n + m) stack.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Merge two sorted lists by splicing nodes (no new nodes). 1→3→5 + 2→4 = 1→2→3→4→5. */
public final class MergeTwoSortedLists {
    private MergeTwoSortedLists() {}

    /** Iterative with a dummy head: always attach the smaller front node. O(n+m), O(1). */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;      // dummy removes the "is result empty?" special case
        while (a != null && b != null) {
            if (a.val <= b.val) {                            // <= keeps the merge stable
                tail.next = a;
                a = a.next;
            } else {
                tail.next = b;
                b = b.next;
            }
            tail = tail.next;
        }
        tail.next = a != null ? a : b;                       // append whatever is left in one go
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Recursive: the smaller head wins, its next is the merge of the rest. O(n+m) time and stack. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        if (a == null) return b;
        if (b == null) return a;
        if (a.val <= b.val) {
            a.next = recursive(a.next, b);
            return a;
        }
        b.next = recursive(a, b.next);
        return b;
    }
}

docs.title: Middle of the linked list
docs.text: Easy Slow / fast pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the middle node. For an even length, return the second middle: 1→2→3→4→5 → 3, 1→2→3→4→5→6 → 4.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: For an even length, which middle? Merge sort's split needs the first middle, so the code has both.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Two passes: count n, then walk n/2 steps. That's O(n) and simple.
  2. One pass: if fast moves twice as fast as slow, then when fast reaches the end slow has gone half as far.
  3. The loop condition fast != null && fast.next != null decides which middle you get. Starting fast at head.next instead shifts the answer to the first middle.

docs.title: Dry run (1→2→3→4→5→6)
docs.text: Step slow fast 0 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 5 3 4 null → stop

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Middle of 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 with slow and fast
  1. slow moves 1 node per step, fast moves 2. When fast runs off the end, slow is halfway.
  2. slow → node 2, fast → node 3.
  3. slow → node 3, fast → node 5.
  4. slow → node 4, fast → null (fell off the end).
  5. fast is null: slow is at node 4, the second middle of an even-length list. One pass, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Middle node; for even length return the SECOND middle (1→2→3→4 gives 3). */
public final class MiddleNode {
    private MiddleNode() {}

    /** Two passes: count, then walk n/2. O(n). */
    public static ListNode twoPass(ListNode head) {
        int n = 0;
        for (ListNode x = head; x != null; x = x.next) n++;
        ListNode x = head;
        for (int i = 0; i < n / 2; i++) x = x.next;
        return x;
    }

    /** Optimal: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast falls off, slow is in the middle. One pass, O(1). */
    public static ListNode slowFast(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }
        return slow;
    }

    /** Variant: FIRST middle for even length (needed when splitting a list for merge sort). */
    public static ListNode firstMiddle(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null) return null;
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head.next;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }
        return slow;
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time and O(1) space for both approaches. The slow/fast version takes a single pass.

docs.title: Palindrome linked list
docs.text: Medium Slow / fast In-place reversal Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if the values read the same forwards and backwards. 1→2→2→1 ✅, 1→2→3→1 ❌. Can you do it in O(1) space?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: copy the values into an ArrayList and use two pointers. O(n) space.
  2. The problem: a singly linked list can't walk backwards.
  3. Insight: make the second half walk "forwards" by reversing it. Find the first middle, reverse everything after it, and compare it node by node with the first half.
  4. Senior touch: reverse the second half back afterwards. A check function shouldn't mutate its input.
  5. Recursive trick: the recursion visits nodes from the tail backwards while a shared front pointer moves forwards, so you compare the outermost pair first.

docs.title: Picture (1→2→3→2→1)
docs.text:
first half: 1 → 2 → 3          second half reversed: 1 → 2
            ↑ compare ↑                              ↑   ↑

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Is the list a palindrome? 1→2→2→1 yes, 1→2 no. */
public final class PalindromeLinkedList {
    private PalindromeLinkedList() {}

    /** Copy values into a list, then two pointers. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean copyToList(ListNode head) {
        List<Integer> v = ListNode.toList(head);
        for (int l = 0, r = v.size() - 1; l < r; l++, r--) if (!v.get(l).equals(v.get(r))) return false;
        return true;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: find the middle, reverse the second half, compare, then reverse it back so the caller's
     * list is unchanged. O(n) time, O(1) space.
     */
    public static boolean reverseHalf(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return true;
        ListNode firstEnd = MiddleNode.firstMiddle(head);
        ListNode second = ReverseLinkedList.iterative(firstEnd.next);
        boolean ok = true;
        for (ListNode p = head, q = second; ok && q != null; p = p.next, q = q.next) ok = p.val == q.val;
        firstEnd.next = ReverseLinkedList.iterative(second); // restore input
        return ok;
    }

    /** Recursive: recursion unwinds from the tail while a "front" pointer walks forward. O(n) stack. */
    public static boolean recursive(ListNode head) {
        ListNode[] front = {head};
        return check(head, front);
    }

    private static boolean check(ListNode node, ListNode[] front) {
        if (node == null) return true;
        if (!check(node.next, front)) return false;          // compare deepest (tail) first
        boolean same = node.val == front[0].val;
        front[0] = front[0].next;
        return same;
    }
}

docs.title: Remove duplicates from a sorted list (I & II)
docs.text: Easy Pointer skipping Dummy node

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given a sorted linked list:

  • I: delete duplicates so each value appears once. 1→1→2→3→3 ⇒ 1→2→3.
  • II (follow-up): delete every node whose value repeats, keeping only distinct values. 1→2→3→3→4→4→5 ⇒ 1→2→5.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input I II 1→1→2 1→2 2 1→1→1→2→3 1→2→3 2→3 1→1 1 empty empty empty empty

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Is the list sorted? That is what makes O(1) space possible. Unsorted lists need a hash set.
  • Can I relink nodes, or must I build a new list?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sorted means duplicates are adjacent. You only ever compare a node with its next.
  2. I: if cur.next.val == cur.val, unlink cur.next and stay on cur (there may be a third copy). Otherwise move on.
  3. II: now the first copy must go too, and it may be the head. A dummy node in front removes that special case. prev is the last node known to be unique. If a run starts at prev.next, skip the whole run and attach prev.next to what follows. Don't advance prev yet, since the next node might start another run.
  4. Recursive I: dedupe the tail, then drop head if it equals the tail's new head.

docs.title: Dry run (II): 1→2→3→3→4→4→5
docs.text:
prev cur run? action dummy 1 no prev = 1 1 2 no prev = 2 2 3 yes (3, 3) prev.next = 4 2 4 yes (4, 4) prev.next = 5 2 5 no prev = 5

Result: 1→2→5.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * Sorted linked list.
 * I: keep one copy of each value (1→1→2→3→3 ⇒ 1→2→3).
 * II: drop EVERY value that repeats (1→2→3→3→4→4→5 ⇒ 1→2→5).
 */
public final class RemoveDuplicatesSortedList {
    private RemoveDuplicatesSortedList() {}

    /** I, iterative: duplicates are adjacent, so unlink next while it equals current. O(n), O(1). */
    public static ListNode keepOne(ListNode head) {
        ListNode cur = head;
        while (cur != null && cur.next != null) {
            if (cur.next.val == cur.val) cur.next = cur.next.next;   // skip the duplicate, stay on cur
            else cur = cur.next;
        }
        return head;
    }

    /** I, recursive: fix the tail first, then decide whether head duplicates the new tail's head. O(n) stack. */
    public static ListNode keepOneRecursive(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;
        head.next = keepOneRecursive(head.next);
        return head.val == head.next.val ? head.next : head;
    }

    /** I, with a set (works even when the list is NOT sorted). O(n) time, O(n) space. Builds a new list. */
    public static ListNode keepOneWithSet(ListNode head) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) seen.add(n.val);
        return ListNode.of(seen.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray());
    }

    /**
     * II: a dummy node lets us delete the head itself. prev is the last node known to be unique; when a run of equal
     * values starts after prev, skip the whole run. O(n), O(1).
     */
    public static ListNode dropAllRepeated(ListNode head) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), prev = dummy;
        while (prev.next != null) {
            ListNode cur = prev.next;
            if (cur.next != null && cur.next.val == cur.val) {
                int v = cur.val;
                while (cur != null && cur.val == v) cur = cur.next;   // skip the entire run of v
                prev.next = cur;                                     // prev stays: cur may start another run
            } else {
                prev = cur;                                          // cur is unique: keep it
            }
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space I iterative O(n) O(1) I recursive O(n) O(n) stack I with a set (unsorted lists too) O(n) O(n) II with a dummy node O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• In I, advancing cur after an unlink misses triples (1→1→1).
  • In II, without the dummy node, a run at the head (1→1→2) needs separate code.
  • In II, advancing prev after skipping a run can keep the start of an immediately following run.

docs.title: Remove Nth node from end
docs.text: Medium Two pointers with a gap Dummy head

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Delete the n-th node from the end and return the head. 1→2→3→4→5, n = 2 → 1→2→3→5. n is always valid.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. To delete a node, you need the node before it.
  2. Two passes: count L, and the target's predecessor is node L − n counting from a dummy. O(n), but two passes.
  3. One pass: move fast n + 1 steps ahead of slow, then advance both together. When fast falls off the end, slow sits right before the target.
  4. Dummy head handles n == L (removing the head) without a special case.

docs.title: Dry run (n = 2)
docs.text: slow fast after the gap of 3 dummy 3 step 1 4 step 2 5 step 3 null → unlink 3.next (4)

docs.title: Recursive
docs.text: Count positions on the way back up the recursion. When the count equals n, return node.next to skip yourself.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Remove the n-th node from the end (1-based; n is valid). 1→2→3→4→5, n=2 gives 1→2→3→5. */
public final class RemoveNthFromEnd {
    private RemoveNthFromEnd() {}

    /** Two passes: length L, then delete node number L-n (0-based) from the front. */
    public static ListNode twoPass(ListNode head, int n) {
        int len = 0;
        for (ListNode x = head; x != null; x = x.next) len++;
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), prev = dummy;
        for (int i = 0; i < len - n; i++) prev = prev.next;
        prev.next = prev.next.next;
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** One pass: keep a gap of n nodes between fast and slow; when fast hits the end, slow is before the target. */
    public static ListNode onePass(ListNode head, int n) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), slow = dummy, fast = dummy;
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) fast = fast.next;       // gap of n+1 so slow stops BEFORE the target
        while (fast != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next;
        }
        slow.next = slow.next.next;
        return dummy.next;                                   // dummy handles "remove the head" too
    }

    /** Recursive: count positions on the way back up; unlink when the count equals n. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode head, int n) {
        int[] fromEnd = {0};
        return remove(head, n, fromEnd);
    }

    private static ListNode remove(ListNode node, int n, int[] fromEnd) {
        if (node == null) return null;
        node.next = remove(node.next, n, fromEnd);
        return ++fromEnd[0] == n ? node.next : node;         // skip myself if I am the n-th from the end
    }
}

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reorder L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → L2 → … in place, by relinking nodes (not by swapping values).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output 1→2→3→4 1→4→2→3 1→2→3→4→5 1→5→2→4→3 1 1

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Must I move nodes, or can I rewrite values? Move nodes. The tests check that the same node objects are relinked.
  • Return a new head? No, the head stays the same, so the method returns void.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: put the nodes in an ArrayList, then link from both ends with two indexes. O(n) extra space.
  2. What do we really need? The second half in reverse, interleaved with the first half.
  3. Three classic sub-problems, chained:
  4. find the middle with slow/fast pointers,
  5. reverse the second half in place,
  6. merge the two halves alternately.
  7. Each step is O(n) time and O(1) space. Combining known building blocks like this is exactly what the interviewer is checking.

docs.title: Dry run: 1→2→3→4→5
docs.text: step first half second half find middle (slow stops at 3) 1→2→3 4→5 reverse second 1→2→3 5→4 weave 1→5→2→4→3

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/** Reorder L0→L1→…→Ln into L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→L2→… in place (relink nodes, don't change values). */
public final class ReorderList {
    private ReorderList() {}

    /** Brute force: copy nodes into a list, then relink with two indexes from both ends. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static void withArray(ListNode head) {
        List<ListNode> nodes = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) nodes.add(n);
        int i = 0, j = nodes.size() - 1;
        while (i < j) {
            nodes.get(i).next = nodes.get(j);
            i++;
            if (i == j) break;
            nodes.get(j).next = nodes.get(i);
            j--;
        }
        if (!nodes.isEmpty()) nodes.get(i).next = null;      // the middle node becomes the new tail
    }

    /** Stack of the second half: pop to interleave from the back. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static void withStack(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null) return;
        Deque<ListNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int n = 0;
        for (ListNode x = head; x != null; x = x.next) { stack.push(x); n++; }
        ListNode cur = head;
        for (int k = 0; k < n / 2; k++) {                    // n/2 back nodes get inserted
            ListNode back = stack.pop(), next = cur.next;
            cur.next = back;
            back.next = next;
            cur = next;
        }
        cur.next = null;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal, O(1) space — three classic steps:
     * 1. find the middle (slow/fast), 2. reverse the second half, 3. merge the halves alternately.
     */
    public static void inPlace(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return;
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null) {  // slow stops at the end of the first half
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }
        ListNode second = reverse(slow.next);
        slow.next = null;                                    // cut: first half is never shorter
        ListNode first = head;
        while (second != null) {                             // weave: first, second, first, second...
            ListNode n1 = first.next, n2 = second.next;
            first.next = second;
            second.next = n1;
            first = n1;
            second = n2;
        }
    }

    private static ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
        ListNode prev = null;
        while (head != null) {
            ListNode next = head.next;
            head.next = prev;
            prev = head;
            head = next;
        }
        return prev;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Array of nodes O(n) O(n) Stack of nodes O(n) O(n) Middle + reverse + merge O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Not cutting the first half (slow.next = null) leaves a cycle. The merged list then never ends.
  • Stop the slow/fast loop with fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null, so the first half is the longer one for odd n.
  • 0, 1 and 2 nodes are all unchanged.

docs.title: Reverse nodes in k-group
docs.text: Hard In-place reversal Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse the list k nodes at a time. A final group shorter than k stays as it is. 1→2→3→4→5: k = 2 gives 2→1→4→3→5, and k = 3 gives 3→2→1→4→5.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. It's reverse a list, repeated on segments, so the hard part is the stitching.
  2. Check first: before reversing, make sure k nodes exist. Otherwise, leave the group alone.
  3. Recursive view: solve the rest of the list first, then reverse my k nodes so the last of them points at that solved remainder. Start prev at the remainder instead of null, and the stitch happens automatically.
  4. Iterative view: keep groupPrev, the node before the current group (initially a dummy). Reverse the group with prev starting at groupNext, point groupPrev.next at the old k-th node, and move groupPrev to the old first node, which is now the group's tail.

docs.title: Picture (k = 2, one group)
docs.text:
dummy → [1 → 2] → 3 → 4 → 5        groupPrev = dummy, kth = 2, groupNext = 3
dummy → [2 → 1] → 3 → 4 → 5        groupPrev = 1 (old first, now the tail)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Reverse nodes k at a time; a final group shorter than k stays as is. 1..5, k=2 gives 2→1→4→3→5. */
public final class ReverseKGroup {
    private ReverseKGroup() {}

    /** Recursive: check k nodes exist, reverse them, attach the recursively solved rest. O(n), O(n/k) stack. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode head, int k) {
        ListNode probe = head;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            if (probe == null) return head;                  // fewer than k left: leave untouched
            probe = probe.next;
        }
        ListNode prev = recursive(probe, k), curr = head;    // prev starts as the solved remainder
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            ListNode next = curr.next;
            curr.next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = next;
        }
        return prev;
    }

    /** Iterative: for each full group, reverse in place and stitch between groupPrev and the next group. O(1) space. */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode head, int k) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), groupPrev = dummy;
        while (true) {
            ListNode kth = groupPrev;
            for (int i = 0; i < k && kth != null; i++) kth = kth.next;
            if (kth == null) break;                          // not a full group
            ListNode groupNext = kth.next, prev = groupNext, curr = groupPrev.next;
            while (curr != groupNext) {                      // reverse, pointing the first node at groupNext
                ListNode next = curr.next;
                curr.next = prev;
                prev = curr;
                curr = next;
            }
            ListNode oldFirst = groupPrev.next;              // becomes the group's tail
            groupPrev.next = kth;
            groupPrev = oldFirst;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time, since each node is reversed once. O(1) extra space iteratively, or O(n/k) stack recursively.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: k = 1 (no change). k = n (a full reversal). k > n (no change). The length is an exact multiple of k.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head. 1→2→3→4→5 → 5→4→3→2→1. Follow-up: reverse only positions left..right (LeetCode 92).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output 1→2→3→4→5 5→4→3→2→1 1 1 empty empty

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: May I modify the input, or should I build a new list? (In place is expected.) Is the list possibly cyclic? (Assume not.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Reversing means every arrow a → b becomes b → a, and the old tail becomes the head.
  2. Brute force: push every node on a stack and pop them to relink. That's correct but uses O(n) memory.
  3. Insight: you only need the previous node to flip the current arrow. The danger is losing the rest of the list when you overwrite curr.next, so save it first.
  4. Pattern: three pointers prev, curr and next, flipping one arrow per step.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Stack
docs.text: Push all nodes, then pop to rebuild the chain. Remember tail.next = null, or the old head still points forward and you get a cycle. O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Iterative three pointers (optimal)
docs.text:
1. prev = null, curr = head.
  2. While curr != null: next = curr.next, curr.next = prev, prev = curr, curr = next.
  3. Return prev.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Recursive
docs.text:
• Base case: 0 or 1 node, so return it.
  • Trust the call: newHead = reverse(head.next) reverses everything after me. My old next is now the tail of that reversed part.
  • My job: head.next.next = head (that tail points back to me), then head.next = null.

docs.title: Dry run (iterative, 1→2→3)
docs.text: Step prev curr Links after the step 0 null 1 1→2→3 1 1 2 null←1  2→3 2 2 3 null←1←2  3 3 3 null null←1←2←3 → return 3

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Reverse 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 with three pointers
  1. prev = null (nothing reversed yet), curr = head.
  2. Save next = curr.next (node 2) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  3. Flip: node 1 now points to null.
  4. Advance both: prev = node 1, curr = node 2.
  5. Save next = curr.next (node 3) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  6. Flip: node 2 now points to node 1.
  7. Advance both: prev = node 2, curr = node 3.
  8. Save next = curr.next (node 4) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  9. Flip: node 3 now points to node 2.
  10. Advance both: prev = node 3, curr = node 4.
  11. Save next = curr.next (node null) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  12. Flip: node 4 now points to node 3.
  13. Advance both: prev = node 4, curr = null.
  14. curr is null, so every arrow is flipped. prev (node 4) is the new head: 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head. 1→2→3 becomes 3→2→1. */
public final class ReverseLinkedList {
    private ReverseLinkedList() {}

    /** Brute force: push nodes on a stack, pop to relink. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static ListNode withStack(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null) return null;
        Deque<ListNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) stack.push(n);
        ListNode newHead = stack.pop(), tail = newHead;
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) tail = tail.next = stack.pop();
        tail.next = null;                                    // old head must now point nowhere
        return newHead;
    }

    /** Optimal: three pointers (prev, curr, next). Flip one arrow per step. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode head) {
        ListNode prev = null, curr = head;
        while (curr != null) {
            ListNode next = curr.next;                       // 1. save the rest
            curr.next = prev;                                // 2. flip the arrow
            prev = curr;                                     // 3. advance prev
            curr = next;                                     // 4. advance curr
        }
        return prev;
    }

    /** Recursive: reverse the rest, then hook the old next back to me. O(n) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return head; // base case: 0 or 1 node
        ListNode newHead = recursive(head.next);
        head.next.next = head;                               // the node after me now points back to me
        head.next = null;
        return newHead;
    }

    /** Follow-up: reverse only positions left..right (1-based). One pass. */
    public static ListNode reverseBetween(ListNode head, int left, int right) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), before = dummy;
        for (int i = 1; i < left; i++) before = before.next;
        ListNode curr = before.next;
        for (int i = 0; i < right - left; i++) {             // move curr.next to the front of the segment
            ListNode moved = curr.next;
            curr.next = moved.next;
            moved.next = before.next;
            before.next = moved;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }
}

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Sort a singly linked list in O(n log n) time. Follow-up: use O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output 4→2→1→3 1→2→3→4 -1→5→3→4→0 -1→0→3→4→5 empty empty

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Stable? The merge sorts here are stable: equal values keep their original order (the tests check this with node identity).
  • Can I copy values into an array? It is allowed as a baseline, but it is O(n) space.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Baseline: copy the values out, sort, write them back. O(n log n), but O(n) space and arguably cheating.
  2. Which sort suits a list? Quicksort needs random access for good pivots. Heapsort needs indexes. Merge sort only needs "split" and "merge", and merging two lists is just relinking with no extra array. Linked lists are merge sort's best case.
  3. Top-down: find the middle (slow/fast), cut, sort both halves recursively, merge. O(log n) recursion stack.
  4. Bottom-up for O(1): skip the recursion. Merge runs of size 1, then 2, then 4…, walking the list each round and relinking merged runs behind a tail pointer.

docs.title: Bottom-up rounds: 4→2→1→3
docs.text: size runs merged list after the round 1 (4)(2) → 2,4 · (1)(3) → 1,3 2→4→1→3 2 (2,4)(1,3) → 1,2,3,4 1→2→3→4

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Sort a linked list in O(n log n). Linked lists favour MERGE sort: merging needs no extra array, only relinking. */
public final class SortList {
    private SortList() {}

    /** Brute force: copy values out, sort the array, write them back. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static ListNode viaArray(ListNode head) {
        List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) vals.add(n.val);
        vals.sort(null);
        ListNode n = head;
        for (int v : vals) { n.val = v; n = n.next; }
        return head;
    }

    /** Insertion sort by relinking. O(n²) worst case, O(1) space, stable. Good for nearly sorted lists. */
    public static ListNode insertionSort(ListNode head) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(Integer.MIN_VALUE);
        while (head != null) {
            ListNode next = head.next, p = dummy;
            while (p.next != null && p.next.val <= head.val) p = p.next;   // "<=" keeps it stable
            head.next = p.next;
            p.next = head;
            head = next;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Top-down merge sort: split at the middle (slow/fast), sort halves recursively, merge. O(n log n), O(log n) stack. */
    public static ListNode mergeSortTopDown(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;      // base case: 0 or 1 node is sorted
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head.next;                   // fast starts one ahead → slow ends at left-middle
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }
        ListNode right = slow.next;
        slow.next = null;                                         // cut into two lists
        return merge(mergeSortTopDown(head), mergeSortTopDown(right));
    }

    /**
     * Bottom-up merge sort: merge runs of size 1, 2, 4, ... iteratively. O(n log n) time and TRUE O(1) extra space —
     * the answer to "can you do it without recursion?".
     */
    public static ListNode mergeSortBottomUp(ListNode head) {
        int n = 0;
        for (ListNode x = head; x != null; x = x.next) n++;
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
        for (int size = 1; size < n; size *= 2) {
            ListNode prevTail = dummy, cur = dummy.next;
            while (cur != null) {
                ListNode left = cur;
                ListNode right = split(left, size);               // left has ≤ size nodes
                cur = split(right, size);                         // right has ≤ size nodes; cur = rest
                prevTail.next = merge(left, right);
                while (prevTail.next != null) prevTail = prevTail.next;
            }
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Cut after `size` nodes; return the head of the remainder. */
    private static ListNode split(ListNode head, int size) {
        for (int i = 1; head != null && i < size; i++) head = head.next;
        if (head == null) return null;
        ListNode rest = head.next;
        head.next = null;
        return rest;
    }

    /** Merge two sorted lists; ties take from `a` first, which keeps the sort stable. */
    private static ListNode merge(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), t = dummy;
        while (a != null && b != null) {
            if (a.val <= b.val) { t.next = a; a = a.next; }
            else { t.next = b; b = b.next; }
            t = t.next;
        }
        t.next = a != null ? a : b;
        return dummy.next;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Copy to array O(n log n) O(n) Insertion sort (relink) O(n²) O(1) Merge sort, top-down O(n log n) O(log n) stack Merge sort, bottom-up O(n log n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• In top-down, start fast at head.next. With fast = head, a 2-node list never splits and recursion never ends.
  • Forgetting to cut (slow.next = null) before recursing.
  • Use a.val <= b.val in the merge (not <) to keep the sort stable.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
Stack (LIFO) Queue (FIFO) Deque Order last in, first out first in, first out both ends Java type ArrayDeque (push/pop/peek) ArrayDeque (offer/poll/peek) ArrayDeque (offerFirst/pollLast…) Typical use undo, recursion, matching brackets, "most recent unresolved" BFS, scheduling, buffering sliding window, monotonic queue

Don't use java.util.Stack

It extends Vector, so every call is synchronised and it allows index access, which breaks the abstraction. Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>() is the modern choice.

docs.title: When should you think "stack"?
docs.text:
1. Something must be matched with the most recent unmatched thing: brackets, tags, operators.
  2. You need the nearest greater or smaller element to the left or right. That's a monotonic stack.
  3. You're converting recursion to iteration. The call stack becomes an explicit stack.
  4. You're evaluating or parsing expressions: postfix, infix, calculators.

docs.title: The monotonic stack template (memorise it)
docs.text:
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();        // indexes; values kept monotonic
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < a[i]) {   // a[i] resolves everyone smaller
        int j = st.pop();
        // a[i] is the NEXT GREATER of a[j]; st.peek() (if any) is the PREVIOUS GREATER-OR-EQUAL of a[j]
    }
    st.push(i);
}
// every index is pushed once and popped at most once → O(n) total, despite the nested while

docs.title: Implement a stack with an array
docs.text: Easy Design Amortised analysis

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build an int stack with push, pop, peek, isEmpty and size, each in O(1). Variant (GfG): implement two stacks in one array without wasting space.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Fixed capacity or growable? What should pop on an empty stack do (throw, or return a sentinel)? Generic or int only?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A stack only ever touches one end, and the end of an array is O(1) to read and write.
  2. Keep top = the index of the top element, with -1 meaning empty. push is data[++top] = x, and pop is data[top--].
  3. Growing: when the array is full, copy it into one twice as big. A single resize costs O(n), but n pushes cost at most n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n copies in total, so push is amortised O(1). Growing by a constant (+10) would make it O(n).
  4. Two stacks in one array: grow stack 1 from the left and stack 2 from the right. Overflow happens only when the two tops meet, so no slot is wasted. Splitting the array in half would waste space whenever one stack is much smaller.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/**
 * Stack backed by a growable int array. push/pop/peek are O(1) (push is amortised O(1) because of doubling).
 * Also shows the classic "two stacks in one array" variant.
 */
public final class ArrayStack {
    private int[] data;
    private int top = -1;                                    // index of the top element; -1 = empty

    public ArrayStack() {
        this(8);
    }

    public ArrayStack(int initialCapacity) {
        data = new int[Math.max(1, initialCapacity)];
    }

    public void push(int x) {
        if (top + 1 == data.length) data = Arrays.copyOf(data, data.length * 2);   // double: amortised O(1)
        data[++top] = x;
    }

    public int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack underflow");
        return data[top--];
    }

    public int peek() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
        return data[top];
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return top == -1;
    }

    public int size() {
        return top + 1;
    }

    /** Two stacks sharing one fixed array: stack 1 grows from the left, stack 2 from the right. */
    public static final class TwoStacks {
        private final int[] arr;
        private int top1, top2;

        public TwoStacks(int capacity) {
            arr = new int[capacity];
            top1 = -1;
            top2 = capacity;
        }

        public void push1(int x) {
            if (top1 + 1 == top2) throw new IllegalStateException("overflow");   // the two tops met
            arr[++top1] = x;
        }

        public void push2(int x) {
            if (top1 + 1 == top2) throw new IllegalStateException("overflow");
            arr[--top2] = x;
        }

        public int pop1() {
            if (top1 < 0) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return arr[top1--];
        }

        public int pop2() {
            if (top2 == arr.length) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return arr[top2++];
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Operation Time push O(1) amortised (O(n) on a resize) pop / peek / isEmpty / size O(1)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Underflow (pop on empty) must be handled explicitly. With object stacks, null out the popped slot (data[top--] = null) or the garbage collector can't free it. This is a classic memory leak from Effective Java.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: A linked-list stack (push and pop at the head) never needs a resize, but each node carries a pointer, so it uses more memory.

docs.title: Asteroid collision
docs.text: Medium Stack simulation Amortised O(n)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Each integer is an asteroid: the absolute value is its size, and the sign is its direction (positive moves right, negative moves left). All move at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one explodes. If they are the same size, both explode. Return the survivors in order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output Why [5, 10, -5] [5, 10] −5 hits 10 and explodes [8, -8] [] equal sizes, both explode [10, 2, -5] [10] −5 destroys 2, then loses to 10 [-2, -1, 1, 2] unchanged left-movers on the left never meet right-movers on the right

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Do two asteroids moving in the same direction ever collide? No, they have the same speed.
  • What about [-1, 1]? They move apart, so nothing collides. Only (+ on the left, − on the right) collides.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: find the first adjacent (+, −) pair, resolve it, and repeat until none remain. Correct but O(n²).
  2. Who can a new asteroid hit? A right-mover never hits anything on its left. A left-mover can only hit the right-movers that are currently the rightmost survivors, and it hits them in reverse order. "Most recent first" means a stack.
  3. Algorithm: for each x, while x is moving left and the stack top is moving right, fight. If the top is smaller, pop it and keep going. If they are equal, pop it and x dies too. If the top is bigger, x dies. Push x if it survives.
  4. Why O(n): each asteroid is pushed once and popped at most once.

docs.title: Dry run: [10, 2, -5]
docs.text: x stack before fights stack after 10 [] — [10] 2 [10] — [10, 2] −5 [10, 2] 2 < 5 → pop 2. 10 > 5 → −5 dies [10]

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Asteroids move along a line: |x| is size, sign is direction (+ right, − left), all at the same speed.
 * When a right-mover meets a left-mover, the smaller explodes; equal sizes both explode. Return the survivors.
 * Only "right-mover on the left, left-mover on the right" ever collide.
 */
public final class AsteroidCollision {
    private AsteroidCollision() {}

    /** Brute force: repeatedly find the first adjacent (+, −) pair and resolve it, until none remain. O(n²). */
    public static int[] simulate(int[] asteroids) {
        List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int x : asteroids) a.add(x);
        boolean changed = true;
        while (changed) {
            changed = false;
            for (int i = 0; i + 1 < a.size(); i++) {
                int l = a.get(i), r = a.get(i + 1);
                if (l > 0 && r < 0) {                   // a collision
                    if (l > -r) a.remove(i + 1);
                    else if (l < -r) a.remove(i);
                    else { a.remove(i + 1); a.remove(i); }
                    changed = true;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        return a.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: a stack of survivors so far. A new left-mover fights the right-movers on top of the stack until it dies,
     * ties, or runs out of opponents. Each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once: O(n).
     */
    public static int[] stack(int[] asteroids) {
        Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int x : asteroids) {
            boolean alive = true;
            while (alive && x < 0 && !st.isEmpty() && st.peek() > 0) {
                int top = st.peek();
                if (top < -x) st.pop();                  // top explodes; x keeps flying left
                else if (top == -x) { st.pop(); alive = false; }   // both explode
                else alive = false;                       // x explodes
            }
            if (alive) st.push(x);
        }
        int[] out = new int[st.size()];
        for (int i = out.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) out[i] = st.pop();   // stack top is the rightmost survivor
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Repeated adjacent resolution O(n²) O(n) Stack O(n) amortised O(n)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pushing a negative onto a stack whose top is also negative is fine: they never meet.
  • A survivor left-mover can destroy several right-movers in a row ([1, 2, 3, -4] → [-4]), so fight in a loop, not with a single if.
  • Popping the stack gives the survivors in reverse. Fill the output array from the back.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Evaluate a string expression with non-negative integers, + - * /, parentheses, spaces and unary minus. Do not use eval or a script engine. "2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)" = 21, "-(2+3)" = −5.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Integer division truncating toward zero? (Yes.) Unary minus allowed? (Yes.) Is the input always valid? (Still, report errors cleanly.) Overflow? (Compute in long.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Only +, − and parentheses (LeetCode 224): keep a running result and the current sign. At (, push (result, sign) and start fresh. At ), combine with outerSign × inner + outerResult. This is one pass with one stack.

  2. With * and /: precedence matters. The cleanest senior answer is to write the grammar, so precedence falls out of the structure:

    • expr := term (('+'|'-') term)*
    • term := factor (('*'|'/') factor)*
    • factor := number | '(' expr ')' | '-' factor

    Each rule becomes one method. This is recursive descent, which is how real compilers parse. 3. Two stacks (Dijkstra): one for operands and one for operators. Apply an operator whenever the one on top has ≥ precedence. It's equivalent to shunting-yard and evaluating in the same pass.

docs.title: How recursive descent handles 2+3*4
docs.text:
expr
├── term → factor 2
├── '+'
└── term
    ├── factor 3
    ├── '*'
    └── factor 4        → 3*4 is computed inside term before expr adds it: 2 + 12 = 14

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Evaluate an infix string with non-negative integers, + - * /, parentheses, unary minus and spaces.
 * "2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)" = 21. Division truncates toward zero. Arithmetic is done in long, result cast to int.
 */
public final class BasicCalculator {
    private BasicCalculator() {}

    /**
     * Calculator I (only + - and parentheses, LeetCode 224): one running result, a sign, and a stack that saves
     * (result, sign) when entering a parenthesis. O(n).
     */
    public static int plusMinusParens(String s) {
        Deque<Long> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        long result = 0, number = 0;
        int sign = 1;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                number = number * 10 + (c - '0');
            } else if (c == '+' || c == '-') {
                result += sign * number;
                number = 0;
                sign = c == '+' ? 1 : -1;
            } else if (c == '(') {
                stack.push(result);                          // save the outer state
                stack.push((long) sign);
                result = 0;
                sign = 1;
            } else if (c == ')') {
                result += sign * number;
                number = 0;
                result = stack.pop() * result + stack.pop(); // outerSign * inner + outerResult
            }
        }
        return (int) (result + sign * number);
    }

    /**
     * Full calculator (LeetCode 772) by recursive descent — the grammar IS the precedence:
     *   expr   := term (('+'|'-') term)*
     *   term   := factor (('*'|'/') factor)*
     *   factor := number | '(' expr ')' | '-' factor
     */
    public static int evaluate(String s) {
        Parser p = new Parser(s.replace(" ", ""));
        long v = p.expr();
        if (p.pos != p.s.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected '" + p.s.charAt(p.pos) + "'");
        return (int) v;
    }

    private static final class Parser {
        final String s;
        int pos;

        Parser(String s) {
            this.s = s;
        }

        long expr() {
            long v = term();
            while (pos < s.length() && (peek() == '+' || peek() == '-')) {
                v = s.charAt(pos++) == '+' ? v + term() : v - term();
            }
            return v;
        }

        long term() {
            long v = factor();
            while (pos < s.length() && (peek() == '*' || peek() == '/')) {
                v = s.charAt(pos++) == '*' ? v * factor() : v / factor();
            }
            return v;
        }

        long factor() {
            if (pos >= s.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected end");
            char c = peek();
            if (c == '-') {
                pos++;
                return -factor();                            // unary minus
            }
            if (c == '(') {
                pos++;
                long v = expr();
                if (pos >= s.length() || s.charAt(pos++) != ')') throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing )");
                return v;
            }
            if (!Character.isDigit(c)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected '" + c + "'");
            long n = 0;
            while (pos < s.length() && Character.isDigit(peek())) n = n * 10 + (s.charAt(pos++) - '0');
            return n;
        }

        char peek() {
            return s.charAt(pos);
        }
    }

    /**
     * Two-stack version (operands + operators), the classic Dijkstra approach: apply an operator whenever the one
     * on the stack has ≥ precedence. Handles + - * / and parentheses (binary operators only).
     */
    public static int twoStacks(String s) {
        Deque<Long> nums = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
        String e = s.replace(" ", "");
        for (int i = 0; i < e.length(); i++) {
            char c = e.charAt(i);
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                long n = 0;
                while (i < e.length() && Character.isDigit(e.charAt(i))) n = n * 10 + (e.charAt(i++) - '0');
                i--;
                nums.push(n);
            } else if (c == '(') {
                ops.push(c);
            } else if (c == ')') {
                while (ops.peek() != '(') apply(nums, ops.pop());
                ops.pop();
            } else {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '(' && prec(ops.peek()) >= prec(c)) apply(nums, ops.pop());
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) apply(nums, ops.pop());
        return (int) (long) nums.pop();
    }

    private static void apply(Deque<Long> nums, char op) {
        long b = nums.pop(), a = nums.pop();
        nums.push(switch (op) {
            case '+' -> a + b;
            case '-' -> a - b;
            case '*' -> a * b;
            default -> a / b;
        });
    }

    private static int prec(char op) {
        return op == '+' || op == '-' ? 1 : 2;
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time for all three approaches. Space is O(n) in the worst case (the nesting depth).

docs.text: You have to handle precedence, associativity, unary minus, multi-digit numbers, whitespace and error reporting at the same time, and explain your choice of design. Being able to state the grammar is the clearest sign of seniority here.

docs.title: Daily temperatures
docs.text: Medium Monotonic stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For each day, return how many days you wait for a warmer temperature, or 0 if none comes. [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73] → [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. This is next greater element, except the answer is a distance. So the stack stores indexes, not values.
  2. Keep days that are still waiting on the stack. Their temperatures are decreasing from bottom to top, because a warmer day would already have resolved them.
  3. When today is warmer than the top, pop it and record today − thatDay. Repeat, then push today.
  4. O(1) extra space trick: walk from right to left. To find day i's answer, start at j = i + 1 and, while t[j] ≤ t[i], jump j += out[j], which skips days already known to be colder.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Daily temperatures with a monotonic stack of indexes
  1. The stack holds days still waiting for a warmer day, temperatures decreasing upwards.
  2. Day 0 (73°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  3. Day 1 (74°) is warmer than day 0 (73°) → wait 1. Pop them.
  4. Day 1 (74°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  5. Day 2 (75°) is warmer than day 1 (74°) → wait 1. Pop them.
  6. Day 2 (75°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  7. Day 3 (71°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  8. Day 4 (69°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  9. Day 5 (72°) is warmer than day 4 (69°) → wait 1, day 3 (71°) → wait 2. Pop them.
  10. Day 5 (72°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  11. Day 6 (76°) is warmer than day 5 (72°) → wait 1, day 2 (75°) → wait 4. Pop them.
  12. Day 6 (76°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  13. Day 7 (73°) now waits for its own warmer day: push it.
  14. Days 6 and 7 are never resolved, so they stay 0. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature (0 if never). [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73] → [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0]. */
public final class DailyTemperatures {
    private DailyTemperatures() {}

    /** Brute force: scan forward for each day. O(n^2). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] t) {
        int[] out = new int[t.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
            for (int j = i + 1; j < t.length; j++) {
                if (t[j] > t[i]) {
                    out[i] = j - i;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Monotonic stack of INDEXES (we need distances, not values). Each index pushed/popped once → O(n). */
    public static int[] monotonicStack(int[] t) {
        int[] out = new int[t.length];
        Deque<Integer> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();         // indexes with decreasing temperatures
        for (int i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && t[waiting.peek()] < t[i]) {
                int day = waiting.pop();
                out[day] = i - day;                          // today is the first warmer day for `day`
            }
            waiting.push(i);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * O(1) extra space: walk right to left and jump using answers already computed
     * (if day j is not warmer, the next candidate is j + out[j]).
     */
    public static int[] backwardJumps(int[] t) {
        int n = t.length;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
            int j = i + 1;
            while (t[j] <= t[i] && out[j] != 0) j += out[j];
            out[i] = t[j] > t[i] ? j - i : 0;
        }
        return out;
    }
}
