docs.title: Decode string
docs.text: Hard Two stacks Recursive descent Nesting

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Decode a string where k[encoded] means repeat encoded exactly k times. Brackets nest.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output 3[a]2[bc] aaabcbc 3[a2[c]] accaccacc 2[abc]3[cd]ef abcabccdcdcdef 10[a] aaaaaaaaaa (multi-digit counts)

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Is the input always valid? Yes: balanced brackets, and digits only appear as counts.
  • Can letters appear outside brackets? Yes (abc3[cd]xyz).
  • Can k be 0, or have several digits? k ≥ 1, and it can have several digits.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: find an innermost k[...] (no [ inside it), replace it with its expansion, and repeat. Easy to reason about, but every replacement rebuilds the whole string.
  2. Nesting means a stack. At [ we start a new inner string, and we must remember two things to resume the outer one later: the count k, and the outer partial string built so far. Push both.
  3. At ]: pop the count and the outer string, then outer.append(inner.repeat(k)). That result becomes the current string again.
  4. Recursive descent is the same idea with the call stack: parse() reads letters and k[ … ] groups until it reaches ], recursing for the inside. It mirrors the grammar seq := (letter | number '[' seq ']')*.

docs.title: Dry run (two stacks): 3[a2[c]]
docs.text: char counts outer strings cur 3 k = 3 [ 3 "" "" a 3 "" a 2 k = 2 [ 3 2 "" a "" c 3 2 "" a c ] 3 "" a + cc = acc ] "" + acc×3 = accaccacc

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Decode k[encoded] repeatedly: "3[a2[c]]" → "accaccacc". Input is valid: digits only appear as repeat counts,
 * brackets are balanced, k ≥ 1 (may have several digits, e.g. "10[a]").
 */
public final class DecodeString {
    private DecodeString() {}

    /** Two stacks: counts and the partial string built before each '['. O(output) time. */
    public static String twoStacks(String s) {
        Deque<Integer> counts = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Deque<StringBuilder> outer = new ArrayDeque<>();
        StringBuilder cur = new StringBuilder();
        int k = 0;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                k = k * 10 + (c - '0');                 // multi-digit counts
            } else if (c == '[') {
                counts.push(k);                          // remember how often to repeat what comes next
                outer.push(cur);                         // and what came before it
                cur = new StringBuilder();
                k = 0;
            } else if (c == ']') {
                String inner = cur.toString();
                cur = outer.pop();
                cur.append(inner.repeat(counts.pop()));  // splice the repeated block back into its parent
            } else {
                cur.append(c);
            }
        }
        return cur.toString();
    }

    /** Recursive descent: decode(i) parses until the matching ']' and returns where it stopped. Mirrors the grammar. */
    public static String recursive(String s) {
        int[] pos = {0};
        return parse(s, pos);
    }

    // grammar: seq := ( letter | number '[' seq ']' )*
    private static String parse(String s, int[] pos) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (pos[0] < s.length() && s.charAt(pos[0]) != ']') {
            char c = s.charAt(pos[0]);
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                int k = 0;
                while (Character.isDigit(s.charAt(pos[0]))) k = k * 10 + (s.charAt(pos[0]++) - '0');
                pos[0]++;                                // skip '['
                String inner = parse(s, pos);
                pos[0]++;                                // skip ']'
                sb.append(inner.repeat(k));
            } else {
                sb.append(c);
                pos[0]++;
            }
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    /** Brute force: repeatedly expand the innermost k[...] (one with no '[' inside) until none remain. */
    public static String innermostFirst(String s) {
        while (s.indexOf('[') >= 0) {
            int close = s.indexOf(']');
            int open = s.lastIndexOf('[', close);        // innermost: the '[' closest before the first ']'
            int start = open;
            while (start > 0 && Character.isDigit(s.charAt(start - 1))) start--;
            int k = Integer.parseInt(s.substring(start, open));
            s = s.substring(0, start) + s.substring(open + 1, close).repeat(k) + s.substring(close + 1);
        }
        return s;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Innermost-first rewriting O(depth · output) O(output) Two stacks O(output) O(output + depth) Recursive descent O(output) O(output + depth) recursion

The output can be exponentially longer than the input (2[2[2[…]]]), so "linear in the output" is the best possible.

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Multi-digit counts: accumulate k = k * 10 + digit. Don't read one char.
  • Reset k = 0 after pushing it at [.
  • String.repeat (Java 11+) beats a manual loop and avoids O(n²) concatenation.

docs.title: Evaluate postfix (Reverse Polish Notation)
docs.text: Medium Stack Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Evaluate a postfix expression of integers with + - * / (division truncates toward zero). ["2","1","+","3","*"] = (2 + 1) × 3 = 9 · ["4","13","5","/","+"] = 4 + 13/5 = 6.

docs.title: Why postfix exists
docs.text: Postfix needs no parentheses and no precedence rules: the order of the tokens is the order of evaluation. Compilers and HP calculators use it, and infix → postfix is how you get there.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. When you read an operator, its operands are the two most recent results. "Most recent" means a stack.
  2. Push a number. For an operator, pop right first, then left, and push left op right. The order matters for − and /.
  3. At the end, exactly one value must remain. Anything else means the expression is malformed.
  4. Recursive view: read the expression backwards. An operator's right operand is the sub-expression just before it, and its left operand is the one before that.

docs.title: Dry run (2 1 + 3 *)
docs.text: Token Stack (top on the right) 2 2 1 2 1 + 3 3 3 3 * 9

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Evaluate a postfix (Reverse Polish) expression of integers with + - * /. Division truncates toward zero.
 * ["2","1","+","3","*"] = (2 + 1) * 3 = 9. Invalid input throws IllegalArgumentException.
 */
public final class EvaluateRpn {
    private EvaluateRpn() {}

    /** Operand stack: numbers are pushed; an operator pops two, applies, pushes the result. O(n). */
    public static int evaluate(String[] tokens) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (String t : tokens) {
            if (t.length() == 1 && "+-*/".contains(t)) {
                if (stack.size() < 2) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not enough operands for " + t);
                int right = stack.pop(), left = stack.pop();    // order matters for - and /
                stack.push(switch (t.charAt(0)) {
                    case '+' -> left + right;
                    case '-' -> left - right;
                    case '*' -> left * right;
                    default -> left / right;
                });
            } else {
                stack.push(Integer.parseInt(t));             // handles negatives like "-11"
            }
        }
        if (stack.size() != 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed expression");
        return stack.pop();
    }

    /** Recursive: read the expression from the END — an operator's operands are the two sub-expressions before it. */
    public static int recursive(String[] tokens) {
        int[] pos = {tokens.length - 1};
        int result = eval(tokens, pos);
        if (pos[0] != -1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed expression");
        return result;
    }

    private static int eval(String[] t, int[] pos) {
        if (pos[0] < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not enough operands");
        String tok = t[pos[0]--];
        if (tok.length() == 1 && "+-*/".contains(tok)) {
            int right = eval(t, pos), left = eval(t, pos);   // right operand is nearer the operator
            return switch (tok.charAt(0)) {
                case '+' -> left + right;
                case '-' -> left - right;
                case '*' -> left * right;
                default -> left / right;
            };
        }
        return Integer.parseInt(tok);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) space, both with the explicit stack and recursively.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: "-11" is a number, not an operator, so check length() == 1 before treating a token as an operator. Popping the operands in the wrong order gives 1 − 2 instead of 2 − 1.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Convert an infix expression (single-character operands, + - * / ^, parentheses) to postfix. a+b*(c^d-e)^(f+g*h)-i → abcd^e-fgh*+^*+i-. Bonus: convert to prefix.

docs.title: Rules you must state
docs.text: Operator Precedence Associativity ^ 3 right (a^b^c = a^(b^c)) * / 2 left + - 1 left

docs.title: Thinking process (Dijkstra's shunting-yard)
docs.text:
1. Operands go straight to the output, because their order never changes between infix and postfix.
  2. Operators wait on a stack until we know nothing with higher priority still needs to be applied first.
  3. When a new operator c arrives, pop to the output every operator on the stack that must run before it: higher precedence, or equal precedence and c is left-associative. Then push c.
  4. ( is pushed as a wall. ) pops to the output until the matching (, then discards both.
  5. At the end, pop everything that's left. A stray ( means the parentheses were unbalanced.

docs.title: Infix → prefix
docs.text: Reverse the string, swap ( and ), run the same algorithm with associativity flipped, then reverse the output. (A-B/C)*(A/K-L) → *-A/BC-/AKL.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Convert an infix expression with single-letter/digit operands, + - * / ^ and parentheses to postfix.
 * "a+b*(c^d-e)^(f+g*h)-i" → "abcd^e-fgh*+^*+i-". ^ is right-associative. Spaces are ignored.
 */
public final class InfixToPostfix {
    private InfixToPostfix() {}

    /** Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm with an operator stack. O(n). */
    public static String convert(String infix) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : infix.toCharArray()) {
            if (c == ' ') continue;
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) {
                out.append(c);                               // operands go straight to the output
            } else if (c == '(') {
                ops.push(c);
            } else if (c == ')') {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '(') out.append(ops.pop());
                if (ops.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unbalanced )");
                ops.pop();                                   // discard '('
            } else {
                // pop operators that must be applied BEFORE c: higher precedence, or equal and left-associative
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '('
                        && (prec(ops.peek()) > prec(c) || (prec(ops.peek()) == prec(c) && c != '^'))) {
                    out.append(ops.pop());
                }
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) {
            char op = ops.pop();
            if (op == '(') throw new IllegalArgumentException("unbalanced (");
            out.append(op);
        }
        return out.toString();
    }

    /** Bonus: infix → prefix = reverse, swap parentheses, convert (treating ^ carefully), reverse. */
    public static String toPrefix(String infix) {
        StringBuilder rev = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = infix.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            char c = infix.charAt(i);
            rev.append(c == '(' ? ')' : c == ')' ? '(' : c);
        }
        // On the reversed string, + - * / become right-associative and ^ left-associative.
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : rev.toString().toCharArray()) {
            if (c == ' ') continue;
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) out.append(c);
            else if (c == '(') ops.push(c);
            else if (c == ')') {
                while (ops.peek() != '(') out.append(ops.pop());
                ops.pop();
            } else {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '('
                        && (prec(ops.peek()) > prec(c) || (prec(ops.peek()) == prec(c) && c == '^'))) {
                    out.append(ops.pop());
                }
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) out.append(ops.pop());
        return out.reverse().toString();
    }

    private static int prec(char op) {
        return switch (op) {
            case '+', '-' -> 1;
            case '*', '/' -> 2;
            case '^' -> 3;
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown operator " + op);
        };
    }
}

docs.title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
docs.text: Expert Monotonic stack Previous / next smaller

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given bar heights (each 1 wide), return the area of the largest rectangle under the histogram. [2,1,5,6,2,3] → 10 (height 5 across the bars 5 and 6).

        █
      █ █
      █ █   █
      █ █ █ █
  █   █ █ █ █
  █ █ █ █ █ █
  2 1 5 6 2 3

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Every optimal rectangle is limited by its shortest bar. So for each bar i, ask: "what is the widest rectangle in which bar i is the shortest?"
  2. That rectangle extends left until the previous smaller bar and right until the next smaller bar. Its area is h[i] × (nextSmaller − prevSmaller − 1).
  3. Brute force: expand left and right for each bar. That's O(n²).
  4. Two monotonic stacks compute every previous-smaller and next-smaller index in O(n). See next greater element.
  5. One pass: keep a stack of indexes with increasing heights. When a lower bar arrives at i, every taller bar popped has just found its right boundary (i), and its left boundary is the element below it on the stack. A sentinel bar of height 0 at the end flushes the stack.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Largest rectangle in a histogram of bar heights (width 1 each). [2,1,5,6,2,3] → 10 (bars 5,6). */
public final class LargestRectangleHistogram {
    private LargestRectangleHistogram() {}

    /** Brute force: for every bar as the shortest, expand left and right. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] h) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
            int l = i, r = i;
            while (l > 0 && h[l - 1] >= h[i]) l--;
            while (r < h.length - 1 && h[r + 1] >= h[i]) r++;
            best = Math.max(best, h[i] * (r - l + 1));
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Two passes of "previous/next smaller index" (monotonic stacks), then one pass for areas. O(n). */
    public static int nearestSmaller(int[] h) {
        int n = h.length;
        int[] left = new int[n], right = new int[n];         // first smaller index on each side (exclusive)
        Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] >= h[i]) st.pop();
            left[i] = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
            st.push(i);
        }
        st.clear();
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] >= h[i]) st.pop();
            right[i] = st.isEmpty() ? n : st.peek();
            st.push(i);
        }
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) best = Math.max(best, h[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1));
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal one pass: stack of indexes with increasing heights. When a lower bar arrives, every taller bar
     * on the stack has found its right boundary (i) and its left boundary is the element below it.
     * A sentinel height 0 at i == n flushes the stack. O(n).
     */
    public static int onePass(int[] h) {
        Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i <= h.length; i++) {
            int cur = i == h.length ? 0 : h[i];
            while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] > cur) {
                int height = h[st.pop()];
                int leftBoundary = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
                best = Math.max(best, height * (i - leftBoundary - 1));
            }
            st.push(i);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Follow-up: maximal rectangle of 1s in a binary matrix — each row is a histogram of column heights. */
    public static int maximalRectangle(char[][] grid) {
        if (grid.length == 0) return 0;
        int[] heights = new int[grid[0].length];
        int best = 0;
        for (char[] row : grid) {
            for (int c = 0; c < row.length; c++) heights[c] = row[c] == '1' ? heights[c] + 1 : 0;
            best = Math.max(best, onePass(heights));
        }
        return best;
    }
}

docs.title: Min stack in O(1)
docs.text: Medium Stack Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and getMin, all in O(1).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Naive: scan the stack in getMin. That's O(n).
  2. Tempting but wrong: keep a single min variable. After you pop the minimum, you don't know the previous minimum.
  3. Insight: a stack only changes at the top, so the minimum below any entry never changes while that entry exists. Store minSoFar alongside each value. getMin is then peek().minSoFar.
  4. Expert, O(1) extra space: keep one min field. When pushing a new minimum x, store the encoded value 2x − oldMin, which is always below x. On pop, a stored value below min means "this was a minimum push", and oldMin = 2·min − stored recovers the previous minimum. Use long so 2x − min can't overflow.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/** Stack with push, pop, top and getMin — all O(1). */
public final class MinStack {
    /** Each entry remembers the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed. */
    private record Entry(int value, int minSoFar) {}

    private final Deque<Entry> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void push(int x) {
        int min = stack.isEmpty() ? x : Math.min(x, stack.peek().minSoFar());
        stack.push(new Entry(x, min));
    }

    public int pop() {
        if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return stack.pop().value();                          // the entry below already knows its own min
    }

    public int top() {
        if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return stack.peek().value();
    }

    public int getMin() {
        if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return stack.peek().minSoFar();
    }

    /**
     * Expert variant: O(1) EXTRA space (one long for the min). When x is a new minimum we store an encoded
     * value 2x - oldMin (always < x), which lets pop recover the previous minimum.
     */
    public static final class Encoded {
        private final Deque<Long> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private long min;

        public void push(int x) {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) {
                stack.push((long) x);
                min = x;
            } else if (x < min) {
                stack.push(2L * x - min);                    // encoded flag: value < current min
                min = x;
            } else {
                stack.push((long) x);
            }
        }

        public int pop() {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            long y = stack.pop();
            if (y < min) {                                   // this slot held the min → restore the previous min
                int popped = (int) min;
                min = 2 * min - y;
                return popped;
            }
            return (int) y;
        }

        public int top() {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            long y = stack.peek();
            return (int) (y < min ? min : y);
        }

        public int getMin() {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return (int) min;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Next greater element
docs.text: Medium Monotonic stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For every element, find the first element to its right that is strictly greater, or −1. [4, 5, 2, 25, 7, 8] → [5, 25, 25, −1, 8, −1]. Variants: circular array (LeetCode 503), and previous smaller element.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each i, scan to the right. That's O(n²).
  2. Waste: scanning right from i, you pass elements that can never be anyone's answer. In … 3, 9 …, the 3 is hidden behind the 9 for every element to the left of both.
  3. Monotonic stack (right to left): keep only the useful candidates, which form a decreasing sequence. For a[i], pop every candidate ≤ a[i] (now useless), and the top is the answer. Then push a[i].
  4. Equivalent left-to-right view: the stack holds indexes still waiting for an answer. A new bigger value resolves every smaller waiting index.
  5. Circular: loop 2n times using i % n, and push only in the first lap.

Next greater element with a monotonic stack (right to left)
  1. Walk from the right. The stack holds candidates in decreasing order: anything smaller than a newcomer can never be anyone's answer again.
  2. i = 5: the stack is empty, so nothing to the right is bigger: out[5] = −1.
  3. Push 8: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  4. i = 4: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[4] = 8.
  5. Push 7: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  6. i = 3, a[i] = 25: pop 7, 8 (≤ 25). 25 is closer and at least as big, so they're useless from here on.
  7. i = 3: the stack is empty, so nothing to the right is bigger: out[3] = −1.
  8. Push 25: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  9. i = 2: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[2] = 25.
  10. Push 2: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  11. i = 1, a[i] = 5: pop 2 (≤ 5). 5 is closer and at least as big, so they're useless from here on.
  12. i = 1: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[1] = 25.
  13. Push 5: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  14. i = 0: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[0] = 5.
  15. Push 4: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  16. Done: [5, 25, 25, −1, 8, −1]. Every value is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Deque;

/** For each element, the first element to its RIGHT that is strictly greater; -1 if none. */
public final class NextGreaterElement {
    private NextGreaterElement() {}

    /** Brute force: scan right for every index. O(n^2). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            out[i] = -1;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) {
                if (a[j] > a[i]) {
                    out[i] = a[j];
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Monotonic stack, right to left: keep a stack of candidates in decreasing order. Pop everything
     * ≤ a[i] (it can never be the answer for anything further left, because a[i] is closer and bigger).
     * Each index is pushed and popped once → O(n).
     */
    public static int[] monotonicStack(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();           // values, decreasing from bottom to top
        for (int i = a.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() <= a[i]) stack.pop();
            out[i] = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek();
            stack.push(a[i]);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Left-to-right form: stack holds indexes still WAITING for their answer; a bigger value resolves them. */
    public static int[] leftToRight(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        Arrays.fill(out, -1);
        Deque<Integer> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && a[waiting.peek()] < a[i]) out[waiting.pop()] = a[i];
            waiting.push(i);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Circular array (LeetCode 503): walk the array twice, only push during the first lap. */
    public static int[] circular(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(out, -1);
        Deque<Integer> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
            int v = a[i % n];
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && a[waiting.peek()] < v) out[waiting.pop()] = v;
            if (i < n) waiting.push(i);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Mirror problem: previous smaller element (nearest strictly smaller to the LEFT). */
    public static int[] previousSmaller(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() >= a[i]) stack.pop();
            out[i] = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek();
            stack.push(a[i]);
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Queue using two stacks
docs.text: Easy Design Amortised O(1)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a FIFO queue (enqueue, dequeue, peek, isEmpty) using only stacks. Reverse variant: a LIFO stack using only a queue.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A stack reverses order. Two reversals cancel out, so pouring stack A into stack B puts the oldest element on top of B.
  2. Use in for every new element and out to serve the oldest.
  3. The key rule: refill out only when it is empty. If you pour while out still holds elements, newer elements land on top of older ones and FIFO order breaks.
  4. Each element is pushed to in once, moved once, and popped from out once. That's 3 operations, so dequeue is amortised O(1), even though a single dequeue can cost O(n).

docs.title: Stack using one queue
docs.text: After offer(x), rotate the queue size − 1 times (poll and re-offer) so x moves to the front. Push is O(n) and pop is O(1).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/**
 * FIFO queue built from two LIFO stacks. Every element is moved from {@code in} to {@code out} at most once,
 * so enqueue/dequeue are amortised O(1). Also: a stack built from one queue.
 */
public final class QueueUsingStacks {
    private final Deque<Integer> in = new ArrayDeque<>();    // receives new elements
    private final Deque<Integer> out = new ArrayDeque<>();   // serves the oldest element on top

    public void enqueue(int x) {
        in.push(x);
    }

    public int dequeue() {
        shiftIfNeeded();
        if (out.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("queue is empty");
        return out.pop();
    }

    public int peek() {
        shiftIfNeeded();
        if (out.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("queue is empty");
        return out.peek();
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return in.isEmpty() && out.isEmpty();
    }

    /** Only refill out when it is EMPTY — refilling earlier would bury older elements under newer ones. */
    private void shiftIfNeeded() {
        if (out.isEmpty()) while (!in.isEmpty()) out.push(in.pop());
    }

    /** Reverse direction: LIFO stack from ONE FIFO queue — rotate the queue after each push. push O(n), pop O(1). */
    public static final class StackUsingQueue {
        private final Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();

        public void push(int x) {
            q.offer(x);
            for (int i = 1; i < q.size(); i++) q.offer(q.poll());   // move older elements behind x
        }

        public int pop() {
            if (q.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return q.poll();
        }

        public int top() {
            if (q.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return q.peek();
        }

        public boolean isEmpty() {
            return q.isEmpty();
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Sliding window maximum
docs.text: Hard Monotonic deque Heap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the maximum of every contiguous window of size k. [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3 → [3,3,5,5,6,7].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: compute the max of each window. That's O(n·k).
  2. Heap: a max-heap of (value, index). Leave expired elements in the heap and discard the top only when its index has left the window (lazy deletion). That's O(n log n).
  3. Insight: when a new element x arrives, every older element smaller than x can never be a maximum again. x is bigger and stays in the window longer. Throw them away.
  4. What's left is decreasing from front to back, so the front is the max. Keep it in a deque of indexes:
    • pop the front if it slid out of the window (index ≤ i − k);
    • pop from the back while a[back] ≤ x;
    • push x at the back; once i ≥ k − 1, record a[front].

Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Sliding window maximum (k = 3) with a monotonic deque
  1. The deque keeps indexes with decreasing values: the front is always the window's max.
  2. i = 0 (1): push it.
  3. i = 1 (3): 3 dominates 1: they can never be a max again. push it.
  4. i = 2 (-1): push it. Window max = 3.
  5. i = 3 (-3): push it. Window max = 3.
  6. i = 4 (5): index 1 slid out of the window; 5 dominates -3, -1: they can never be a max again. push it. Window max = 5.
  7. i = 5 (3): push it. Window max = 5.
  8. i = 6 (6): 6 dominates 3, 5: they can never be a max again. push it. Window max = 6.
  9. i = 7 (7): 7 dominates 6: they can never be a max again. push it. Window max = 7.
  10. [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]. Every index enters and leaves the deque once: O(n), O(k) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Maximum of every window of size k. [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k=3 → [3,3,5,5,6,7]. */
public final class SlidingWindowMaximum {
    private SlidingWindowMaximum() {}

    /** Brute force: max of each window. O(n·k). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0 || k <= 0) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i + k <= a.length; i++) {
            int max = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
            for (int j = i; j < i + k; j++) max = Math.max(max, a[j]);
            out[i] = max;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Max-heap of (value, index); lazily discard tops that slid out. O(n log n). */
    public static int[] heap(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0 || k <= 0) return new int[0];
        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Integer.compare(y[0], x[0]));
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            pq.offer(new int[]{a[i], i});
            if (i >= k - 1) {
                while (pq.peek()[1] <= i - k) pq.poll();     // stale: index left the window
                out[i - k + 1] = pq.peek()[0];
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: monotonic deque of indexes with DECREASING values. Front = current max.
     * Pop back while smaller than the new element (they can never be a max again), pop front if it slid out.
     * Each index enters and leaves once → O(n), O(k) space.
     */
    public static int[] monotonicDeque(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0 || k <= 0) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();   // front fell out of the window
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) dq.pollLast(); // dominated by a[i]
            dq.offerLast(i);
            if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Stack using queues
docs.text: Easy Design Amortisation trade-off

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a LIFO stack (push, pop, top, isEmpty) using only queue operations: offer to the back, poll / peek from the front, size, isEmpty.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: push(1), push(2)  → top() = 2, pop() = 2, isEmpty() = false, pop() = 1, isEmpty() = true

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Which operation should be cheap? You can make push O(1) or pop O(1), but not both. Ask which one the caller uses more.
  • What happens on an empty pop? Here it throws NoSuchElementException, like ArrayDeque.pop().

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Mismatch: a queue hands back the oldest element and a stack the newest. We have to reverse the order somewhere.
  2. Option A, push-costly (one queue): after offer(x), rotate the n − 1 older elements from the front to the back. Now x is at the front, so pop and top are plain poll and peek.
  3. Option B, pop-costly (two queues): push is a plain offer. To pop, move all but the last element to a helper queue, take the last one, then swap the two queue references (no copying back). Cache the top so top() stays O(1).
  4. Compare with queue using stacks: there, the two-stack version is amortised O(1) because each element moves at most once. Here, elements move on every expensive operation, so the cost is really O(n). That asymmetry is a good thing to point out.

docs.title: Dry run (one queue)
docs.text: op queue (front → back) push 1 1 push 2 offer → 1 2, rotate 1 → 2 1 push 3 offer → 2 1 3, rotate 2 → 3 2 1 pop 3, queue 2 1

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;
import java.util.Queue;

/** LIFO stack built only from FIFO queue operations (offer, poll, peek, size, isEmpty). */
public final class StackUsingQueues {
    private StackUsingQueues() {}

    /** Common interface so tests can run every variant through the same script. */
    public interface IntStack {
        void push(int x);
        int pop();
        int top();
        boolean isEmpty();
    }

    /**
     * One queue, push-costly: after offering x, rotate the n-1 older elements behind it, so the queue front is always
     * the stack top. push O(n), pop/top O(1).
     */
    public static final class OneQueue implements IntStack {
        private final Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();

        @Override public void push(int x) {
            q.offer(x);
            for (int i = 1; i < q.size(); i++) q.offer(q.poll());   // move older elements behind x
        }

        @Override public int pop() {
            if (q.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
            return q.poll();
        }

        @Override public int top() {
            if (q.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
            return q.peek();
        }

        @Override public boolean isEmpty() {
            return q.isEmpty();
        }
    }

    /**
     * Two queues, pop-costly: push is a plain offer (O(1)). To pop, move all but the last element to the helper queue,
     * take the last one, then swap the queues' roles. pop O(n). The top is cached so top() is O(1).
     */
    public static final class TwoQueues implements IntStack {
        private Queue<Integer> main = new ArrayDeque<>(), helper = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private int top;

        @Override public void push(int x) {
            main.offer(x);
            top = x;
        }

        @Override public int pop() {
            if (main.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
            while (main.size() > 1) {
                top = main.poll();                 // the last one moved becomes the new top
                helper.offer(top);
            }
            int result = main.poll();
            Queue<Integer> t = main;               // swap roles instead of copying back
            main = helper;
            helper = t;
            return result;
        }

        @Override public int top() {
            if (main.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
            return top;
        }

        @Override public boolean isEmpty() {
            return main.isEmpty();
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• In the two-queue version, popping the last element leaves the cached top stale. Guard top() with isEmpty().
  • Copying the helper back into the main queue doubles the work. Swap the references instead.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• A hash table turns a key into an array index (hash(key) & (capacity − 1)), so put, get and contains are O(1) on average. Collisions share a bucket. Java chains them in a list and turns a long chain into a red-black tree (8+ nodes), which caps the worst case at O(log n).
  • The trade: you pay O(n) memory to turn "search" from O(n) into O(1). Most "brute force O(n²) → optimal O(n)" improvements in interviews are exactly this trade.
  • Contract: if a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Break it, and HashMap silently loses entries.

docs.title: Intersection of two arrays
docs.text: Easy HashSet Count map Two pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Unique (LeetCode 349): each common value once. [4,9,5] ∩ [9,4,9,8,4] → [4,9].
  2. With counts (LeetCode 350): each value as many times as it appears in both. [1,2,2,1] ∩ [2,2] → [2,2].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each value of a, search b. O(n·m).
  2. Unique: put a in a HashSet, then keep the values of b that are in it, collecting them in another set to remove repeats. O(n + m). Set.retainAll is the library version.
  3. With counts: a set loses the counts, so use a count map for a. While walking b, take a value only if its count is still > 0, then decrement.
  4. Both arrays sorted: two pointers, advancing the smaller side and taking the value when they're equal. O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * Intersection of two arrays.
 * {@link #unique}: each common value once (LeetCode 349). {@link #withCounts}: as many times as it appears in BOTH (LeetCode 350).
 * Results are sorted so they are easy to compare.
 */
public final class ArrayIntersection {
    private ArrayIntersection() {}

    /** Brute force: for each value of a, linear search in b. O(n·m). */
    public static int[] bruteForceUnique(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> out = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a)
            for (int y : b)
                if (x == y) {
                    out.add(x);
                    break;
                }
        return sorted(out);
    }

    /** Set of a, then keep values of b that are in it. O(n + m). */
    public static int[] unique(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> setA = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) setA.add(x);
        Set<Integer> out = new HashSet<>();
        for (int y : b) if (setA.contains(y)) out.add(y);
        return sorted(out);
    }

    /** Library: Set.retainAll does exactly "keep only what is also in the other collection". */
    public static int[] retainAll(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> setA = new HashSet<>(Arrays.stream(a).boxed().toList());
        setA.retainAll(Arrays.stream(b).boxed().toList());
        return sorted(setA);
    }

    /** With multiplicity: count a, then consume counts while walking b. O(n + m). */
    public static int[] withCounts(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) count.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int y : b) {
            int c = count.getOrDefault(y, 0);
            if (c > 0) {
                out.add(y);
                count.put(y, c - 1);                         // each copy in a can be used once
            }
        }
        return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sorted().toArray();
    }

    /** Both arrays already sorted: two pointers, O(1) extra space. Follow-up interviewers love. */
    public static int[] sortedTwoPointers(int[] a, int[] b) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int i = 0, j = 0;
        while (i < a.length && j < b.length) {
            if (a[i] < b[j]) i++;
            else if (a[i] > b[j]) j++;
            else {
                out.add(a[i]);
                i++;
                j++;
            }
        }
        return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    private static int[] sorted(Set<Integer> s) {
        return s.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sorted().toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Contains duplicate
docs.text: Easy HashSet Sorting Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if any value appears at least twice. [1,2,3,1] → true, [1,2,3,4] → false. Variant (LeetCode 219): two equal values whose indexes are at most k apart.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Can I modify the array (sorting in place saves memory)? How large is n? Do I need the duplicate itself or just yes/no?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: compare every pair. O(n²) time, O(1) space.
  2. Sort: equal values become neighbours, so one scan is enough. O(n log n) time, and O(1) extra if sorting in place is allowed.
  3. HashSet: remember what you've seen. Set.add already returns false for a repeat, so there's no separate contains call. O(n) time, O(n) space, and it exits early on the first duplicate.
  4. Within distance k: store the last index of each value. map.put returns the previous index, so you get it for free.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/** Does any value appear at least twice? Plus the "within distance k" variant (LeetCode 219). */
public final class ContainsDuplicate {
    private ContainsDuplicate() {}

    /** Brute force: compare every pair. O(n^2), O(1). */
    public static boolean bruteForce(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++)
                if (a[i] == a[j]) return true;
        return false;
    }

    /** Sort a copy: duplicates become neighbours. O(n log n), O(n) for the copy (O(1) if mutation is allowed). */
    public static boolean sorting(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        for (int i = 1; i < c.length; i++) if (c[i] == c[i - 1]) return true;
        return false;
    }

    /** Optimal: HashSet.add returns false when the value is already present. O(n), O(n). */
    public static boolean hashSet(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) if (!seen.add(x)) return true;      // early exit on the first repeat
        return false;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: distinct count smaller than total count. Always scans everything. */
    public static boolean streams(int[] a) {
        return Arrays.stream(a).distinct().count() < a.length;
    }

    /** Variant: two equal values whose indexes differ by at most k. Map value → last index. O(n). */
    public static boolean withinDistance(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> lastIndex = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            Integer prev = lastIndex.put(a[i], i);           // put returns the previous mapping
            if (prev != null && i - prev <= k) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Early exit? Brute force O(n²) O(1) yes Sort O(n log n) O(1)–O(n) yes HashSet O(n) O(n) yes Streams distinct().count() O(n) O(n) no: it always scans everything

docs.title: Talking point
docs.text: The three approaches are a clean demonstration of the time vs. space trade-off: O(n²)/O(1), O(n log n)/O(1) and O(n)/O(n). Say this out loud.

docs.title: Distinct elements in every window
docs.text: Medium Sliding window Frequency map

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For every window of size k, count how many distinct values it contains.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: a k Output [1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 3] 4 [3, 4, 4, 3] [7, 7, 7] 1 [1, 1, 1] [1, 2] 3 [] (no full window)

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• k larger than n? Then there are no windows, so return an empty array.
  • Value range? If values are small and non-negative, a counts array beats a map.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: a fresh HashSet for each window. O(n · k).
  2. Waste: consecutive windows share k − 1 elements. Only one element enters and one leaves.
  3. Keep a frequency map of the current window: increment the entering value and decrement the leaving one. The number of distinct values is the number of keys with a count above zero, so delete a key when its count hits 0. Then map.size() is the answer.
  4. Map-free version: with a counts array, keep a distinct counter. A count going 0 → 1 means +1, and 1 → 0 means −1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/** Number of distinct elements in every window of size k. [1,2,1,3,4,2,3], k=4 → [3,4,4,3]. */
public final class DistinctInWindow {
    private DistinctInWindow() {}

    /** Brute force: a fresh set per window. O(n·k). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        if (k <= 0 || k > a.length) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i + k <= a.length; i++) {
            Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
            for (int j = i; j < i + k; j++) set.add(a[j]);
            out[i] = set.size();
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Sliding window + frequency map: add the entering element, remove the leaving one, and delete keys whose
     * count drops to zero so that map.size() is always the distinct count. O(n) time, O(k) space.
     */
    public static int[] slidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
        if (k <= 0 || k > a.length) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            freq.merge(a[i], 1, Integer::sum);                          // element entering
            if (i >= k) {
                // merge returning null removes the key: the count reached zero
                freq.merge(a[i - k], -1, (old, d) -> old + d == 0 ? null : old + d);
            }
            if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = freq.size();
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Variant without a map when values are small and non-negative: a counts array + a running distinct counter. */
    public static int[] countsArray(int[] a, int k, int maxValue) {
        if (k <= 0 || k > a.length) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1], count = new int[maxValue + 1];
        int distinct = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (count[a[i]]++ == 0) distinct++;                        // first copy in the window
            if (i >= k && --count[a[i - k]] == 0) distinct--;          // last copy left the window
            if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = distinct;
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Set per window O(n · k) O(k) Sliding frequency map O(n) O(k) Counts array + counter O(n) O(max value)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting to remove zero-count keys makes map.size() count values that have already left.
  • map.merge(key, -1, (old, d) -> old + d == 0 ? null : old + d): a merge function that returns null deletes the key. That is the neatest way to do it.
  • Remove the leaving element only once i ≥ k.

docs.title: 4Sum II (count zero-sum tuples)
docs.text: Hard Meet in the middle HashMap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given four arrays of length n, count the tuples (i,j,k,l) with a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] = 0. a=[1,2] b=[−2,−1] c=[−1,2] d=[0,2] → 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: four nested loops. O(n⁴). With n = 200 that's 1.6 billion iterations, which is too slow.
  2. Hash one array: three loops plus a lookup of −(x+y+z) in a count map of d. O(n³).
  3. Meet in the middle: split the four arrays into two pairs. Count every sum a[i] + b[j] in a map (n² entries). Then for every c[k] + d[l], add map[−(c[k] + d[l])]. O(n²) time and space.
  4. General principle: when you combine m independent choices, hash half of them and enumerate the other half. That turns O(Nᵐ) into O(N^(m/2)).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Count tuples (i, j, k, l) with a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] == 0 across four equal-length arrays (LeetCode 454). */
public final class FourSumCount {
    private FourSumCount() {}

    /** Brute force: four nested loops. O(n^4). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c, int[] d) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int x : a) for (int y : b) for (int z : c) for (int w : d) if ((long) x + y + z + w == 0) count++;
        return count;
    }

    /** Hash one array: three loops + lookup. O(n^3). A useful middle step when explaining. */
    public static int threeLoops(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c, int[] d) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> dCount = new HashMap<>();
        for (int w : d) dCount.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
        int count = 0;
        for (int x : a) for (int y : b) for (int z : c) count += dCount.getOrDefault(-(x + y + z), 0);
        return count;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal meet-in-the-middle: count every pair sum of (a, b), then for each pair sum of (c, d) look up its
     * negation. O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space.
     */
    public static int meetInTheMiddle(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c, int[] d) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> abSums = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) for (int y : b) abSums.merge(x + y, 1, Integer::sum);
        int count = 0;
        for (int z : c) for (int w : d) count += abSums.getOrDefault(-(z + w), 0);
        return count;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Four loops O(n⁴) O(1) Three loops + map O(n³) O(n) Meet in the middle O(n²) O(n²)

docs.title: Contrast with 4Sum (one array, list the unique quadruplets)
docs.text: That variant asks for distinct value tuples from a single array. Sort it, fix two indexes, and run two pointers, for O(n³) with duplicate skipping. The hashing trick above fits counting across separate arrays.

docs.title: Isomorphic strings
docs.text: Easy Bijection Two maps Canonical form

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Two strings are isomorphic if you can replace characters of s to get t, where every occurrence of a character is replaced by the same character, and no two characters map to the same one. A character may map to itself.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: s t isomorphic? Why egg add yes e→a, g→d paper title yes p→t, a→i, e→l, r→e foo bar no o would need to map to both a and r badc baba no b→b and d→b: two letters onto one

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Same length required? Yes, otherwise the answer is false immediately.
  • Character set? Any char. The int[65536] version covers all of them.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. One map s→t is not enough. badc/baba passes a one-way check, because each s-letter maps consistently, but b and d both map to b. The relation must be a bijection, so keep a second map t→s too.
  2. Structural view: two strings are isomorphic iff they have the same shape. Replace each char by the index of its first occurrence (paper → 0 1 0 3 4, title → 0 1 0 3 4) and compare. Elegant, and it groups many strings at once.
  3. No maps at all: walk both strings together and store, for each char, the position where it was last seen. At every index the two "last seen" values must agree, otherwise the histories differ.

docs.title: Dry run (two maps): badc / baba
docs.text: i pair s→t t→s conflict? 0 b, b b→b b→b 1 a, a a→a a→a 2 d, b d→b b is already →b, but now needs →d yes → false

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * s and t are isomorphic if the characters of s can be replaced (consistently, one-to-one) to get t.
 * "egg"/"add" → true; "foo"/"bar" → false; "badc"/"baba" → false (two letters can't map to the same one).
 */
public final class IsomorphicStrings {
    private IsomorphicStrings() {}

    /** Two maps: s→t and t→s must both stay consistent (a bijection). O(n) time, O(alphabet) space. */
    public static boolean twoMaps(String s, String t) {
        if (s.length() != t.length()) return false;
        Map<Character, Character> st = new HashMap<>(), ts = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char a = s.charAt(i), b = t.charAt(i);
            Character mappedA = st.putIfAbsent(a, b), mappedB = ts.putIfAbsent(b, a);
            if ((mappedA != null && mappedA != b) || (mappedB != null && mappedB != a)) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    /**
     * Last-seen positions: two strings are isomorphic iff every position has the same "pattern" — each char was last
     * seen at the same index in both strings. One int[] per string, no maps. O(n).
     */
    public static boolean lastSeen(String s, String t) {
        if (s.length() != t.length()) return false;
        int[] ls = new int[65536], lt = new int[65536];          // full char range; 0 = never seen
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char a = s.charAt(i), b = t.charAt(i);
            if (ls[a] != lt[b]) return false;                     // different history → different structure
            ls[a] = lt[b] = i + 1;                                 // +1 so that 0 keeps meaning "unseen"
        }
        return true;
    }

    /** Canonical form: replace each char by the index of its first occurrence. "paper" → [0,1,0,3,4]. */
    public static boolean canonical(String s, String t) {
        return s.length() == t.length() && Arrays.equals(pattern(s), pattern(t));
    }

    static int[] pattern(String s) {
        Map<Character, Integer> first = new HashMap<>();
        int[] p = new int[s.length()];
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) p[i] = first.computeIfAbsent(s.charAt(i), c -> first.size());
        return p;
    }
}

docs.title: Longest consecutive sequence
docs.text: Medium HashSet

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, in O(n). [100,4,200,1,3,2] → 4 (1,2,3,4). Duplicates don't break or extend a run.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each x, look for x+1, x+2, … with a linear search each time. O(n³) in the worst case.
  2. Sort: runs become contiguous. Skip duplicates, extend when c[i] == c[i−1] + 1, otherwise reset. O(n log n). That's good, but the problem asks for O(n).
  3. HashSet makes "is x+1 present?" O(1). But counting upward from every x is still O(n²) on 1..n, because each run is re-walked from each of its elements.
  4. Key insight: only start counting at a sequence start, an x where x − 1 is absent. Each run is then walked exactly once, so the total work is O(n), even though the loop looks nested.

docs.title: Dry run ({100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2})
docs.text: x x−1 present? Action Length 100 no count 100 1 4 yes (3) skip 200 no count 200 1 1 no count 1,2,3,4 4 3, 2 yes skip

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Longest consecutive sequence with a HashSet
  1. Put everything in a set for O(1) lookups. Only count from the start of a run, so each number is walked at most once overall.
  2. 100 starts a run: 100, length 1. best = 1.
  3. 4: 3 is in the set, so 4 isn't a start. Skip, its run gets counted from its start.
  4. 200 starts a run: 200, length 1. best = 1.
  5. 1 starts a run: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, length 4. best = 4.
  6. 3: 2 is in the set, so 3 isn't a start. Skip, its run gets counted from its start.
  7. 2: 1 is in the set, so 2 isn't a start. Skip, its run gets counted from its start.
  8. Answer 4 (1, 2, 3, 4). Each element is touched O(1) times: O(n) without sorting. (Java iterates the set in its own order; the result is the same.)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Length of the longest run of consecutive integers (any order, duplicates allowed). [100,4,200,1,3,2] → 4 (1..4). */
public final class LongestConsecutiveSequence {
    private LongestConsecutiveSequence() {}

    /** Brute force: for each x, count x+1, x+2, … with a linear search each time. O(n^3) worst case. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int len = 1;
            long next = (long) x + 1;
            while (contains(a, next)) {
                len++;
                next++;
            }
            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Sort, then count runs, skipping duplicates. O(n log n). */
    public static int sorting(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 0) return 0;
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        int best = 1, run = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < c.length; i++) {
            if (c[i] == c[i - 1]) continue;                  // duplicate: neither extends nor breaks
            run = (long) c[i] == (long) c[i - 1] + 1 ? run + 1 : 1;
            best = Math.max(best, run);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: put everything in a HashSet. Only start counting at a sequence START (x-1 not present),
     * so every element is walked at most once overall. O(n) time, O(n) space.
     */
    public static int hashSet(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) set.add(x);
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : set) {                                  // iterate the set: duplicates already removed
            if (x != Integer.MIN_VALUE && set.contains(x - 1)) continue;   // not a start
            int len = 1;
            for (int y = x; y != Integer.MAX_VALUE && set.contains(y + 1); y++) len++;
            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;
    }

    private static boolean contains(int[] a, long v) {
        for (int x : a) if (x == v) return true;
        return false;
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n³) O(1) Sort O(n log n) O(n) copy HashSet (starts only) O(n) O(n)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: x − 1 and y + 1 overflow at Integer.MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE, so the code guards them. Iterating the original array instead of the set re-processes duplicates, which is still correct but wasteful.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: Union-Find also solves it in near-O(n): union x with x+1 when both exist, and the answer is the largest component.

docs.title: Longest subarray with sum 0 / equal 0s and 1s
docs.text: Hard Prefix sum First-index map

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Longest subarray with sum 0 (GfG): [15,−2,2,−8,1,7,10,23] → 5 (−2,2,−8,1,7).
  2. Equal 0s and 1s (LeetCode 525): [0,1,1,1,1,1,0,0,0] → 6.

The code solves the general case, the longest subarray with sum k, which covers both.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: every start with a running sum. O(n²).
  2. Prefix-sum view: a[i+1..j] sums to k ⇔ prefix[j] − prefix[i] = k.
  3. To make that subarray longest for a fixed j, you want the smallest i, so store the first index at which each prefix value appears, and never overwrite it (putIfAbsent).
  4. Seed {0: −1}, so a subarray starting at index 0 has length j − (−1) = j + 1.
  5. Equal 0s and 1s: replace 0 with −1. Equal counts then means the sum is 0, so it's the same problem.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Longest subarray with sum 0 (GfG) and its twin: longest subarray with equal numbers of 0s and 1s
 * (LeetCode 525 — map 0 → -1 and it becomes the same problem). Generalised to sum k.
 */
public final class LongestZeroSumSubarray {
    private LongestZeroSumSubarray() {}

    /** Brute force: every start, running sum. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                if (sum == k) best = Math.max(best, j - i + 1);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: prefix sums with the FIRST index each prefix was seen. If prefix[j] - k was first seen at i,
     * a[i+1..j] sums to k and is the longest such subarray ending at j. Never overwrite → keeps it longest. O(n).
     */
    public static int longestWithSum(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Long, Integer> firstIndex = new HashMap<>();
        firstIndex.put(0L, -1);                              // empty prefix "ends" before index 0
        long prefix = 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) {
            prefix += a[j];
            Integer i = firstIndex.get(prefix - k);
            if (i != null) best = Math.max(best, j - i);
            firstIndex.putIfAbsent(prefix, j);               // FIRST occurrence only
        }
        return best;
    }

    public static int longestZeroSum(int[] a) {
        return longestWithSum(a, 0);
    }

    /** Equal 0s and 1s: treat 0 as -1, then it is "longest subarray with sum 0". */
    public static int longestEqualZerosOnes(int[] bits) {
        int[] mapped = new int[bits.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < bits.length; i++) mapped[i] = bits[i] == 0 ? -1 : 1;
        return longestZeroSum(mapped);
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) space with the map, versus O(n²) and O(1) for brute force.

docs.title: Design a HashMap from scratch
docs.text: Expert Design Separate chaining Resizing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement put, get, remove, containsKey and size with average O(1) operations, without using any built-in hash table. Support any key type, including null.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Generic keys or only int? Must it grow? (Yes.) Null keys? Thread safety? (No. Mention ConcurrentHashMap as a follow-up.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Array of buckets: the index is derived from key.hashCode(). Different keys can land in the same bucket, a collision, so each bucket holds a small linked list of entries (separate chaining).
  2. Index: hash & (capacity − 1). With a power-of-two capacity this equals hash mod capacity, is never negative, and costs one CPU instruction.
  3. Spread the bits: h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes the high bits into the low bits. Without it, hash codes that differ only in their high bits would all collide, because the mask only keeps the low bits. This is the same trick java.util.HashMap uses.
  4. Lookup: walk the chain comparing the stored hash first (a cheap int comparison), then Objects.equals (which is null-safe and possibly expensive).
  5. Load factor 0.75: once size > capacity × 0.75, chains start growing. Double the table and re-bucket. A single resize is O(n), but doubling makes put amortised O(1), for the same reason as an array stack.
  6. Store the hash in each node, so a resize never calls hashCode() again.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
table (capacity 8)
[0] → null
[1] → ("b", 2) → ("j", 9) → null      ← collision chain
[2] → null
[3] → ("d", 4) → null
 …

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Objects;

/**
 * A HashMap from scratch: array of buckets with separate chaining, hash spreading, load-factor resize.
 * Supports null keys like java.util.HashMap. Not thread-safe.
 */
public final class MyHashMap<K, V> {
    private static final int DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 16;          // always a power of two
    private static final float LOAD_FACTOR = 0.75f;

    /** One entry in a bucket's singly linked chain. */
    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final int hash;
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> next;

        Node(int hash, K key, V value, Node<K, V> next) {
            this.hash = hash;
            this.key = key;
            this.value = value;
            this.next = next;
        }
    }

    private Node<K, V>[] table;
    private int size;

    public MyHashMap() {
        this(DEFAULT_CAPACITY);
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public MyHashMap(int initialCapacity) {
        int cap = 1;
        while (cap < Math.max(1, initialCapacity)) cap <<= 1; // round up to a power of two
        table = (Node<K, V>[]) new Node[cap];
    }

    /**
     * Spread the high bits into the low bits (same trick as java.util.HashMap): the index uses only the low bits,
     * so without this, hashCodes differing only in high bits would all collide.
     */
    static int hash(Object key) {
        int h = key == null ? 0 : key.hashCode();
        return h ^ (h >>> 16);
    }

    /** index = hash mod capacity; with a power-of-two capacity that is a cheap bit mask, and never negative. */
    private static int indexFor(int hash, int capacity) {
        return hash & (capacity - 1);
    }

    /** Insert or replace. Returns the previous value or null. Average O(1). */
    public V put(K key, V value) {
        int h = hash(key);
        int i = indexFor(h, table.length);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next) {
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) { // cheap hash check first, then equals
                V old = n.value;
                n.value = value;
                return old;
            }
        }
        table[i] = new Node<>(h, key, value, table[i]);      // prepend to the chain
        if (++size > table.length * LOAD_FACTOR) resize();
        return null;
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        Node<K, V> n = find(key);
        return n == null ? null : n.value;
    }

    public boolean containsKey(K key) {
        return find(key) != null;                            // distinguishes "absent" from "mapped to null"
    }

    /** Remove the mapping; returns the old value or null. Average O(1). */
    public V remove(K key) {
        int h = hash(key);
        int i = indexFor(h, table.length);
        Node<K, V> prev = null;
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[i]; n != null; prev = n, n = n.next) {
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) {
                if (prev == null) table[i] = n.next;
                else prev.next = n.next;
                size--;
                return n.value;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

    public int size() {
        return size;
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    /** Current bucket count (exposed for tests and teaching). */
    int capacity() {
        return table.length;
    }

    private Node<K, V> find(K key) {
        int h = hash(key);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[indexFor(h, table.length)]; n != null; n = n.next) {
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) return n;
        }
        return null;
    }

    /** Double the table and re-bucket every node. O(n), but happens rarely enough to be amortised O(1) per put. */
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    private void resize() {
        Node<K, V>[] old = table;
        table = (Node<K, V>[]) new Node[old.length * 2];
        for (Node<K, V> head : old) {
            for (Node<K, V> n = head; n != null; ) {
                Node<K, V> next = n.next;
                int i = indexFor(n.hash, table.length);      // stored hash: no need to call hashCode() again
                n.next = table[i];
                table[i] = n;
                n = next;
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Operation Average Worst case (everything collides) put / get / remove O(1) O(n). Java 8 caps this at O(log n) by turning long chains into trees resize O(n), amortised O(1) per put

docs.title: How it's tested
docs.text: The test runs a differential check: 20,000 random put/remove/get calls applied to both MyHashMap and java.util.HashMap, asserting identical results and sizes through many resizes. It also uses a key class whose hashCode() always returns 7, to stress the collision chains.

docs.title: What java.util.HashMap adds on top
docs.text:
• Treeification: a chain with 8 or more nodes becomes a red-black tree, when the table has 64 or more buckets.
  • Resize splitting: after doubling, each node either keeps its index or moves to index + oldCapacity, decided by one bit.
  • Fail-fast iterators using modCount.

docs.title: Alternative: open addressing
docs.text: Store the entries in the array itself, and on a collision probe the next slot (linear or quadratic probing). It's cache-friendly, but deletion needs tombstones, and performance drops sharply above about 70% load. ThreadLocal and Python's dict use variants of it.

docs.title: Subarray sum equals K
docs.text: Medium Prefix sum HashMap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values can be negative. [1,1,1], k = 2 → 2 · [3,4,7,2,−3,1,4,2], k = 7 → 4.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Negative numbers? (Yes, which rules out a plain sliding window.) Count or list them? Overflow? (Use long sums.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: every start i, extending j with a running sum. O(n²).
  2. Why not a sliding window? A window works only if growing it always increases the sum. With negative numbers, shrinking might increase the sum, so the window logic breaks.
  3. Prefix-sum insight: sum(i+1..j) = prefix[j] − prefix[i]. So a subarray ending at j sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals prefix[j] − k.
  4. Keep a map prefix value → how many times seen. At each j, add map[prefix − k] to the count, then record prefix.
  5. Seed the map with {0: 1} (the empty prefix), so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.

Subarray sum = 7 with prefix sums and a hash map

  2. j = 0: prefix = 3, need an earlier prefix of 3 − 7 = -4: none.
  3. j = 1: prefix = 7, need an earlier prefix of 7 − 7 = 0: seen 1× → count = 1.
  4. j = 2: prefix = 14, need an earlier prefix of 14 − 7 = 7: seen 1× → count = 2.
  5. j = 3: prefix = 16, need an earlier prefix of 16 − 7 = 9: none.
  6. j = 4: prefix = 13, need an earlier prefix of 13 − 7 = 6: none.
  7. j = 5: prefix = 14, need an earlier prefix of 14 − 7 = 7: seen 1× → count = 3.
  8. j = 6: prefix = 18, need an earlier prefix of 18 − 7 = 11: none.
  9. j = 7: prefix = 20, need an earlier prefix of 20 − 7 = 13: seen 1× → count = 4.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values may be negative. [1,1,1], k=2 → 2. */
public final class SubarraySumEqualsK {
    private SubarraySumEqualsK() {}

    /** Brute force: every (start, end) with a running sum. O(n^2), O(1). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                if (sum == k) count++;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: prefix sums + hash map. sum(i+1..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i], so a subarray ending at j sums to k
     * exactly when an EARLIER prefix equals prefix[j] - k. Count those with a map prefix → occurrences. O(n), O(n).
     */
    public static int prefixSumMap(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        seen.put(0L, 1);                                     // empty prefix: lets subarrays starting at index 0 count
        long prefix = 0;
        int count = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            prefix += x;
            count += seen.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0);       // look up BEFORE inserting the current prefix
            seen.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return count;
    }

    /** Only valid for NON-NEGATIVE values: sliding window (shrink while sum > k). O(n), O(1). */
    public static int slidingWindowNonNegative(int[] a, int k) {
        int count = 0, left = 0;
        long sum = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < a.length; right++) {
            sum += a[right];
            while (sum > k && left <= right) sum -= a[left++];
            if (sum == k && left <= right) {                // left > right means an EMPTY window (k == 0)
                count++;
                // zeros at the left edge give extra windows with the same sum
                for (int l = left; l < right && a[l] == 0; l++) count++;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }
}

docs.title: Subarray sums divisible by K
docs.text: Hard Prefix sum Remainder buckets Negative modulo

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k (k ≥ 1). Values can be negative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
a k Output [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1] 5 7 [5] 9 0 [-5] 5 1

The 7 subarrays for the first example: [4,5,0,-2,-3,1], [5], [5,0], [5,0,-2,-3], [0], [0,-2,-3], [-2,-3].

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Negative values? Yes. This is exactly where most solutions break.
  • Count or list? Count. Listing them could be O(n²) output.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: every (i, j) with a running sum. O(n²).
  2. Prefix sums: sum(i..j) = P[j+1] − P[i]. That is divisible by k exactly when P[j+1] mod k == P[i] mod k.
  3. So it is a counting problem: walking left to right, each new prefix pairs with every earlier prefix that has the same remainder. Keep a count per remainder. Seed remainder 0 → 1 for the empty prefix, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.
  4. The trap: in Java, -1 % 5 == -1, not 4. Two prefixes with remainders −1 and 4 are congruent but would land in different buckets. Normalise with ((p % k) + k) % k or Math.floorMod(p, k).
  5. Closed form: a bucket holding c prefixes contributes C(c, 2) pairs, so sum c·(c−1)/2 over the buckets.

package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Count non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k (k ≥ 1). Values may be negative.
 * [4,5,0,-2,-3,1], k=5 → 7.
 */
public final class SubarraysDivisibleByK {
    private SubarraysDivisibleByK() {}

    /** Brute force: every (i, j) with a running sum. O(n²). */
    public static long bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        long count = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                if (sum % k == 0) count++;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    /**
     * Prefix sums + remainder counts. sum(i..j) = P[j+1] − P[i] is divisible by k ⇔ P[j+1] ≡ P[i] (mod k).
     * So for each prefix, add the number of EARLIER prefixes with the same remainder. Seed remainder 0 with count 1
     * (the empty prefix). Normalise negative remainders: Java's % keeps the sign of the dividend. O(n) time, O(k) space.
     */
    public static long prefixRemainders(int[] a, int k) {
        long[] seen = new long[k];
        seen[0] = 1;                                     // empty prefix P[0] = 0
        long count = 0, prefix = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            prefix += x;
            int r = (int) (((prefix % k) + k) % k);      // −1 % 5 is −1 in Java; we want 4
            count += seen[r];                            // pair with every earlier prefix of the same remainder
            seen[r]++;
        }
        return count;
    }

    /** Same idea with a HashMap — what you'd write when k is huge and an array of size k is too big. */
    public static long prefixRemaindersMap(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Long, Long> seen = new HashMap<>();
        seen.put(0L, 1L);
        long count = 0, prefix = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            prefix += x;
            long r = Math.floorMod(prefix, (long) k);   // floorMod is always non-negative for k > 0
            long earlier = seen.getOrDefault(r, 0L);
            count += earlier;
            seen.put(r, earlier + 1);
        }
        return count;
    }

    /** Closed form: a remainder bucket with c prefixes contributes C(c, 2) pairs. Same O(n), two passes. */
    public static long combinatorial(int[] a, int k) {
        long[] bucket = new long[k];
        bucket[0] = 1;
        long prefix = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            prefix += x;
            bucket[(int) Math.floorMod(prefix, (long) k)]++;
        }
        long count = 0;
        for (long c : bucket) count += c * (c - 1) / 2;
        return count;
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n²) O(1) Prefix remainders (array) O(n) O(k) Prefix remainders (map) O(n) O(min(n, k)) C(c, 2) per bucket O(n + k) O(k)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Raw % with negative prefixes. The random tests use values in −10..10 to catch this.
  • Forgetting the seed seen[0] = 1 misses every subarray that starts at index 0.
  • Sum overflow on long arrays: keep the prefix in a long.
