docs.title: Burst balloons
docs.text: Expert Interval DP Think backwards

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Burst balloons one at a time. Bursting balloon i earns left × nums[i] × right, where left and right are its current neighbours (1 beyond the ends). Maximise the total. [3,1,5,8] → 167.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every order, n! of them. The tests use this as the reference for small n.
  2. Why "first to burst" fails as a DP state: bursting balloon k first makes its neighbours adjacent, so the left and right sides aren't independent anymore.
  3. The flip: choose the balloon to burst last in an interval. While everything else inside (i, j) bursts, k is still standing, so the left part and right part never touch each other. When k finally bursts, its neighbours are exactly the interval boundaries i and j.
  4. So dp[i][j] = max over k in (i, j) of dp[i][k] + a[i]·a[k]·a[j] + dp[k][j], over an array padded with a 1 at each end.
  5. Fill by increasing interval length, the interval-DP pattern again. That's O(n³).

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: The algorithm is ordinary interval DP. The insight, reverse the time direction to make subproblems independent, is not. Spotting when "first" breaks independence and "last" restores it is a reusable senior-level trick. It also appears in "minimum cost to cut a stick".

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Burst balloon i to earn left·nums[i]·right (neighbours at that moment; outside = 1). Max total coins.
 * [3,1,5,8] → 167. (LeetCode 312)
 */
public final class BurstBalloons {
    private BurstBalloons() {}

    /** Brute force: try every balloon as the NEXT one to burst, recursively. O(n!). Only for tiny inputs. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] nums) {
        List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int x : nums) list.add(x);
        return brute(list);
    }

    private static int brute(List<Integer> b) {
        if (b.isEmpty()) return 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < b.size(); i++) {
            int left = i == 0 ? 1 : b.get(i - 1), right = i == b.size() - 1 ? 1 : b.get(i + 1);
            int coins = left * b.get(i) * right;
            Integer removed = b.remove(i);
            best = Math.max(best, coins + brute(b));
            b.add(i, removed);                               // backtrack
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Interval DP, thinking BACKWARDS: choose k = the LAST balloon to burst inside the open interval (i, j).
     * When k bursts last, its neighbours are exactly the interval boundaries i and j — fixed, independent of the order
     * inside. So dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + a[i]·a[k]·a[j] + dp[k][j]. O(n^3).
     */
    public static int intervalDp(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] a = new int[n + 2];
        a[0] = a[n + 1] = 1;                                 // virtual boundary balloons
        System.arraycopy(nums, 0, a, 1, n);
        int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2];
        for (int len = 2; len <= n + 1; len++)               // len = j - i
            for (int i = 0; i + len <= n + 1; i++) {
                int j = i + len;
                for (int k = i + 1; k < j; k++)
                    dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + a[i] * a[k] * a[j] + dp[k][j]);
            }
        return dp[0][n + 1];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Brute force O(n!) · interval DP O(n³) time, O(n²) space.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: 200 random arrays of up to 6 balloons (including zeros), where the interval DP must match the brute force over all orders.

docs.title: Climbing stairs
docs.text: Easy 1D DP Recursion → memo → table → O(1)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to reach step n? n = 3 → 3 (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1). Generalisation: any set of allowed step sizes.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Last decision: the final move onto step n was a 1-step (from n−1) or a 2-step (from n−2). Those two groups don't overlap and together cover every way, so f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) with f(0) = f(1) = 1. It's Fibonacci.
  2. Recursion recomputes the same values exponentially often, so cache them (memo), which is O(n).
  3. Table: dp[i] only needs dp[i−1] and dp[i−2], so fill it left to right.
  4. O(1) space: keep just the two previous values.
  5. Any step set {s₁…sₖ}: dp[i] = Σ dp[i − s], for O(n·k).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps (n ≥ 0; 0 stairs → 1 way). The "hello world" of DP. */
public final class ClimbingStairs {
    private ClimbingStairs() {}

    /** 1. Plain recursion: last move was 1 or 2 steps → f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2). O(2^n). */
    public static long recursive(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;
        return recursive(n - 1) + recursive(n - 2);
    }

    /** 2. Memoization (top-down): cache each f(k). O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static long memo(int n) {
        long[] cache = new long[n + 1];
        Arrays.fill(cache, -1);
        return memo(n, cache);
    }

    private static long memo(int n, long[] cache) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;
        if (cache[n] != -1) return cache[n];
        return cache[n] = memo(n - 1, cache) + memo(n - 2, cache);
    }

    /** 3. Tabulation (bottom-up): fill dp[0..n] in order. O(n), O(n). */
    public static long table(int n) {
        long[] dp = new long[Math.max(2, n + 1)];
        dp[0] = dp[1] = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2];
        return dp[n];
    }

    /** 4. Space-optimised: only the last two values matter. O(n), O(1). */
    public static long optimal(int n) {
        long prev2 = 1, prev1 = 1;                           // f(0), f(1)
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            long cur = prev1 + prev2;
            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = cur;
        }
        return prev1;
    }

    /** Generalisation: allowed step sizes are given (e.g. {1, 3, 5}). dp[i] = Σ dp[i - s]. O(n·k). */
    public static long withSteps(int n, int[] steps) {
        long[] dp = new long[n + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) for (int s : steps) if (i >= s) dp[i] += dp[i - s];
        return dp[n];
    }
}

docs.text: Version Time Space Recursive O(2ⁿ) O(n) stack Memo O(n) O(n) Table O(n) O(n) Optimal O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Coin change: fewest coins & number of ways
docs.text: Medium Unbounded knapsack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Each coin denomination can be used any number of times. 1. Fewest coins to make amount, or −1 (LeetCode 322): [1,2,5], 11 → 3 (5 + 5 + 1). 2. Number of combinations (LeetCode 518): [1,2,5], 5 → 4.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Why greedy fails: with [1,3,4] and 6, "largest coin first" gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 = 2. You have to try every option.
  2. Last decision: the last coin used was some c, so f(a) = 1 + min over c of f(a − c), with f(0) = 0.
  3. State = the remaining amount alone, giving amount + 1 states × #coins transitions.
  4. Table: fill dp[1..amount] upward. Use amount + 1 as "infinity", since no answer can use more coins than the amount.
  5. Counting ways, the loop-order subtlety:
    • coins outer, amounts inner: each coin is added in a fixed order, so {1,2} and {2,1} count once. Those are combinations.
    • amounts outer, coins inner: every ordering is counted. Those are permutations (5 → 9).

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Fewest coins for 11 using [1, 2, 5], bottom-up
  1. dp[0] = 0 (no coins for amount 0). Everything else starts at ∞ (amount + 1, which no real answer can reach).
  2. a = 1: try every coin as the last one: dp[0]+1 = 1. Best is coin 1 → dp[1] = 1.
  3. a = 2: try every coin as the last one: dp[1]+1 = 2, dp[0]+1 = 1. Best is coin 2 → dp[2] = 1.
  4. a = 3: try every coin as the last one: dp[2]+1 = 2, dp[1]+1 = 2. Best is coin 1 → dp[3] = 2.
  5. a = 4: try every coin as the last one: dp[3]+1 = 3, dp[2]+1 = 2. Best is coin 2 → dp[4] = 2.
  6. a = 5: try every coin as the last one: dp[4]+1 = 3, dp[3]+1 = 3, dp[0]+1 = 1. Best is coin 5 → dp[5] = 1.
  7. a = 6: try every coin as the last one: dp[5]+1 = 2, dp[4]+1 = 3, dp[1]+1 = 2. Best is coin 1 → dp[6] = 2.
  8. a = 7: try every coin as the last one: dp[6]+1 = 3, dp[5]+1 = 2, dp[2]+1 = 2. Best is coin 2 → dp[7] = 2.
  9. a = 8: try every coin as the last one: dp[7]+1 = 3, dp[6]+1 = 3, dp[3]+1 = 3. Best is coin 1 → dp[8] = 3.
  10. a = 9: try every coin as the last one: dp[8]+1 = 4, dp[7]+1 = 3, dp[4]+1 = 3. Best is coin 2 → dp[9] = 3.
  11. a = 10: try every coin as the last one: dp[9]+1 = 4, dp[8]+1 = 4, dp[5]+1 = 2. Best is coin 5 → dp[10] = 2.
  12. a = 11: try every coin as the last one: dp[10]+1 = 3, dp[9]+1 = 4, dp[6]+1 = 3. Best is coin 1 → dp[11] = 3.
  13. dp[11] = 3 (5 + 5 + 1). O(amount × coins) time, O(amount) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Unlimited coins of each denomination. (1) fewest coins for amount, -1 if impossible. (2) number of combinations. */
public final class CoinChange {
    private CoinChange() {}

    /** Recursion: try every coin as the last one. Exponential. */
    public static int minCoinsRecursive(int[] coins, int amount) {
        if (amount == 0) return 0;
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int c : coins) {
            if (c > amount) continue;
            int sub = minCoinsRecursive(coins, amount - c);
            if (sub != -1) best = Math.min(best, sub + 1);
        }
        return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : best;
    }

    /** Memoized: cache by remaining amount. O(amount · coins). */
    public static int minCoinsMemo(int[] coins, int amount) {
        int[] cache = new int[amount + 1];
        Arrays.fill(cache, -2);                              // -2 = not computed, -1 = impossible
        return memo(coins, amount, cache);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] coins, int amount, int[] cache) {
        if (amount == 0) return 0;
        if (cache[amount] != -2) return cache[amount];
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int c : coins) {
            if (c > amount) continue;
            int sub = memo(coins, amount - c, cache);
            if (sub != -1) best = Math.min(best, sub + 1);
        }
        return cache[amount] = best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : best;
    }

    /** Bottom-up: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]). "amount + 1" acts as infinity (can never be reached). O(amount · coins). */
    public static int minCoins(int[] coins, int amount) {
        int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
        Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
            for (int c : coins) if (c <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
        return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
    }

    /**
     * Number of COMBINATIONS (order doesn't matter, LeetCode 518). Coins in the OUTER loop: each coin is "unlocked" once,
     * so {1,2} and {2,1} are counted once. Swapping the loops counts permutations instead.
     */
    public static long combinations(int[] coins, int amount) {
        long[] dp = new long[amount + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (int c : coins) for (int a = c; a <= amount; a++) dp[a] += dp[a - c];
        return dp[amount];
    }

    /** Number of ordered sequences (permutations) — loops swapped. */
    public static long permutations(int[] coins, int amount) {
        long[] dp = new long[amount + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++) for (int c : coins) if (c <= a) dp[a] += dp[a - c];
        return dp[amount];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(amount × coins) time and O(amount) space for the memo and table versions. The plain recursion is exponential.

docs.title: Edit distance (Levenshtein)
docs.text: Hard Two-string DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The minimum number of single-character inserts, deletes and replacements to turn a into b. "horse" → "ros" = 3 (replace h→r, delete r, delete e).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. State = prefixes (i, j). Base cases: turning i characters into an empty string takes i deletes, and turning an empty string into j characters takes j inserts.
  2. Last characters equal cost nothing: f(i−1, j−1).
  3. Different: try all three operations on the last position and take the cheapest:
    • replace a's last character with b's: 1 + f(i−1, j−1);
    • delete a's last character: 1 + f(i−1, j);
    • insert b's last character at the end of a: 1 + f(i, j−1).
  4. One row: each cell needs its left, upper and upper-left neighbours. Save the upper-left value in a diag variable before it's overwritten.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Edit distance "horse" → "ros"
  1. Border: turning a prefix into the empty string costs its length (deletes), and vice versa (inserts).
  2. dp[1][1]: h ≠ r: 1 + min(replace 0, delete 1, insert 1) = 1.
  3. dp[1][2]: h ≠ o: 1 + min(replace 1, delete 2, insert 1) = 2.
  4. dp[1][3]: h ≠ s: 1 + min(replace 2, delete 3, insert 2) = 3.
  5. dp[2][1]: o ≠ r: 1 + min(replace 1, delete 1, insert 2) = 2.
  6. dp[2][2]: o = o: free, copy the diagonal → 1.
  7. dp[2][3]: o ≠ s: 1 + min(replace 2, delete 3, insert 1) = 2.
  8. dp[3][1]: r = r: free, copy the diagonal → 2.
  9. dp[3][2]: r ≠ o: 1 + min(replace 2, delete 1, insert 2) = 2.
  10. dp[3][3]: r ≠ s: 1 + min(replace 1, delete 2, insert 2) = 2.
  11. dp[4][1]: s ≠ r: 1 + min(replace 3, delete 2, insert 4) = 3.
  12. dp[4][2]: s ≠ o: 1 + min(replace 2, delete 2, insert 3) = 3.
  13. dp[4][3]: s = s: free, copy the diagonal → 2.
  14. dp[5][1]: e ≠ r: 1 + min(replace 4, delete 3, insert 5) = 4.
  15. dp[5][2]: e ≠ o: 1 + min(replace 3, delete 3, insert 4) = 4.
  16. dp[5][3]: e ≠ s: 1 + min(replace 3, delete 2, insert 4) = 3.
  17. Answer dp[5][3] = 3: replace h → r, delete r, delete e. O(m·n); one row is enough for O(n) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** Minimum insert/delete/replace operations to turn a into b ("horse" → "ros" = 3). Levenshtein distance. */
public final class EditDistance {
    private EditDistance() {}

    /** Recursion on prefixes. O(3^(m+n)). */
    public static int recursive(String a, String b) {
        return rec(a, b, a.length(), b.length());
    }

    private static int rec(String a, String b, int i, int j) {
        if (i == 0) return j;                                // insert the remaining j chars
        if (j == 0) return i;                                // delete the remaining i chars
        if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) return rec(a, b, i - 1, j - 1);   // free match
        return 1 + Math.min(rec(a, b, i - 1, j - 1),        // replace
                Math.min(rec(a, b, i - 1, j),                // delete from a
                        rec(a, b, i, j - 1)));               // insert into a
    }

    /** Table dp[i][j] = distance between a[0..i) and b[0..j). O(m·n). */
    public static int table(String a, String b) {
        int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
        int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;
        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
                dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1]
                        : 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1], Math.min(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]));
        return dp[m][n];
    }

    /** One row + a saved diagonal. O(m·n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static int oneRow(String a, String b) {
        int n = b.length();
        int[] row = new int[n + 1];
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) row[j] = j;
        for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
            int diag = row[0];                               // dp[i-1][j-1]
            row[0] = i;
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
                int above = row[j];                          // dp[i-1][j], about to be overwritten
                row[j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? diag : 1 + Math.min(diag, Math.min(above, row[j - 1]));
                diag = above;
            }
        }
        return row[n];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Recursion O(3^(m+n)) · table O(m·n) time and space · one row O(m·n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Real-world uses
docs.text: Spell checkers ("did you mean…"), DNA alignment, fuzzy search. Related: one edit distance (O(n) two pointers) · delete operation for two strings (LCS-based).

docs.title: Egg drop
docs.text: Expert Minimax DP Binary search in DP Invert the question

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You have k eggs and a building with n floors. There is a highest floor f (0 ≤ f ≤ n) from which an egg survives a drop. An egg that survives can be reused, and a broken one can't. Find the minimum number of drops that guarantees you find f, whatever it is.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: k n answer 1 2 2 (floor by floor) 2 6 3 2 100 14, the classic puzzle 3 14 4

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• "Guarantee" means the worst case over all possible f. That is a minimax.
  • Size? n up to 10⁴ (or 10⁹ for the moves formulation), k up to 100.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. One egg: you can't risk skipping floors, so you need n drops.
  2. Recurrence: drop from floor x. If it breaks, search floors below x with e − 1 eggs. If it survives, search floors above x with e eggs. You pay for the worse case, and you choose the best x: dp[e][f] = 1 + min over x of max(dp[e−1][x−1], dp[e][f−x]). That is O(k · n²).
  3. Binary search the x: dp[e−1][x−1] grows with x and dp[e][f−x] shrinks with x. The max of the two is smallest where they cross, so binary search for that crossing: O(k · n log n).
  4. Invert the question: instead of "the fewest moves for n floors", ask "the most floors I can cover with m moves and e eggs": cover(m, e) = cover(m−1, e−1) + 1 + cover(m−1, e). The floors below if it breaks, plus this floor, plus the floors above if it survives. Increase m until cover(m, k) ≥ n. That is O(k · m), and m is tiny (14 for 2 eggs and 100 floors, 30 for 10⁹ floors with plenty of eggs).

docs.title: The moves table: cover[m][e]
docs.text:
moves m 1 egg 2 eggs 3 eggs 1 1 1 1 2 2 3 3 3 3 6 7 4 4 10 14 … 14 14 105 ≥ 100

With 2 eggs, 13 moves cover 91 floors and 14 moves cover 105, so 100 floors need 14 drops.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/**
 * Egg drop: k eggs, a building with n floors. Some floor f (0..n) is the highest safe floor. Find the minimum number of
 * drops that GUARANTEES finding f in the worst case. A dropped egg that survives can be reused.
 */
public final class EggDrop {
    private EggDrop() {}

    /**
     * Classic DP over (eggs, floors): dp[e][f] = 1 + min over x in 1..f of max(dp[e−1][x−1] (breaks: below x),
     * dp[e][f−x] (survives: above x)). O(k · n²).
     */
    public static int classic(int k, int n) {
        int[][] dp = new int[k + 1][n + 1];
        for (int f = 1; f <= n; f++) dp[1][f] = f;            // one egg: must go floor by floor
        for (int e = 2; e <= k; e++) {
            for (int f = 1; f <= n; f++) {
                int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int x = 1; x <= f; x++) {
                    int worst = 1 + Math.max(dp[e - 1][x - 1], dp[e][f - x]);
                    best = Math.min(best, worst);
                }
                dp[e][f] = best;
            }
        }
        return k == 0 ? (n == 0 ? 0 : Integer.MAX_VALUE) : dp[k][n];
    }

    /**
     * Same recurrence, but binary search the drop floor x: "breaks" cost grows with x, "survives" cost shrinks with x,
     * so the max is minimised where they cross. O(k · n log n).
     */
    public static int binarySearch(int k, int n) {
        int[][] memo = new int[k + 1][n + 1];
        for (int[] row : memo) Arrays.fill(row, -1);
        return solve(k, n, memo);
    }

    private static int solve(int e, int f, int[][] memo) {
        if (f == 0) return 0;
        if (e == 1) return f;
        if (memo[e][f] != -1) return memo[e][f];
        int lo = 1, hi = f;
        while (lo + 1 < hi) {                                 // find the crossing of an increasing and a decreasing curve
            int x = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            int breaks = solve(e - 1, x - 1, memo), survives = solve(e, f - x, memo);
            if (breaks < survives) lo = x;
            else if (breaks > survives) hi = x;
            else lo = hi = x;
        }
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int x = lo; x <= hi; x++) best = Math.min(best, 1 + Math.max(solve(e - 1, x - 1, memo), solve(e, f - x, memo)));
        return memo[e][f] = best;
    }

    /**
     * Flip the question: with m moves and e eggs, how many floors can I fully cover?
     *   cover[m][e] = cover[m−1][e−1] (floors below, if it breaks) + 1 (this floor) + cover[m−1][e] (floors above).
     * The answer is the smallest m with cover[m][k] ≥ n. m ≤ n, and with ≥ log₂ n eggs, m ≈ log₂ n. O(k · m) time, O(k) space.
     */
    public static int movesDp(int k, int n) {
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        if (k == 0) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        long[] cover = new long[k + 1];                       // cover[e] for the current number of moves
        int m = 0;
        while (cover[k] < n) {
            m++;
            for (int e = k; e >= 1; e--) cover[e] = cover[e - 1] + 1 + cover[e];   // right-to-left: uses m−1 values
        }
        return m;
    }
}

• n = 0 needs 0 drops. k = 1 needs n drops.
  • cover grows fast. Keep it in a long.
  • In the inverted DP, update e from high to low so cover[e−1] still holds the m − 1 value.

docs.title: House robber
docs.text: Easy 1D DP Take / skip

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Houses in a row hold money, and you can't rob two adjacent houses. Maximise the total. [2,7,9,3,1] → 12 (2 + 9 + 1). Variant: the houses are in a circle (LeetCode 213).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Last decision at house i: skip it (best up to i−1), or take it (a[i] plus the best up to i−2, since i−1 is now forbidden). f(i) = max(f(i−1), a[i] + f(i−2)).
  2. Recursion → memo → table, then only two values are needed, so use O(1) space.
  3. Circle: the first and last houses are now adjacent, so you can't take both. Solve two straight-line problems, without the last and without the first, and take the larger.

House robber in O(1) space
  1. For each house: skip it (keep prev1) or rob it (prev2 + x, since the neighbour is off-limits).
  2. House 0 (2): skip → 0, take → 0 + 2 = 2. best = 2 (take).
  3. House 1 (7): skip → 2, take → 0 + 7 = 7. best = 7 (take).
  4. House 2 (9): skip → 7, take → 2 + 9 = 11. best = 11 (take).
  5. House 3 (3): skip → 11, take → 7 + 3 = 10. best = 11 (skip).
  6. House 4 (1): skip → 11, take → 11 + 1 = 12. best = 12 (take).
  7. Answer 12: rob houses 0, 2 and 4 (2 + 9 + 1). O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Max money robbing houses in a row without robbing two adjacent ones. [2,7,9,3,1] → 12 (2 + 9 + 1). */
public final class HouseRobber {
    private HouseRobber() {}

    /** Recursion from the end: rob house i (skip i-1) or skip it. O(2^n). */
    public static int recursive(int[] a) {
        return rob(a, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int rob(int[] a, int i) {
        if (i < 0) return 0;
        return Math.max(rob(a, i - 1), a[i] + rob(a, i - 2));
    }

    /** Memoized. O(n). */
    public static int memo(int[] a) {
        int[] cache = new int[a.length];
        Arrays.fill(cache, -1);
        return memo(a, a.length - 1, cache);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] a, int i, int[] cache) {
        if (i < 0) return 0;
        if (cache[i] != -1) return cache[i];
        return cache[i] = Math.max(memo(a, i - 1, cache), a[i] + memo(a, i - 2, cache));
    }

    /** Tabulation with O(1) space: best including up to previous house, and up to the one before. */
    public static int optimal(int[] a) {
        int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev2 + x);            // skip x, or take x on top of best two back
            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = cur;
        }
        return prev1;
    }

    /** Circular street (LeetCode 213): first and last are neighbours → max(rob without last, rob without first). */
    public static int circular(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 1) return a[0];
        return Math.max(optimal(Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 0, a.length - 1)), optimal(Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, a.length)));
    }
}

docs.title: 0/1 knapsack
docs.text: Medium Knapsack 2D → 1D

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Items have a weight and a value, and each can be used at most once. Maximise the value with total weight ≤ capacity. weights [10,20,30], values [60,100,120], capacity 50 → 220 (items 2 and 3).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Greedy by value/weight ratio fails for 0/1 (it works for the fractional knapsack in the Greedy topic).
  2. Decision per item: skip it, giving f(i−1, w), or take it if it fits, giving val[i] + f(i−1, w − wt[i]).
  3. State = (item index, remaining capacity), so there are n × W states with O(1) work each: O(n·W). That's pseudo-polynomial, since it depends on the value of W.
  4. 2D table: dp[i][w] uses only row i−1, so one row is enough.
  5. The direction trick: in the 1D version, iterate w downward. That way dp[w − wt] is still the previous item's value, and each item is used once. Iterating upward lets an item be reused, which turns it into the unbounded knapsack.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** 0/1 knapsack: each item once; maximise value with total weight ≤ capacity. */
public final class Knapsack01 {
    private Knapsack01() {}

    /** Recursion: for item i, skip it or take it (if it fits). O(2^n). */
    public static int recursive(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        return rec(wt, val, wt.length - 1, cap);
    }

    private static int rec(int[] wt, int[] val, int i, int cap) {
        if (i < 0 || cap == 0) return 0;
        int skip = rec(wt, val, i - 1, cap);
        if (wt[i] > cap) return skip;
        return Math.max(skip, val[i] + rec(wt, val, i - 1, cap - wt[i]));
    }

    /** Memoized on (item, capacity). O(n·W). */
    public static int memo(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        Integer[][] cache = new Integer[wt.length][cap + 1];
        return memo(wt, val, wt.length - 1, cap, cache);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] wt, int[] val, int i, int cap, Integer[][] cache) {
        if (i < 0 || cap == 0) return 0;
        if (cache[i][cap] != null) return cache[i][cap];
        int skip = memo(wt, val, i - 1, cap, cache);
        int best = wt[i] > cap ? skip : Math.max(skip, val[i] + memo(wt, val, i - 1, cap - wt[i], cache));
        return cache[i][cap] = best;
    }

    /** 2D table: dp[i][w] = best using the first i items with capacity w. O(n·W) time and space. */
    public static int table(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        int n = wt.length;
        int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][cap + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
            for (int w = 0; w <= cap; w++) {
                dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w];
                if (wt[i - 1] <= w) dp[i][w] = Math.max(dp[i][w], val[i - 1] + dp[i - 1][w - wt[i - 1]]);
            }
        return dp[n][cap];
    }

    /**
     * 1D: one row, capacity iterated DOWNWARD so dp[w - wt] still holds the previous item's row
     * (iterating upward would let an item be reused = unbounded knapsack). O(n·W) time, O(W) space.
     */
    public static int optimal(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++)
            for (int w = cap; w >= wt[i]; w--) dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]]);
        return dp[cap];
    }

    /** Unbounded knapsack (items reusable): the same loop, capacity iterated UPWARD. */
    public static int unbounded(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++)
            for (int w = wt[i]; w <= cap; w++) dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]]);
        return dp[cap];
    }
}

docs.title: Longest common subsequence
docs.text: Hard Two-string DP Reconstruction

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The length of the longest sequence that appears, in order, in both strings, and the sequence itself. "abcde", "ace" → 3, "ace".

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. State = two prefix lengths (i, j): a[0..i) and b[0..j).
  2. Compare the last characters:
    • equal: they can both end the LCS, giving 1 + f(i−1, j−1);
    • different: at least one of them isn't in the LCS, giving max(f(i−1, j), f(i, j−1)).
  3. The base case is an empty prefix, giving 0. That's (m+1)(n+1) states with O(1) work each, so O(m·n).
  4. Reconstruction: walk back from dp[m][n]. On equal characters, take the character and move diagonally. Otherwise move toward the larger neighbour.
  5. Space: for the length only, keep two rows, and make the shorter string the columns.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

LCS table for "abcde" and "ace"
  1. Row 0 and column 0 are 0: an empty prefix has nothing in common with anything.
  2. dp[1][1]: a = a: take the diagonal + 1 → 1.
  3. dp[1][2]: a ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 0, left 1) = 1.
  4. dp[1][3]: a ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 0, left 1) = 1.
  5. dp[2][1]: b ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  6. dp[2][2]: b ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 1) = 1.
  7. dp[2][3]: b ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 1) = 1.
  8. dp[3][1]: c ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  9. dp[3][2]: c = c: take the diagonal + 1 → 2.
  10. dp[3][3]: c ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 2) = 2.
  11. dp[4][1]: d ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  12. dp[4][2]: d ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 2, left 1) = 2.
  13. dp[4][3]: d ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 2, left 2) = 2.
  14. dp[5][1]: e ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  15. dp[5][2]: e ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 2, left 1) = 2.
  16. dp[5][3]: e = e: take the diagonal + 1 → 3.
  17. Answer: dp[5][3] = 3. Walking back from the corner (diagonal on a match) spells the LCS "ace". O(m·n) time and space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** Longest common subsequence of two strings ("abcde", "ace" → 3, "ace"). */
public final class LongestCommonSubsequence {
    private LongestCommonSubsequence() {}

    /** Recursion on prefixes: last chars equal → 1 + lcs(both shorter); else max(drop one from either). O(2^(m+n)). */
    public static int recursive(String a, String b) {
        return rec(a, b, a.length(), b.length());
    }

    private static int rec(String a, String b, int i, int j) {
        if (i == 0 || j == 0) return 0;
        if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) return 1 + rec(a, b, i - 1, j - 1);
        return Math.max(rec(a, b, i - 1, j), rec(a, b, i, j - 1));
    }

    /** Memoized. O(m·n). */
    public static int memo(String a, String b) {
        Integer[][] cache = new Integer[a.length() + 1][b.length() + 1];
        return memo(a, b, a.length(), b.length(), cache);
    }

    private static int memo(String a, String b, int i, int j, Integer[][] cache) {
        if (i == 0 || j == 0) return 0;
        if (cache[i][j] != null) return cache[i][j];
        int r = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? 1 + memo(a, b, i - 1, j - 1, cache)
                : Math.max(memo(a, b, i - 1, j, cache), memo(a, b, i, j - 1, cache));
        return cache[i][j] = r;
    }

    /** Table dp[i][j] = LCS of a[0..i) and b[0..j). O(m·n). */
    public static int[][] table(String a, String b) {
        int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
        int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
                dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
        return dp;
    }

    public static int length(String a, String b) {
        return table(a, b)[a.length()][b.length()];
    }

    /** Reconstruct one LCS by walking the table back from the bottom-right corner. */
    public static String sequence(String a, String b) {
        int[][] dp = table(a, b);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = a.length(), j = b.length(); i > 0 && j > 0; ) {
            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
                sb.append(a.charAt(i - 1));
                i--;
                j--;
            } else if (dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]) i--;
            else j--;
        }
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    /** Two rows instead of a full table: O(min(m,n)) space when only the length is needed. */
    public static int twoRows(String a, String b) {
        if (b.length() > a.length()) return twoRows(b, a);
        int[] prev = new int[b.length() + 1], cur = new int[b.length() + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= b.length(); j++)
                cur[j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? prev[j - 1] + 1 : Math.max(prev[j], cur[j - 1]);
            int[] t = prev;
            prev = cur;
            cur = t;
        }
        return prev[b.length()];
    }
}

docs.title: Longest increasing subsequence
docs.text: Medium 1D DP Binary search Patience sorting

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (not necessarily contiguous). [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] → 4 (2,3,7,18).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Recursion: for each element, skip it or take it (if it's bigger than the last one taken). O(2ⁿ).
  2. DP O(n²): dp[i] = the length of the LIS ending exactly at i = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with a[j] < a[i]. The answer is max(dp).
  3. O(n log n) insight: for each length k, only the smallest possible tail matters, because a smaller tail is easier to extend. Keep tails[k], which is always sorted. For each x, binary-search the first tail ≥ x and replace it with x. If x is bigger than every tail, append it.
  4. Careful: tails is not an actual LIS. Only its length is the answer. (Rebuilding the sequence needs parent pointers.)

docs.title: Patience trace
docs.text: x tails 10 [10] 9 [9] replace 2 [2] replace 5 [2, 5] append 3 [2, 3] replace 7 [2, 3, 7] append 101 [2, 3, 7, 101] append 18 [2, 3, 7, 18] replace → length 4

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Length of the longest STRICTLY increasing subsequence. [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] → 4 (2,3,7,18). */
public final class LongestIncreasingSubsequence {
    private LongestIncreasingSubsequence() {}

    /** Recursion: take or skip each element, remembering the last taken value. O(2^n). */
    public static int recursive(int[] a) {
        return rec(a, 0, -1);
    }

    private static int rec(int[] a, int i, int prevIdx) {
        if (i == a.length) return 0;
        int skip = rec(a, i + 1, prevIdx);
        int take = prevIdx == -1 || a[i] > a[prevIdx] ? 1 + rec(a, i + 1, i) : 0;
        return Math.max(skip, take);
    }

    /** DP O(n^2): dp[i] = LIS ending exactly at i = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with a[j] < a[i]. */
    public static int quadratic(int[] a) {
        int[] dp = new int[a.length];
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            dp[i] = 1;
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j] < a[i]) dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Patience sorting O(n log n): tails[k] = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.
     * tails is sorted, so binary-search where each element goes (replace the first tail ≥ x, or extend).
     */
    public static int patience(int[] a) {
        int[] tails = new int[a.length];
        int len = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int pos = Arrays.binarySearch(tails, 0, len, x);
            if (pos < 0) pos = -pos - 1;                     // insertion point = first tail >= x (strictly increasing)
            tails[pos] = x;
            if (pos == len) len++;
        }
        return len;
    }
}

docs.title: Longest palindromic subsequence
docs.text: Hard Interval DP LCS reduction

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the length of the longest subsequence of s that is a palindrome. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip characters.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: s answer one palindrome bbbab 4 bbbb cbbd 2 bb racecar 7 itself

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Subsequence or substring? A subsequence (characters can be skipped). The substring version is a different problem.
  • Return the length or the string? The length. The string can be rebuilt from the table.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Look at both ends of s[i..j]:
  2. if s[i] == s[j], both can wrap the best palindrome inside: 2 + LPS(i+1, j−1),
  3. otherwise at least one end isn't used: max(LPS(i+1, j), LPS(i, j−1)).
  4. Plain recursion is exponential, but there are only n² intervals. That is interval DP.
  5. Fill order: dp[i][j] needs dp[i+1][…] (the row below) and dp[i][j−1] (to its left). So loop i from n−1 down to 0, and j upward from i+1.
  6. Space: each row only needs the row below, so two rows are enough (O(n) space).
  7. The reduction: a palindromic subsequence reads the same backwards, so LPS(s) = LCS(s, reverse(s)). Good to mention, and it reuses LCS.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/**
 * Longest palindromic SUBSEQUENCE (characters need not be contiguous). "bbbab" → 4 ("bbbb"); "cbbd" → 2.
 * Contrast: longest palindromic SUBSTRING is contiguous (see strings).
 */
public final class LongestPalindromicSubsequence {
    private LongestPalindromicSubsequence() {}

    /** Recursion on the interval [i, j]. O(2ⁿ). */
    public static int recursive(String s) {
        return s.isEmpty() ? 0 : go(s, 0, s.length() - 1);
    }

    private static int go(String s, int i, int j) {
        if (i > j) return 0;
        if (i == j) return 1;
        if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)) return 2 + go(s, i + 1, j - 1);   // both ends join the palindrome
        return Math.max(go(s, i + 1, j), go(s, i, j - 1));               // drop one end
    }

    /**
     * Interval DP. dp[i][j] = LPS of s[i..j]. Fill by i from right to left so dp[i+1][*] is ready. O(n²) time/space.
     */
    public static int intervalDp(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        int[][] dp = new int[n][n];
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            dp[i][i] = 1;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                dp[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)
                        ? 2 + dp[i + 1][j - 1]                  // for j == i+1 this reads dp[i+1][i] = 0
                        : Math.max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }
        return dp[0][n - 1];
    }

    /** Same DP with two rows: dp[i][*] needs only dp[i+1][*] and the current row. O(n) space. */
    public static int twoRows(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        int[] next = new int[n], cur = new int[n];
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            cur[i] = 1;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                cur[j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j) ? 2 + next[j - 1] : Math.max(next[j], cur[j - 1]);
            }
            int[] t = next; next = cur; cur = t;
        }
        return next[n - 1];
    }

    /** The classic trick: LPS(s) = LCS(s, reverse(s)). O(n²). */
    public static int viaLcs(String s) {
        String r = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
        int n = s.length();
        int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][n + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
                dp[i][j] = s.charAt(i - 1) == r.charAt(j - 1) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
        return dp[n][n];
    }

    /** Follow-up: minimum insertions (or deletions) to make s a palindrome = n − LPS. */
    public static int minInsertionsToPalindrome(String s) {
        return s.length() - intervalDp(s);
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Recursion O(2ⁿ) O(n) Interval DP O(n²) O(n²) Two rows O(n²) O(n) LCS with reverse O(n²) O(n²)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• For j == i + 1 with equal chars, dp[i+1][j−1] is dp[i+1][i], an empty interval. It must read as 0, which the zero-initialised array gives for free.
  • Filling i upward reads rows that haven't been computed yet.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: Minimum insertions (or deletions) to make s a palindrome = n − LPS(s). Whatever isn't in the longest palindromic subsequence needs a partner.

docs.title: Matrix chain multiplication
docs.text: Expert Interval DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Matrices A₁…Aₙ, where Aᵢ has dimensions dims[i−1] × dims[i]. Multiplication is associative, so choose the parenthesisation that minimises scalar multiplications. dims = [10,30,5,60] → 4500, from (A₁A₂)A₃, versus 27,000 for A₁(A₂A₃).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Multiplying a p×q matrix by a q×r one costs p·q·r.
  2. Last decision: the final multiplication splits the chain i..j at some k: (Aᵢ…Aₖ)(Aₖ₊₁…Aⱼ). The cost is f(i,k) + f(k+1,j) + dims[i−1]·dims[k]·dims[j]. Try every k.
  3. State = the interval (i, j): O(n²) states with O(n) choices of k each, so O(n³).
  4. Fill order: a chain needs shorter chains first, so loop over length, then the start. That's the signature of interval DP.

docs.title: Interval DP fill order
docs.text:
len 2: (1,2) (2,3) …          ← pairs first
len 3: (1,3) (2,4) …          ← uses len-2 results
…
len n: (1,n)                  ← the answer

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/**
 * Matrices A1..An where Ai has dims[i-1] × dims[i]. Minimum scalar multiplications to compute the product
 * (choosing the parenthesisation). dims = [10, 30, 5, 60] → 4500: (A1·A2)·A3.
 */
public final class MatrixChainMultiplication {
    private MatrixChainMultiplication() {}

    /** Recursion: try every split point k for the chain i..j. Exponential (Catalan number of orders). */
    public static long recursive(int[] dims) {
        return rec(dims, 1, dims.length - 1);
    }

    private static long rec(int[] d, int i, int j) {
        if (i >= j) return 0;                                // one matrix: no multiplication
        long best = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int k = i; k < j; k++)
            best = Math.min(best, rec(d, i, k) + rec(d, k + 1, j) + (long) d[i - 1] * d[k] * d[j]);
        return best;
    }

    /** Memoized on (i, j). O(n^3). */
    public static long memo(int[] dims) {
        int n = dims.length;
        return memo(dims, 1, n - 1, new long[n][n]);
    }

    private static long memo(int[] d, int i, int j, long[][] cache) {
        if (i >= j) return 0;
        if (cache[i][j] != 0) return cache[i][j];
        long best = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int k = i; k < j; k++)
            best = Math.min(best, memo(d, i, k, cache) + memo(d, k + 1, j, cache) + (long) d[i - 1] * d[k] * d[j]);
        return cache[i][j] = best;
    }

    /** Interval DP: solve chains by increasing LENGTH so sub-chains are always ready. O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space. */
    public static long table(int[] dims) {
        int n = dims.length - 1;                             // number of matrices
        long[][] dp = new long[n + 1][n + 1];
        for (int len = 2; len <= n; len++)
            for (int i = 1; i + len - 1 <= n; i++) {
                int j = i + len - 1;
                dp[i][j] = Long.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int k = i; k < j; k++)
                    dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + (long) dims[i - 1] * dims[k] * dims[j]);
            }
        return dp[1][n];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Recursion: exponential (Catalan) · memo/table: O(n³) time, O(n²) space.

docs.title: Partition equal subset sum
docs.text: Hard Subset sum 0/1 knapsack Bitset

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Can positive integers be split into two subsets with equal sums? [1,5,11,5] → true ([11] and [1,5,5]). [1,2,3,5] → false.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Reduce it: an odd total can't be split. Otherwise the question becomes: is there a subset summing to total/2? That's the subset-sum problem.
  2. Recursion: for each number, take it or skip it. O(2ⁿ).
  3. DP: can[s] = "some subset seen so far sums to s". For each x, can[s] |= can[s − x]. Iterate s downward so each number is used at most once, exactly as in the 0/1 knapsack.
  4. Bitset: represent can as bits, so adding x becomes bits |= bits << x. That handles 64 sums per machine word, a constant-factor speed-up worth mentioning.

docs.title: DP trace ([1,5,11,5], target 11)
docs.text: After Reachable sums start 0 1 0 1 5 0 1 5 6 11 0 1 5 6 11 ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.BitSet;

/** Can the positive numbers be split into two subsets of equal sum? [1,5,11,5] → true (11 | 1+5+5). */
public final class PartitionEqualSubset {
    private PartitionEqualSubset() {}

    /** Reduce to subset-sum: is there a subset summing to total/2? Recursive take/skip. O(2^n). */
    public static boolean recursive(int[] a) {
        int total = sum(a);
        return total % 2 == 0 && subset(a, a.length - 1, total / 2);
    }

    private static boolean subset(int[] a, int i, int target) {
        if (target == 0) return true;
        if (i < 0 || target < 0) return false;
        return subset(a, i - 1, target - a[i]) || subset(a, i - 1, target);
    }

    /** 1D boolean DP, sums iterated DOWNWARD (each number used once, like 0/1 knapsack). O(n · sum). */
    public static boolean dp(int[] a) {
        int total = sum(a);
        if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
        int target = total / 2;
        boolean[] can = new boolean[target + 1];
        can[0] = true;
        for (int x : a)
            for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) can[s] |= can[s - x];
        return can[target];
    }

    /** Bitset trick: bit s set = sum s reachable. Adding x is (bits | bits << x) — 64 sums per machine word. */
    public static boolean bitset(int[] a) {
        int total = sum(a);
        if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
        BitSet reachable = new BitSet(total + 1);
        reachable.set(0);
        for (int x : a) {
            BitSet shifted = new BitSet(total + 1);
            for (int s = reachable.nextSetBit(0); s >= 0 && s + x <= total; s = reachable.nextSetBit(s + 1)) shifted.set(s + x);
            reachable.or(shifted);
        }
        return reachable.get(total / 2);
    }

    private static int sum(int[] a) {
        int s = 0;
        for (int x : a) s += x;
        return s;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Recursion O(2ⁿ) · DP O(n · sum) time, O(sum) space · bitset O(n · sum / 64).

docs.title: Buy & sell stock with cooldown
docs.text: Medium State machine DP O(1) space

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given daily prices, make as many buy/sell transactions as you like, but hold at most one share, and after you sell you must skip the next day before buying again. Return the maximum profit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: prices profit how [1, 2, 3, 0, 2] 3 buy 1, sell 2, cooldown, buy 0, sell 2 [1] 0 [5, 4, 3] 0 never buy

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Can I buy and sell on the same day? No.
  • Does the cooldown follow a sell or a buy? Only a sell.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Recursion over decisions: on each day you're either holding or not. If holding: skip, or sell (and jump 2 days ahead, because of the cooldown). If not holding: skip, or buy. Exponential.
  2. Overlapping states: the future only depends on (day, holding), which is just 2n states. Memoise them and it is O(n).
  3. Name the states at the end of each day, and the DP becomes a small state machine:
  4. hold: I own a share,
  5. sold: I sold today (so tomorrow I can't buy),
  6. rest: I own nothing and I'm free to buy.
  7. Transitions: hold' = max(hold, rest − p), sold' = hold + p, rest' = max(rest, sold). The cooldown lives in one detail: you can only buy from rest, never straight from sold.

docs.title: State diagram
docs.text:
buy (−p)            sell (+p)
 rest ───────────▶ hold ───────────▶ sold
  ▲ ⟲ wait          ⟲ keep             │
  └────────────── cooldown day ◀───────┘

docs.title: Dry run: [1, 2, 3, 0, 2]
docs.text:
day price hold sold rest 0 1 −1 −∞ 0 1 2 −1 1 0 2 3 −1 2 1 3 0 1 (rest 1 − 0) −1 2 4 2 1 3 2

Answer: max(sold, rest) = 3.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/**
 * Best time to buy and sell stock with cooldown: unlimited transactions, hold at most one share, and after a SELL
 * you must skip the next day before buying again. Return the maximum profit.
 */
public final class StockWithCooldown {
    private StockWithCooldown() {}

    /** Plain recursion over (day, holding): try every action. O(2ⁿ). */
    public static int recursive(int[] prices) {
        return go(prices, 0, false);
    }

    private static int go(int[] p, int day, boolean holding) {
        if (day >= p.length) return 0;
        int skip = go(p, day + 1, holding);
        int act = holding
                ? p[day] + go(p, day + 2, false)          // sell today, day+1 is the cooldown
                : -p[day] + go(p, day + 1, true);         // buy today
        return Math.max(skip, act);
    }

    /** Memoised recursion: only 2·n distinct states. O(n). */
    public static int memo(int[] prices) {
        int[][] m = new int[prices.length][2];
        for (int[] row : m) Arrays.fill(row, Integer.MIN_VALUE);
        return memo(prices, 0, 0, m);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] p, int day, int holding, int[][] m) {
        if (day >= p.length) return 0;
        if (m[day][holding] != Integer.MIN_VALUE) return m[day][holding];
        int skip = memo(p, day + 1, holding, m);
        int act = holding == 1 ? p[day] + memo(p, day + 2, 0, m) : -p[day] + memo(p, day + 1, 1, m);
        return m[day][holding] = Math.max(skip, act);
    }

    /**
     * State machine, O(n) time and O(1) space. Three states at the END of each day:
     *   hold — I own a share;   sold — I sold today (so tomorrow is a cooldown);   rest — no share, free to buy.
     *   hold' = max(hold, rest − price)     (keep, or buy — only from rest, never straight after selling)
     *   sold' = hold + price                (sell)
     *   rest' = max(rest, sold)             (do nothing, or finish a cooldown)
     */
    public static int stateMachine(int[] prices) {
        if (prices.length == 0) return 0;
        int hold = -prices[0], sold = Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2, rest = 0;   // can't have sold on day 0
        for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) {
            int prevHold = hold, prevSold = sold;
            hold = Math.max(hold, rest - prices[i]);
            sold = prevHold + prices[i];
            rest = Math.max(rest, prevSold);
        }
        return Math.max(sold, rest);                    // ending while holding is never optimal
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Recursion O(2ⁿ) O(n) Memo over (day, holding) O(n) O(n) State machine O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• Updating hold from the new rest lets you buy on the day right after a sale. Save the previous values first, as the code does.
  • Initialise sold to a very negative number (you can't have sold on day 0). Use MIN_VALUE / 2 so adding a price can't overflow.

docs.title: The whole stock family, one framework
docs.text: Variant Change to the state machine One transaction buy only from a profit of 0 Unlimited no sold state, so hold' = max(hold, rest − p) Cooldown buy only from rest (this page) Transaction fee sold' = hold + p − fee At most k transactions add a transaction count to the state

docs.title: Unique paths in a grid
docs.text: Medium Grid DP Combinatorics

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A robot at the top-left of an m×n grid moves only right or down. How many paths reach the bottom-right? 3×7 → 28. Variant: some cells are blocked.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Last move into (r, c) came from above or from the left, so f(r,c) = f(r−1,c) + f(r,c−1). The first row and first column are 1.
  2. Recursion → memo → 2D table, filled row by row.
  3. 1D rolling row: before you update row[c], it still holds the value from the row above. Add row[c−1] (from the left, already updated). That's O(n) space.
  4. Maths shortcut: every path is a sequence of (m−1) downs and (n−1) rights, so the count is C(m+n−2, m−1). Compute it incrementally so it stays an integer at every step.
  5. Obstacles: a blocked cell has 0 paths. The same rolling row handles it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** Robot moves only right/down in an m×n grid from top-left to bottom-right. Count paths; variant with obstacles. */
public final class UniquePaths {
    private UniquePaths() {}

    /** Recursion: paths(r, c) = paths(r-1, c) + paths(r, c-1). O(2^(m+n)). */
    public static long recursive(int m, int n) {
        if (m == 1 || n == 1) return 1;
        return recursive(m - 1, n) + recursive(m, n - 1);
    }

    /** Memoized. O(m·n). */
    public static long memo(int m, int n) {
        return memo(m, n, new long[m + 1][n + 1]);
    }

    private static long memo(int m, int n, long[][] cache) {
        if (m == 1 || n == 1) return 1;
        if (cache[m][n] != 0) return cache[m][n];
        return cache[m][n] = memo(m - 1, n, cache) + memo(m, n - 1, cache);
    }

    /** 2D table. O(m·n) time and space. */
    public static long table(int m, int n) {
        long[][] dp = new long[m][n];
        for (int r = 0; r < m; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) dp[r][c] = (r == 0 || c == 0) ? 1 : dp[r - 1][c] + dp[r][c - 1];
        return dp[m - 1][n - 1];
    }

    /** 1D rolling row: row[c] already holds "from above"; add "from the left". O(m·n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static long rolling(int m, int n) {
        long[] row = new long[n];
        java.util.Arrays.fill(row, 1);
        for (int r = 1; r < m; r++) for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) row[c] += row[c - 1];
        return row[n - 1];
    }

    /** Combinatorics: choose which (m-1) of the (m+n-2) moves are "down". O(min(m, n)). */
    public static long combinatorics(int m, int n) {
        long result = 1;
        int moves = m + n - 2, k = Math.min(m - 1, n - 1);
        for (int i = 1; i <= k; i++) result = result * (moves - k + i) / i;   // stays an integer at every step
        return result;
    }

    /** With obstacles (1 = blocked): same rolling row, but a blocked cell has 0 paths. */
    public static long withObstacles(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid[0].length;
        long[] row = new long[n];
        row[0] = grid[0][0] == 1 ? 0 : 1;
        for (int[] cells : grid)
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                if (cells[c] == 1) row[c] = 0;
                else if (c > 0) row[c] += row[c - 1];
            }
        return row[n - 1];
    }
}

docs.text: Version Time Space Recursion O(2^(m+n)) O(m+n) Memo / table O(m·n) O(m·n) Rolling row O(m·n) O(n) Combinatorics O(min(m,n)) O(1)

docs.title: Word break
docs.text: Expert 1D DP over prefixes Memoization

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Can s be split into a sequence of dictionary words (each reusable)? "leetcode", [leet, code] → true · "catsandog", [cats, dog, sand, and, cat] → false.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Recursion: try every dictionary word that is a prefix of s, then solve the rest.
  2. Why it explodes: "aaaa…ab" with [a, aa, aaa, aaaa] reaches the same suffix along exponentially many paths, and every one fails.
  3. State = the start index of the remaining suffix, so there are only n + 1 states. Memoize on it.
  4. Bottom-up: dp[i] = "the prefix s[0..i) can be segmented". dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] and s[j..i) is a word.
  5. Optimisation: only check j ≥ i − maxWordLength, and use a HashSet for O(1) word lookups.

docs.title: dp for "leetcode"
docs.text: i 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 dp T F F F T ("leet") F F F T ("code")

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.HashSet;

/** Can s be segmented into dictionary words (reusable)? "leetcode", [leet, code] → true. */
public final class WordBreak {
    private WordBreak() {}

    /** Recursion: try every dictionary word as a prefix. Exponential on inputs like "aaaa…ab". */
    public static boolean recursive(String s, List<String> dict) {
        if (s.isEmpty()) return true;
        for (String w : dict) if (s.startsWith(w) && recursive(s.substring(w.length()), dict)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    /** Memoized on the start index. O(n · |dict| · L). */
    public static boolean memo(String s, List<String> dict) {
        return memo(s, 0, dict, new HashMap<>());
    }

    private static boolean memo(String s, int start, List<String> dict, Map<Integer, Boolean> cache) {
        if (start == s.length()) return true;
        Boolean hit = cache.get(start);
        if (hit != null) return hit;
        boolean ok = false;
        for (String w : dict) {
            if (s.startsWith(w, start) && memo(s, start + w.length(), dict, cache)) {
                ok = true;
                break;
            }
        }
        cache.put(start, ok);
        return ok;
    }

    /**
     * Bottom-up: dp[i] = prefix s[0..i) can be segmented. dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] and s[j..i) is a word.
     * Limit j to the longest word length. O(n · maxLen) substring checks.
     */
    public static boolean dp(String s, List<String> dict) {
        Set<String> words = new HashSet<>(dict);
        int maxLen = 0;
        for (String w : dict) maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, w.length());
        boolean[] can = new boolean[s.length() + 1];
        can[0] = true;
        for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++)
            for (int j = Math.max(0, i - maxLen); j < i && !can[i]; j++)
                can[i] = can[j] && words.contains(s.substring(j, i));
        return can[s.length()];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Recursion: exponential · memo: O(n · |dict| · L) · DP: O(n · maxLen) substring checks (each substring is O(maxLen) to hash).

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: You have to see the hidden overlap, choose the right state (the index, not the substring), and handle the adversarial input. The tests include "a"×40 + "b", which the memoized versions answer instantly. Word break II (return every sentence) adds memoized lists of sentences, and its output can be exponential.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it. When it works, it's usually the simplest and fastest solution (often just a sort plus one pass). When it doesn't, it's silently wrong.

docs.title: How to know greedy is safe
docs.text:
1. Try to break it: look for a small counter-example. Greedy coin change fails on [1,3,4] for amount 6 (4+1+1 vs 3+3), and greedy-by-ratio fails on the 0/1 knapsack.
  2. Exchange argument: take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one at the first choice, swap in the greedy choice, and show it's no worse. If you can, greedy is optimal.
  3. If the exchange fails, the problem needs DP.

The most common greedy shapes

Sort by end time (intervals), sort both lists and match (cookies, boats), track the furthest reach (jump game), reset when a running total goes negative (gas station, Kadane), always combine the two smallest (Huffman, ropes).

docs.text:

docs.title: Activity selection / non-overlapping intervals
docs.text: Medium Sort by end Exchange argument

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals [start, end) (touching is allowed). Twin (LeetCode 435): the minimum number to remove so the rest don't overlap, which is n − max kept.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every subset, 2ⁿ of them.
  2. DP O(n²): sort by end, then dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over compatible j.
  3. Which greedy? Try the candidates against counter-examples:
    • shortest first fails: [0,5) [4,6) [5,10) keeps 1 instead of 2.
    • earliest start fails: [0,100) [1,2) [2,3) keeps 1 instead of 2.
    • earliest finish works.
  4. Why earliest finish is safe: the activity that ends first leaves the most time for everything else. Swap it into any optimal solution in place of that solution's first activity, and nothing else conflicts.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;

/**
 * Activity selection: max number of non-overlapping intervals [start, end) (touching is fine).
 * Twin (LeetCode 435): minimum intervals to REMOVE so the rest don't overlap = n - max kept.
 */
public final class ActivitySelection {
    private ActivitySelection() {}

    /** Brute force: try every subset (2^n) — reference for small n. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[][] iv) {
        int n = iv.length, best = 0;
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {
            if (Integer.bitCount(mask) <= best) continue;
            boolean ok = true;
            for (int i = 0; i < n && ok; i++)
                for (int j = i + 1; j < n && ok; j++)
                    if ((mask >> i & 1) == 1 && (mask >> j & 1) == 1 && iv[i][0] < iv[j][1] && iv[j][0] < iv[i][1]) ok = false;
            if (ok) best = Integer.bitCount(mask);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** DP O(n^2): sort by end; dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] with end[j] ≤ start[i]. Correct but slower than greedy. */
    public static int dp(int[][] iv) {
        int[][] a = sortedByEnd(iv);
        int[] dp = new int[a.length];
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            dp[i] = 1;
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j][1] <= a[i][0]) dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Greedy: sort by END time, always take the activity that finishes first among those that fit.
     * Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument). O(n log n).
     */
    public static int greedy(int[][] iv) {
        int count = 0;
        long lastEnd = Long.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int[] x : sortedByEnd(iv)) {
            if (x[0] >= lastEnd) {
                count++;
                lastEnd = x[1];
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    public static int minRemovals(int[][] iv) {
        return iv.length - greedy(iv);
    }

    private static int[][] sortedByEnd(int[][] iv) {
        int[][] a = iv.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a, Comparator.comparingInt(x -> x[1]));
        return a;
    }
}

docs.title: Assign cookies
docs.text: Easy Sort + two pointers Exchange argument

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Child i is content with a cookie of size ≥ greed[i]. Each child gets at most one cookie. Maximise the number of content children. greed [1,2,3], cookies [1,1] → 1 · greed [1,2], cookies [1,2,3] → 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every assignment. Exponential.
  2. Intuition: don't waste a big cookie on an easy child, and don't skip an easy child that a small cookie can satisfy.
  3. Greedy: sort both lists. Walk the cookies from smallest to largest. If the current cookie satisfies the least greedy unsatisfied child, give it to them. Otherwise the cookie is too small for everyone left, so discard it.
  4. Exchange argument: if an optimal solution gives the least greedy child a bigger cookie, swapping it for the smallest cookie that works never makes things worse.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Child i is content with a cookie of size ≥ greed[i]; each child gets at most one cookie. Max content children. */
public final class AssignCookies {
    private AssignCookies() {}

    /** Brute force: try giving each child each unused cookie (or nothing). Exponential — reference only. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] greed, int[] cookies) {
        return brute(greed, 0, cookies, new boolean[cookies.length]);
    }

    private static int brute(int[] g, int i, int[] s, boolean[] used) {
        if (i == g.length) return 0;
        int best = brute(g, i + 1, s, used);                 // child i gets nothing
        for (int j = 0; j < s.length; j++) {
            if (!used[j] && s[j] >= g[i]) {
                used[j] = true;
                best = Math.max(best, 1 + brute(g, i + 1, s, used));
                used[j] = false;
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Greedy: sort both; give the SMALLEST cookie that satisfies the LEAST greedy remaining child.
     * Exchange argument: any optimal assignment can be rearranged into this one without losing a child. O(n log n).
     */
    public static int greedy(int[] greed, int[] cookies) {
        int[] g = greed.clone(), s = cookies.clone();
        Arrays.sort(g);
        Arrays.sort(s);
        int child = 0;
        for (int cookie = 0; cookie < s.length && child < g.length; cookie++) {
            if (s[cookie] >= g[child]) child++;              // satisfied; otherwise this cookie is too small for everyone left
        }
        return child;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n log n + m log m) for the sorting, plus an O(n + m) scan. Brute force is exponential.

docs.title: Candy
docs.text: Hard Two-pass greedy Slopes / mountains

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Children stand in a line, each with a rating. Give each child at least one candy, and any child with a higher rating than a neighbour must get more candy than that neighbour. Return the minimum total.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: ratings candies total [1, 0, 2] 2 1 2 5 [1, 2, 2] 1 2 1 4 (equal neighbours have no constraint) [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] 1 2 3 4 1 11

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Equal ratings? No constraint between them, so they can get different amounts.
  • Is the line circular? No.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force (relaxation): give everyone 1, then repeatedly fix any child who should have more than a neighbour, until nothing changes. Correct, but O(n²).
  2. Split the constraints: each child has a left rule (more than the left neighbour if rated higher) and a right rule.
  3. Left pass: going left to right, c[i] = c[i−1] + 1 on a rise. Every left rule now holds with the smallest values possible.
  4. Right pass: going right to left, on a fall set c[i] = max(c[i], c[i+1] + 1). The max keeps the left rule satisfied. Each child ends with the larger of its two slope lengths, which is the least that satisfies both rules.
  5. O(1) space: walk the "mountains". An up-slope of length u costs 1 + 2 + … + u. A down-slope does the same counting down, and when the down-slope gets longer than the up-slope, the peak has to rise by one as well.

docs.title: Dry run (two passes): [1, 0, 2]
docs.text:
pass c start 1 1 1 left → right (0 → 2 rises) 1 1 2 right → left (1 → 0 falls) 2 1 2

Total 5.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;

/**
 * Children stand in a line with ratings. Each gets ≥ 1 candy; a child with a HIGHER rating than a neighbour must get
 * MORE candy than that neighbour. Minimum total candies?
 */
public final class Candy {
    private Candy() {}

    /** Brute force: start everyone at 1 and keep fixing violations until stable. O(n²) worst case. */
    public static int relaxation(int[] ratings) {
        int n = ratings.length;
        int[] c = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(c, 1);
        boolean changed = true;
        while (changed) {
            changed = false;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                if (i > 0 && ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1] && c[i] <= c[i - 1]) { c[i] = c[i - 1] + 1; changed = true; }
                if (i + 1 < n && ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1] && c[i] <= c[i + 1]) { c[i] = c[i + 1] + 1; changed = true; }
            }
        }
        return Arrays.stream(c).sum();
    }

    /**
     * Two passes: left→right satisfies every "higher than LEFT neighbour" rule; right→left satisfies every
     * "higher than RIGHT neighbour" rule while keeping the first (take the max). Each child gets exactly the larger
     * of its two run lengths, which is the minimum possible. O(n) time, O(n) space.
     */
    public static int twoPass(int[] ratings) {
        int n = ratings.length;
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        int[] c = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(c, 1);
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) if (ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]) c[i] = c[i - 1] + 1;
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) if (ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1]) c[i] = Math.max(c[i], c[i + 1] + 1);
        int total = 0;
        for (int x : c) total += x;
        return total;
    }

    /**
     * One pass, O(1) space: walk the "mountains". Track the current up-run length, down-run length, and the peak
     * height. A down-run of length d costs 1+2+…+d; when it grows past the peak, the peak must grow too (+1).
     */
    public static int onePass(int[] ratings) {
        int n = ratings.length;
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        int total = 1, up = 0, down = 0, peak = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            if (ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]) {
                up++;
                down = 0;
                peak = up;
                total += 1 + up;                 // this child gets one more than the previous
            } else if (ratings[i] == ratings[i - 1]) {
                up = down = peak = 0;
                total += 1;                      // equal neighbours: no constraint, reset to 1
            } else {
                up = 0;
                down++;
                // the new child gets 1 and the earlier children of this down-run each rise by 1: that is +down.
                // Once the down-run is longer than the climb to the peak, the peak must rise as well: +1.
                total += down + (down > peak ? 1 : 0);
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Relaxation (oracle) O(n²) O(n) Two passes O(n) O(n) One pass (slopes) O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Edge cases & pitfalls
docs.text:
• In the right pass, overwriting c[i] = c[i+1] + 1 without the max breaks the left-pass result at peaks.
  • Equal neighbours reset everything: the next child can drop back to 1.
  • The one-pass peak adjustment is the subtle part. The random tests cross-check it against relaxation on 3,000 arrays.
